constraints: Eligibility thresholds and effective dates are authoritative outside the model.
The assistant should explain a result and expose uncertainty rather than invent a determination.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: This division gives up automatic eligibility decisions, but it keeps the appealable calculation reproducible while preserving useful explanation.
details.errorCorrection: Keep the policy decision outside the model and validate the explanatory output; this reduces model flexibility but protects reproducibility and appeals.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A versioned rules service can evaluate dates and thresholds reproducibly, while the model receives structured results for explanation and citation.
details.scenarioApplication: The assistant can state the rule version, explain the returned inputs and outcome, and route missing or conflicting records to a caseworker.
details.transfer: The same boundary applies when a model summarizes a regulated calculation: computation and authorization remain in the system of record.

messages.text: Examples do not encode every threshold or effective-date rule and make the authority path unreproducible.
Prompted tables give context but do not provide a separately enforced calculation or guarantee that all rule conditions were applied.
Review after a disputed decision leaves the model as the initial authority and does not prevent an incorrect eligibility outcome.

feedback.reason: The deterministic service owns the consequence-bearing calculation; Claude performs the language work that benefits from context and can hand off an exception.

options.text: Ask Claude to infer the applicable threshold from examples and return the final eligibility decision as text.
Put the rule tables in the prompt and allow Claude to apply them without a separately validated calculation.
Have a rules service calculate eligibility, then give Claude the inputs and result to explain, cite, and route exceptions.
Have Claude decide eligibility and use a post hoc reviewer only when a claimant disputes the result.

questions.prompt: A benefits assistant must explain eligibility while deterministic, versioned income and date rules remain authoritative. Which design puts Claude at the right boundary?

constraints: The request names an aspiration but no testable outcome.
The prototype can change before production investment.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Discovery and evaluation delay broad rollout, but they prevent optimization of a system whose value cannot yet be demonstrated.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat interface polish, tool count, or subjective enthusiasm as the business requirement; define the behavior change and evidence first.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A baseline and representative test set turn a broad value word into a feedback loop for accuracy, time saved, handoff rate, and failure cases.
details.scenarioApplication: For scheduling, measure correctly proposed slots, time per appointment, and escalation across real case types against today's process.
details.transfer: Whenever a sponsor says productivity or transformation, ask what behavior changes, for whom, and how the current process will be compared.

messages.text: Usage and action completion can show activity but do not define a comparable scheduling outcome or establish whether the work became faster or better.
Model effort and favorable comments are proxies; neither supplies a task baseline or a reproducible quality criterion.
A cohort comparison without a defined task, baseline, or objective criteria can reflect novelty or workflow pressure rather than productivity.

feedback.reason: The team cannot diagnose a productivity effect until it defines the work unit and compares it with current practice. A task-specific evaluation should precede prompt or architecture changes.

options.text: Define a scheduling task, measurable success criteria, representative cases, and a baseline before tuning the prompt or architecture.
Instrument the prototype and run a limited pilot using usage and action completion as initial indicators while leaving the current process unmeasured.
Increase model effort and choose the version that receives the most favorable reviewer comments.
Roll the prototype to a representative scheduler cohort and compare self-reported usefulness and usage before defining a formal productivity baseline.

questions.prompt: A hospital scheduling team asks for a Claude assistant to “improve productivity.” The prototype has a polished chat screen, reviewers disagree about usefulness, and there is no current-process baseline. What should the architect do next?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Ease of prompt changes is not a reason to replace a functioning data source.
details.errorCorrection: One blended score can conceal a failure in either user task.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Routing can separate distinct categories when specialized paths fit them better.
details.scenarioApplication: A status API and policy interpretation need different evidence and quality measures.
details.transfer: Segment service outcomes before choosing a shared front end or separate solution paths.

messages.text: The status API is already the source for live account facts; routing every request through Claude risks replacing that authoritative lookup without improving the policy task.
One average score can hide that repeat status checks and changing-policy interpretations have different evidence and user outcomes.
Ease of prompt iteration does not justify replacing the authoritative API for current account status.

feedback.reason: The two categories have different solution mechanisms and evaluation contracts. Separating them prevents deterministic status accuracy from hiding weaknesses in policy interpretation.

options.text: Have Claude answer every question and call the status API when useful.
Separate status and policy paths; measure them independently.
Optimize a single average answer-quality score across both categories.
Defer the status API because LLM answers are easier to iterate.

questions.prompt: A tax-support team requests an assistant that “answers more questions.” The audit finds that 30% of inbound questions are repeated status checks already answered by an API, while the rest require policy interpretation from changing guidance. What is the strongest initial framing?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automation volume rewards a behavior without showing whether it reduced contacts or stayed within loss limits.
details.errorCorrection: A single survey does not measure the operational or financial condition described.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success criteria can include multiple use-case-specific dimensions such as task fidelity and latency.
details.scenarioApplication: The stated metrics and guardrail cover each stakeholder concern.
details.transfer: A value contract should make each trade-off measurable and identify which stakeholder owns it.

messages.text: Response speed omits repeat contacts, policy support, and the finance limit named by the stakeholders.
A post-deployment survey alone cannot set measurable operating thresholds or compare against the current process.
Automatic approval volume measures automation, not whether customers needed fewer contacts or refund loss stayed within the limit.

feedback.reason: The stakeholders named separate outcomes and a financial constraint, so a single speed or satisfaction measure would omit material requirements. A baseline and ownership make trade-offs visible.

options.text: Set separate outcome targets, owners, and refund-loss guardrails before a pilot.
Pick the fastest response time and treat the other outcomes as secondary observations.
Use a single satisfaction survey after deployment to decide whether the project worked.
Measure the number of refunds approved automatically.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants a Claude assistant for returns. Supervisors ask for fewer repeat contacts; operators say policy lookup is slow; finance needs refund loss to stay below its existing limit. Which success contract should be set before implementation?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Benchmarks and production evidence answer different questions and can complement one another.
details.errorCorrection: Expanding to excluded complex cases increases uncertainty rather than resolving it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evals should use tasks that reflect the system and establish expected behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The changed case mix and staffing are concrete alternative causes of the measured difference.
details.transfer: When a measured outcome has changed alongside workload conditions, test attribution before claiming value.

messages.text: Ticket mix, monthly volume, and staffing all changed, so the 25% difference cannot be attributed to the assistant.
The complex cases were excluded, so the result provides no evidence that the system handles them safely or effectively.
Ticket-type adjustment addresses volume, but the complex cases were excluded and staffing still changed, so the remaining difference cannot be attributed to the assistant.

feedback.reason: The observed difference is confounded by changed workload and staffing, so it cannot be attributed to the assistant. A comparable test should preserve representative cases and relevant operating conditions.

options.text: The pilot demonstrated a 25% service improvement.
The model is likely better, so roll out to the excluded complex tickets next.
Use ticket-type averages to adjust for lower volume, then attribute the remaining 25% difference to the assistant despite the staffing change.
The result is inconclusive because ticket mix, volume, and staffing changed; use a comparable evaluation before attributing the gain.

questions.prompt: A customer-support sponsor claims an AI pilot “cut resolution time by 25%.” In the pilot, complex tickets were excluded, the comparison month had lower volume, and agent staffing changed. Which conclusion should the architect present?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The result supports broader testing only while the quality floor and staff decision boundary remain intact.
details.errorCorrection: First-review speed alone would hide rework, while the observed net result now includes it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Value should be judged across the complete task and its quality constraints.
details.scenarioApplication: The held-out result includes correction time and completed-appointment quality.
details.transfer: Change the decision when end-to-end outcomes and quality guardrails—not a local proxy—show improvement.

messages.text: The single held-out study justifies a bounded next comparison, but it does not establish that other clinics have the same workflow or outcomes.
The measured total includes correction work; abandoning that measure would recreate the local-speed mistake the study was designed to avoid.
The observed queue workflow already improved the measured outcome; changing the user surface adds an untested variable and does not follow from the evidence.

feedback.reason: The new evidence includes the correction work: total handling time improved while quality stayed above its agreed floor. That supports a bounded next evaluation, not automatic rollout or a rule that every correction increase is disqualifying.

options.text: Expand to all clinics now because the held-out study meets the time and quality criteria; no further clinic-level evaluation is needed.
Promote the system based on first-review time and stop tracking correction work, since the completed summaries remain above the quality floor.
Expand through the queue with quality and end-to-end measures; compare clinic types before broad rollout.
Replace the queue with chat so staff can correct more fields in conversation.

questions.prompt: A clinic referral desk pilots an extractor. First review drops from 6.0 to 4.5 minutes, correction rate rises from 4% to 6%, but a held-out study that includes correction work shows total staff time falling from 8.0 to 7.1 minutes per referral while completed-appointment quality stays above its agreed floor. Scheduling authority remains with staff. What should the architect recommend?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Prompt wording cannot remove the stated service overhead by assumption.
details.errorCorrection: An ongoing production comparison is unnecessary when the pilot already measures no added value; monitoring can use an approved evaluation design.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An AI component should address a measured language or reasoning need rather than be present by default.
details.scenarioApplication: The rules service meets the stated task requirement and Claude adds latency without a demonstrated benefit.
details.transfer: Reassess when input shape, measured failures, or service requirements change.

messages.text: Future extensibility is not evidence that the current structured workflow benefits from Claude.
The case provides a representative pilot comparison; production experimentation should have a defined purpose and authorization.
The case identifies added request overhead, not an untested prompt defect.

feedback.reason: The records are structured, the existing service meets the measured field requirement, and Claude breaches a hard synchronous latency limit without improving the outcome. The evidence supports leaving this workload on the simpler path.

options.text: Keep Claude because natural-language solutions are easier to extend later.
Use deterministic extraction unless representative cases need language reasoning.
Route every fifth referral through Claude to preserve a comparison sample in production.
Increase the prompt detail until Claude’s added latency becomes acceptable.

questions.prompt: A clinic wants an assistant to summarize referrals. A 500-case pilot shows referral text is already structured, a deterministic rules service extracts every required field with 99.9% accuracy, and Claude adds no measurable improvement while adding 700 ms to a synchronous 1-second p95 limit. What is the best next step?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Claude may still help the smaller note-interpretation task if representative cases show value, but it does not fix queue assignment.
details.errorCorrection: A summarizer that leaves the queue delay unchanged does not address the measured bottleneck.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Measurable success criteria should reflect the business outcome the solution is meant to change.
details.scenarioApplication: The time study locates most delay in queue ownership and handoffs rather than interpretation of language.
details.transfer: Use process and task evidence to identify where AI can change end-to-end outcomes before selecting a solution.

messages.text: The complaint describes slow processing, but the measured delay identifies a non-language handoff bottleneck.
A faster model would affect only the small interpretation segment and does not change queue ownership.
Summary volume is activity and does not show shorter end-to-end referral time.

feedback.reason: The dominant measured delay is queue handoff, not note interpretation, and the summarizer pilot did not change that bottleneck. The solution framing should address the process constraint before introducing a model that cannot remove it.

options.text: Deploy Claude to draft every referral because all work is described as slow.
Select a larger model to summarize notes faster and treat the queue delay as an adoption issue.
Measure and redesign the queue assignment and ownership workflow first; consider Claude for note interpretation only if that is a material, evidenced source of delay.
Count the number of referral summaries generated as the primary productivity target.

questions.prompt: A hospital’s referral team reports slow “AI-ready” processing. A time study finds that 72% of elapsed time is spent waiting for a human to assign cases between queues, while clinicians spend only 8% interpreting free-form notes; a small pilot summarizer does not reduce handoff delay. What should the architect frame as the first solution opportunity?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A narrow interpretation assistant may still help if accuracy and staff time improve, but it cannot be credited with document-wait reduction unless the workflow changes.
details.errorCorrection: Choosing the only language-heavy task because it looks like an LLM use case confuses technical fit with business impact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Problem framing connects a baseline, a controllable cause, and a measurable result before choosing an AI component.
details.scenarioApplication: The wait dominates labor but the proposed assistant cannot directly change the case system’s follow-up behavior. The architecture should test a permitted integration or choose a different bottleneck.
details.transfer: Map work time and ownership by stage; select a target the proposed system can influence, then evaluate quality and end-to-end outcome.

messages.text: The language-heavy 24% is not the largest delay; an intervention must be linked to the measured case-level outcome and its actual control boundary.
A general benchmark does not show whether the candidate changes missing-document wait or policy work in this process.
A chat surface does not itself shorten the separate system’s document wait and could add an unmeasured handoff.

feedback.reason: The largest measured loss is document wait, and that step belongs to another system. First define the outcome and test an intervention that can reach it; separately measure the smaller interpretation task.

options.text: Automate the policy interpretation first because it is the only task that requires language understanding.
Compare model sizes on a general claims benchmark and select the highest-scoring one.
Define a case-level outcome and test an intervention that can change the dominant wait.
Replace the case system with a Claude chat so all work is in one interface.

questions.prompt: A claims center says its new assistant should ‘improve productivity.’ A 3-week audit finds 61% of labor is spent waiting for missing documents, 24% on policy interpretation, and 15% on entry; missing-document follow-up is controlled by a separate case system. What should the architect do before selecting a model pattern?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A randomized production trial may be unnecessary if a representative, controlled replay can answer the question; safety and workload variation may still require staged deployment.
details.errorCorrection: A faster mean or median cannot stand in for a tail SLA or prove the system caused the change.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An evaluation must match the stated outcome, population, and comparison needed for a decision.
details.scenarioApplication: The pilot mixes routing changes with case difficulty and reports average first response rather than p95 resolution or reopens.
details.transfer: Predefine the target population, comparator, success and guardrail metrics, and decision rule before interpreting a pilot.

messages.text: Average response time is neither the stated p95 resolution outcome nor evidence that the routing groups were comparable.
A full rollout would retain the selection bias and still omit the service-level and quality measures.
The pilot provides no evidence that model capability caused the difficult-case difference.

feedback.reason: Easy cases were selected into the pilot, and the reported metric is different from the p95 resolution promise. The evidence needs a comparable target-workload evaluation before a causal or rollout claim.

options.text: Run a comparable target-workload trial; report p95 resolution and reopens.
The 19% average improvement is sufficient because faster first responses generally reduce resolution time.
Deploy to all tickets and ask agents to flag cases that feel slower.
Choose a larger model for the difficult tickets, since the pilot excluded them.

questions.prompt: A support pilot reports a 19% faster average response. During the pilot, easy tickets were routed to Claude while difficult cases stayed with experts; the median improved, but p95 resolution time and reopen rate were not reported. The service promise is a 2-hour p95 resolution. Which conclusion is justified?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the time study instead showed policy lookup as the dominant controllable delay, a policy-retrieval intervention would deserve the pilot.
details.errorCorrection: A high answer rate can coexist with an unchanged backlog when waiting for documents is the main constraint.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Problem framing links observed work and its cause to a measurable outcome before selecting a model or interface.
details.scenarioApplication: Here, missing documents dominate elapsed delay; map where requests stall and whether a bounded assistant action can shorten that stage.
details.transfer: Measure the full workflow outcome and its relevant slices, not a model activity count alone.

messages.text: The answer-rate target measures model output, not whether the missing-document queue shrinks.
The largest share is waiting on claimants; automating a smaller lookup may leave the measured bottleneck intact.
Model choice is premature while the goal and the part of the process that can change remain unclear.

feedback.reason: The observed queue is dominated by missing-document waits, so an answer-rate target may not address the measured cause. First connect the operational bottleneck to an intervention and outcome that the owner values.

options.text: Set a target for Claude to answer 90% of claims and use answer rate as the pilot success measure.
Automate policy lookup first because it is the largest task Claude can perform without process changes.
Map time and rework by stage, test which intervention changes the bottleneck, and agree an outcome measure with operations.
Compare three Claude models on a claims benchmark before deciding what the backlog problem is.

questions.prompt: A claims operations sponsor asks for a Claude pilot after a 12% rise in backlog. A two-week sample shows 70% of work is waiting for claimant documents, 20% is policy lookup, and 10% is clerical summarization. Which discovery step best converts the request into a testable business problem?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the pilot already captured all cases and end-to-end labor, model latency and adoption could help explain the outcome.
details.errorCorrection: Increasing the same selected sample only narrows uncertainty around a biased estimate.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value is measured across the workflow and representative workload, including exceptions and correction costs.
details.scenarioApplication: The reported four minutes apply only to accepted unedited cases; omitted rejected summaries and repairs may reduce or reverse the net saving.
details.transfer: Inspect who entered the metric denominator and which costs were excluded before accepting a productivity claim.

messages.text: A larger accepted-only sample would still exclude the work most likely to reverse the estimate.
Inference latency is not staff time saved, especially when rework is missing from the measurement.
Voluntary satisfaction can reveal usability but does not establish net labor change or representative performance.

feedback.reason: The accepted-only pilot excludes rejection and repair work, so it cannot establish net productivity. Compare representative end-to-end staff labor with a comparable baseline before claiming a saving.

options.text: Measure representative end-to-end labor, including rejected summaries and repairs, against a comparable baseline.
Expand the accepted-only sample to estimate time savings more precisely, then report its scope as accepted summaries.
Use latency and token logs to quantify model efficiency, then pair that with a smaller sample of agent time.
Use agent satisfaction as an adoption signal, while the accepted-summary pilot estimates time saved.

questions.prompt: A service team says its summarizer saves 4 minutes per case. The pilot contains only cases that agents accepted without edits; rejected summaries and time spent repairing them were excluded. What evidence should the architect request before claiming productivity value?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the service objective explicitly prioritizes median latency and accepts higher tail/escalation, that tradeoff must be agreed and measured.
details.errorCorrection: A paired sample helps control case mix but does not make the median a complete productivity measure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value depends on representative end-to-end outcomes and relevant workload slices, not a single favorable statistic.
details.scenarioApplication: The median improves, but p90 and escalations worsen and resolution work is unmeasured.
details.transfer: State what the observed metric supports and what additional evidence is needed before broad value claims.

messages.text: The median alone ignores slower tail cases, escalations, and unknown downstream work.
A release gate may reasonably prioritize tail latency, but this alone does not establish that total business value worsened.
Pairing improves comparability, but excluding p90 and escalations would omit material outcomes.

feedback.reason: The paired sample supports a distributional comparison: the median improved while the tail and escalation rate worsened. It does not establish net value without downstream work and outcome data.

options.text: The new workflow improves productivity because median handling time fell by 1.5 minutes.
The pilot shows a faster median but slower p90 and more escalations; collect resolution and total-work data before claiming net value.
Treat the p90 breach as a release blocker until the slower tail is explained, even though the median improved.
Use the paired cases to compare medians only; that controls case mix and avoids overreacting to a few tail cases.

questions.prompt: The same 600 completed cases were replayed through the current and proposed workflow. The new workflow reduced median handling time from 7.0 to 5.5 minutes, but p90 rose from 14 to 18 minutes; 30% of cases were escalated in the new workflow, and no downstream resolution outcome was measured. Which conclusion is supported?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Actual-mix results remain important for staffing and total weekly labor even when standardized results isolate workflow effect.
details.errorCorrection: The summary’s claimed saving cannot be trusted without denominator, class mix, and per-class values.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Disaggregate outcomes when case composition changes, then distinguish actual workload impact from like-for-like treatment effect.
details.scenarioApplication: High-complexity cases doubled while low-complexity volume fell, changing the weighted average.
details.transfer: Use a common-mix comparison to estimate like-for-like effects and actual mix to plan operational capacity.

messages.text: Actual workload burden matters for staffing, but the composition changed while per-class times stayed flat.
A single headline is insufficient because the supplied class counts and unchanged per-class times alter its interpretation.
Actual mix describes workload, but a changed mix can confound a like-for-like comparison.

feedback.reason: Class mix shifted materially, so aggregate time can change even when class-specific time does not. Both actual operational burden and a standardized comparison are useful, but they answer different questions.

options.text: Attribute the aggregate increase to the assistant because the post-change average is the actual weekly burden.
Use the reported 18% saving as the pilot result, then investigate the mix change only if it repeats.
Use only the pilot’s overall average; it reflects the observed workload.
Show class-specific effects and a common-mix comparison; use actual-mix results for staffing.

questions.prompt: A claims pilot reports 18% lower average agent time. The event table shows: low-complexity cases 1,000→800/week at 4 minutes each; high-complexity cases 200→400/week at 18 minutes each. The proposed assistant’s per-class time is unchanged, but high-complexity cases now make up more traffic. What is the safest interpretation of the overall average change?

constraints: All required inputs are structured and the validated rules service meets the 40 ms p95 target.
No measured language task is missing from the current posting path.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The design gives up speculative model coverage but protects a proven latency and correctness path and avoids redundant spend.
details.errorCorrection: Match the solution mechanism to the information shape and outcome; model presence is not itself a business benefit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Structured validation is already handled by ordinary code; Claude becomes useful only where unstructured interpretation or explanation creates measured value.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the 40 ms rules path, monitor correctness and exception volume, and separately test Claude on a concrete explanation or investigation workload if one exists.
details.transfer: Before adding an LLM, ask whether every input and decision rule are already deterministic and whether any language task has measurable value.

messages.text: An advisory second classifier still adds a redundant language path when no measured language task is missing; disagreement data does not establish a defined explanation need.
Replacing a deterministic validator with a language model weakens reproducibility and makes post-posting review the safety net.
Sampling every record still adds cost and does not identify a missing language task or an acceptance criterion.

feedback.reason: Introducing a model adds latency and an unmeasured failure mode without a language-shaped problem to solve. The existing deterministic path should remain canonical while evidence guides any later language capability.

options.text: Run an advisory Claude classifier alongside the rules service, compare disagreements, and keep the deterministic result authoritative.
Keep the deterministic service in the posting path, measure its correctness and exceptions, and reserve Claude for an evidenced unstructured explanation task.
Replace the rules service with Claude and recover disagreements through manual review after posting.
Send a sample of every record to Claude first, then choose the route from whichever result appears more descriptive.

questions.prompt: A utility billing service receives 200,000 normalized records per day. A deterministic rules service already validates them in 40 ms p95, and all required fields are structured. The team proposes adding Claude to classify each record before posting. Which decision is best?

constraints: The alert deadline is 100 ms p95 and the immediate alert uses structured event codes.
Claude narrative latency is measured at about 600 ms; the source snapshot has a version and freshness boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Use synchronous Claude only if a paired benchmark shows completion and freshness fit the 100 ms contract; otherwise retain the asynchronous boundary.
details.errorCorrection: The split path adds coordination and a stale-result state, but it preserves both the operational deadline and the measured business value of narrative analysis.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A synchronous structured alert preserves the hard SLA; an asynchronous Claude job can analyze the immutable snapshot and attach provenance so commanders know what evidence it used.
details.scenarioApplication: Publish the code-derived alert at once, queue the narrative with snapshot version and completion time, and show it as supplemental until a commander reviews it.
details.transfer: When a language result is valuable but misses a hard deadline, isolate it behind a versioned asynchronous contract instead of weakening the deadline.

messages.text: Negotiating away the stated deadline makes the slower narrative the gate and breaks the existing alert contract.
Without the immutable snapshot version and freshness marker, a later narrative can describe a different incident state and cannot be safely joined to the alert.
First-token latency is not a complete validated alert; streaming partial narrative text leaves the required decision and evidence unfinished.

feedback.reason: The value-bearing narrative is real but its measured latency cannot satisfy the immediate alert contract. Separate the deterministic deadline path from an asynchronous, freshness-labeled language result.

options.text: Put Claude in the synchronous alert path and negotiate a longer deadline so its narrative can accompany the alert.
Emit the deterministic alert within the deadline, then run Claude asynchronously on the immutable snapshot and attach its versioned narrative for commander review.
Compute a synchronous deterministic alert and attach an asynchronous Claude narrative from current logs, but omit the incident snapshot version and freshness marker.
Stream Claude's first narrative tokens into the alert dashboard so operators see useful text within 100 ms while final validation continues.

questions.prompt: A warehouse alert service must emit a structured alert within 100 ms p95 from event codes. Incident commanders also gain material value from a Claude narrative over unstructured incident notes, but measured Claude completion is about 600 ms. The notes are stored as an immutable, versioned snapshot. Which design meets both needs?

constraints: Free text is the only ambiguous input; normalized codes already meet the latency target.
The existing rules service must remain the authority for validation and posting.
Notes can be labeled for a bounded held-out evaluation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the notes were removed or fully normalized before arrival, retain the rules-only design from CCARP-D01-O01-scenario-01.
details.errorCorrection: It preserves deterministic authority but leaves the measured unstructured bottleneck unsolved even though a bounded extraction experiment is available.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest solution and adding agentic complexity only when it is needed, because agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Language ambiguity exists only in the note field, while the deterministic service must retain authority for final posting.
details.scenarioApplication: Use Claude to extract candidate structured facts from the notes with evidence and an explicit uncertainty state, then send them through the existing deterministic validation and posting path.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: This preserves deterministic authority but leaves the measured unstructured bottleneck unsolved even though a bounded extraction experiment is available.
A model confidence threshold does not replace the existing validation and posting authority; it would move the consequential write outside the proven rules path.
A brittle parser does not provide evidenced language extraction for the unclassified fault and still bypasses the deterministic validation and posting boundary.

feedback.reason: The business need now includes an evidenced unstructured extraction step, so a narrowly augmented model adds value without replacing the proven decision service.

options.text: Extract evidenced facts with Claude, then use the existing deterministic validation and posting path; flag uncertainty.
Keep the rules-only path and send every note-bearing record to manual entry until upstream codes cover the fault.
Replace deterministic posting with a Claude call that classifies the note and posts the normalized result whenever its confidence exceeds a threshold.
Use a keyword and regular-expression parser for notes and post its normalized fields directly, reserving manual review only for parser errors.

questions.prompt:
A billing service receives free-form technician notes alongside normalized codes. The deterministic posting rules meet their latency target for coded records, but the notes contain the only description of an unclassified fault.

Which architecture addresses the note bottleneck while preserving the posting authority?

constraints: The only workable user surface is an asynchronous queue item, not a conversational chat.
Missing fields must be visible to staff before scheduling, and the desk retains scheduling authority.
Expansion is judged on total handling time and completed-appointment quality, including corrections.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If correction rate returned to baseline and total handling time fell while completed-appointment quality held, expansion of the queue workflow would be justified.
details.errorCorrection: Chat is unavailable in the operating process, and the higher correction rate means the local gain may increase total work rather than improve the business outcome.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends clear success criteria and empirical tests before prompt improvement, making the business objective testable. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Translate the request into a queue-based intake workflow and keep expansion gated on end-to-end handling and appointment outcomes, not on shorter first review alone.
details.scenarioApplication: Build a structured referral extractor that flags missing fields for staff, keeps scheduling authority with the desk, and expand only if total handling time and completed-appointment quality improve against baseline.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: Chat is unavailable in the operating process, and the higher correction rate means the local gain may increase total work rather than improve the business outcome.
The correction increase can erase the local time gain, so first-review time alone is not the required end-to-end business measure.
Throughput alone omits the required handling-time and completed-appointment quality measures and does not test whether structured extraction can reduce the actual bottleneck.

feedback.reason: The decision fits the actual work surface and prevents a local summarization gain from being mistaken for business value.

options.text: Launch a conversational assistant because first-review time improved and let staff adapt their workflow around it.
Pilot a structured queue extractor that flags missing fields, leaves scheduling to staff, and expand only if end-to-end outcomes improve.
Keep the queue surface but expand the summarizer solely because first review fell from 6.0 to 4.5 minutes; treat the extra corrections as normal staff work.
Leave the current manual queue unchanged and measure only forms completed per hour until the correction rate returns to baseline.

questions.prompt:
A clinic referral desk processes 3,000 forms each week. Staff work from a queue, never from chat; they correct missing fields before scheduling. A summarizer pilot cuts first review from 6.0 to 4.5 minutes but raises correction rate from 4% to 9%.

Which next step translates this request into a safe, measurable workflow and value decision?

constraints: Triage speed is the measured outcome.
Equipment switching remains outside Claude's authority.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The bounded design leaves switching with existing controls, which limits immediate automation but reduces operational risk while the team learns where autonomy is justified.
details.errorCorrection: State the business result, authority limit, and acceptance evidence before selecting a model pattern or implementation investment.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A bounded extraction, retrieval, and drafting workflow can expose structured fields, preserve an operator handoff, and feed measured outcomes back into design.
details.scenarioApplication: The utility can compare minutes per incident, severity accuracy, and escalation rate with the current process before expanding capability.
details.transfer: Use the same framing for claims or support: name the work unit to improve, the authority the system has, and the evidence that will show improvement.

messages.text: Usage and feedback from a general chat pilot do not establish the triage outcome, authority boundary, or a reproducible acceptance test.

feedback.reason: The scope starts with the measurable triage job and makes the authority boundary executable. It gives the team an observable first release instead of treating more autonomy or more training as the business requirement.

options.text: Start with a general operator chat pilot, collect usage and feedback, and defer a formal triage measure until the pilot reveals which workflow matters.
Build a bounded workflow that extracts location and severity, retrieves the runbook, drafts a triage summary, routes uncertainty to an operator, and measures time and classification quality.
Let an agent choose and execute switching commands whenever its outage classification confidence exceeds the launch threshold.
Fine-tune on historical outage emails first, use existing analyst judgments as an interim signal, and define the triage handoff after the model stabilizes.

questions.prompt: A regional utility receives 18,000 free-form outage emails each day. Which initial solution best translates the business problem into a production scope?

constraints: The release should target policy lookup time and recommendation quality.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A narrower release defers refund automation but lowers exposure and produces evidence for the next investment.

feedback.reason: The first release pairs the measured bottleneck with an observable workflow and preserves the supervisor's consequential decision. Both value evidence and responsibility are explicit.

options.text: Measure message throughput and handling time for the workflow, then capture policy grounding and supervisor acceptance in a later review.
Define handling-time, policy-grounding, and supervisor-acceptance measures against the current returns process.
Give Claude permission to approve refunds after it retrieves a policy passage.
Use Claude to summarize the case, retrieve the applicable policy, and draft a recommendation while the supervisor decides.
Index every internal data source before measuring whether policy retrieval is the returns bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A retailer is redesigning returns operations. Which TWO decisions best translate this problem into a coherent first release? Select TWO.

constraints: The output shape is valid but the missed decision is not attributable.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More structured logging and labeling costs storage and review time, but it prevents blind prompt changes and makes improvement attributable.
details.errorCorrection: Separate transport or schema success from task success and capture the evidence required to locate the failing stage.

details.scenarioApplication: Join each missed renewal clause to its document revision, retrieved passage, prompt release, lawyer correction, and eventual case outcome before comparing fixes.
details.transfer: When a system appears correct syntactically but fails business decisions, add stage-level provenance and outcome labels before changing the model.

messages.text: More model effort cannot reveal which source or release caused a miss when the service has discarded the relevant provenance.

feedback.reason: Valid JSON only proves serialization. The missing links prevent the team from determining whether the defect came from source version, retrieval, prompt behavior, or review, so traceable outcome data is the first diagnosis.

options.text: Record document and policy versions, prompt release, retrieved evidence, lawyer accept/edit/reject outcome, and link those fields to held-out evaluation cases.
Increase model effort and inspect a few fluent summaries without changing the event data captured by the service.
Add every contract repository as a tool and treat the resulting JSON validity rate as the quality measure.
Compare monthly renewal-clause recall on a labeled sample and tune the highest-recall prompt, then track the aggregate result by month.

questions.prompt: A contract review service logs valid JSON output but still misses renewal clauses. The logs cannot identify the document revision, prompt release, or lawyer outcome associated with each miss. What should the architect diagnose first?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Blind repetition does not repair a missing input and can create duplicate work.
details.errorCorrection: Similar cases do not establish facts about this claimant’s source document.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A reliable path needs ground truth and controlled checkpoints at the step where uncertainty arises.
details.scenarioApplication: Field validation is an application boundary before retrieval and generation.
details.transfer: For each stage, define its accepted input, failure state, and owner for recovery.

messages.text: A dashboard finds correction patterns after the fact; it does not stop an empty extraction from being treated as valid evidence now.
A similar claim cannot establish facts missing from this claim’s source document.
Retries cannot recreate fields missing from the source extraction, and repeated generation can keep forwarding an unsupported empty result.

feedback.reason: The workflow must distinguish missing evidence from a valid negative result before downstream reasoning. An explicit incomplete-input state prevents false recommendations and supports correction.

options.text: Add a post-hoc dashboard showing how often adjusters correct the recommendation.
Validate fields before retrieval; route incomplete inputs to review with the source attached.
Ask Claude to infer missing policy fields from similar claims.
Increase the generation retry limit until the response has all required fields, then let the adjuster resolve any source gaps.

questions.prompt: A claims assistant retrieves policy text, drafts a recommendation, and sends it to an adjuster. Some incoming PDFs fail extraction, but the service currently forwards empty fields as if the claim had no evidence. Where should the end-to-end design change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A static summary can become stale and lose the specific passage required for the case.

details.scenarioApplication: The device and version determine the source slice before generation.

feedback.reason: The answer depends on which manual applies to the user’s device, not simply on the latest content. Version-aware retrieval makes the evidence relevant to the installed product.

options.text: Resolve the device, then retrieve its applicable manual revision.
Search the newest manual for every question and label all answers as current.
Ask Claude to blend passages from every manual revision into one answer.
Store a summary of the newest manual in the system prompt and skip retrieval.

questions.prompt: A support assistant must answer from a versioned product manual. The manual is updated weekly; users can ask general questions or ask about a device installed two years ago. Which retrieval step should the architecture add?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Persisting only the rendered text loses provenance and machine-readable state.
details.errorCorrection: Model size does not restore fields discarded downstream.

messages.text: The problem is not summary length; the screen removes citations and missing-evidence state that reviewers need.
A larger model cannot restore fields that the presentation layer discards.
Keeping only rendered prose loses the evidence and uncertainty needed to verify the result.

feedback.reason: The workflow’s useful output includes its evidence and uncertainty, not just a fluent summary. Dropping those fields breaks the contract between processing and review.

options.text: The model output is too short to be useful.
The assistant should use a larger model before changing the screen.
The service should store only the rendered summary to keep its schema stable.
Preserve evidence and uncertainty in the reviewer-facing response.

questions.prompt: A contract assistant returns a valid structured summary, but its user-facing screen shows only the summary and drops source citations and “not found” fields. What is the key end-to-end defect?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The model cannot override the stated vendor eligibility rule.

messages.text: Changing the extracted vendor to force acceptance misstates the invoice rather than resolving the authoritative rejection.
Hiding the ERP rejection presents an unposted invoice as complete.
The inactive-vendor rule belongs to the authoritative business validator, not the model’s guess.

feedback.reason: Schema-valid output can still violate a business rule. The ERP or an authoritative validation service should own that rule and return a recoverable correction state.

options.text: The extraction prompt should infer a different vendor until the ERP accepts the record.
The display layer should hide the ERP rejection and show the extracted invoice as complete.
Return a typed vendor rejection and require correction before another post.
The model should decide whether an inactive vendor is probably still acceptable.

questions.prompt: A document-processing workflow extracts invoice fields, validates them, then posts to an ERP. The ERP occasionally rejects a validly shaped record because a vendor is inactive. Which stage should own the response?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Removing the timestamp hides a material boundary from the technician.
details.errorCorrection: Plausibility does not determine whether operational evidence remains current.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Ground truth must be relevant to the current step, not merely returned by a tool.
details.scenarioApplication: Freshness and policy applicability should gate the downstream answer.
details.transfer: Pass source timestamp and version alongside content when they affect the decision.

messages.text: An approved tool can still return data that is too old for the current safety decision.
Plausibility does not show that the reading or threshold is current.
Removing the timestamp hides a fact needed to judge whether the recommendation is safe.

feedback.reason: A trusted source can still be stale for the present decision. Freshness and applicable policy version are part of the evidence contract before an operational recommendation.

options.text: Use the reading because it came from an approved tool.
Refresh stale readings or escalate; retain their timestamp.
Ask Claude whether the old reading still seems plausible.
Use the reading but omit its timestamp to avoid confusing the technician.

questions.prompt: A field-service assistant calls a device status tool, then advises a technician. The status tool returns a reading timestamped 40 minutes before the request, and the safety threshold may have changed since then. What should the processing stage do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A post-publication survey cannot decide whether the current report is ready.
details.errorCorrection: Repeating all answers ignores which ones need more work.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Agents can pause for feedback and use stopping conditions to maintain control.
details.scenarioApplication: These states close the loop between reviewer evidence and the next workflow action.
details.transfer: Use reviewer outcomes to determine the next evidence or release step, then stop when the acceptance criteria are met or a human must resolve the case.

messages.text: A second call on every answer ignores the analyst’s signal and adds work where no revision is needed.
A survey after publication arrives too late to decide whether this report is ready for release.
“Be comprehensive” does not specify what evidence is missing or when the workflow should stop.

feedback.reason: The review outcome should drive a bounded next step rather than being recorded after publication. An explicit state and stop condition let the loop respond to evidence without retrying indefinitely.

options.text: Revise, gather evidence, or stop based on review; set a limit.
A second Claude call on every answer regardless of the analyst’s decision.
A satisfaction survey after publication.
A prompt instruction that says “be comprehensive.”

questions.prompt: A research workflow has an input queue, Claude synthesis, a citations check, and analyst review. The analyst requests more evidence in some cases, but the workflow always publishes after one pass. What feedback-loop behavior is missing?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Without a status endpoint, an unresolved result may require an operational path rather than an invented confirmation.
details.errorCorrection: A timeout is not evidence of failure, and a new key would bypass the provider’s duplicate protection.

details.scenarioApplication: Persist the key and intent before the request, reuse that identity for the permitted retry, and keep the user state unresolved until a result is received.
details.transfer: Retry behavior follows the specific external contract; change the recovery path when same-key semantics or status lookup availability changes.

messages.text: A new key can be treated as a distinct charge, and an unbounded retry loop has no stopping or support path.
The provider may have committed the charge before the response was lost; the timeout cannot establish failure.
Account history does not reveal whether this particular provider operation committed.

feedback.reason: The provider’s stated same-key behavior reduces duplicate-charge risk, but a timeout still does not reveal the result. Durable intent, contract-bounded same-key recovery, and an explicit unresolved state preserve that distinction.

options.text: Generate a new key and retry until a response arrives, then show the final response.
Treat the timeout as a failed charge because the provider returned no operation ID.
Ask Claude to infer from the customer’s account history whether the charge likely succeeded.

Persist the intent and key before submission; after timeout, keep the result unresolved, retry only with that same key under a bounded policy, and route it for reconciliation or support if still unresolved.

questions.prompt: The fictional payment service contract supplied for this case states that repeated submissions with the same idempotency key return the original operation result and do not create another charge. details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Within the supplied deduplication window, bounded same-key retries may be permitted by the case contract; after it expires, reconciliation is needed before another mutation. These guarantees are case premises, not claims about a named payment provider.
details.errorCorrection: A timeout does not prove failure, and a new key can duplicate a completed payment. Reusing the old key beyond the supplied deduplication window also no longer establishes safe retry.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The safe retry window follows the provider’s stated contract; it does not imply unlimited retention or exactly-once semantics.

details.transfer: Design recovery around documented idempotency scope, response ambiguity, and an owner for unresolved outcomes.

messages.text: The provider only deduplicates within the stated 24-hour window and does not promise exactly-once processing.
A new identity defeats deduplication precisely when the earlier request may have succeeded.
A timeout is ambiguous; changing descriptive content does not resolve payment state.

feedback.reason: The documented deduplication window limits when same-key retry is safe, and the absence of status lookup means a late timeout cannot prove failure. Persisting intent and reconciling an unknown outcome prevents a second payment from being issued blindly.

options.text: Retry indefinitely with the same key because idempotency guarantees exactly-once execution.
Create a new key after each timeout so the provider can distinguish attempts.
Persist the submission intent and key, retry within the documented window, then preserve an unknown state and require reconciliation before any new mutation.
Assume timeout means rejection and allow the model to submit again after changing the memo.

messages.text: The gateway log proves the provider could not have processed this attempt, so the outcome is not unknown.

The local validation record is authoritative for the dispatch boundary; model inference adds no evidence.

Reuse a provider idempotency key from an unrelated refund to prevent duplicates.
Ask Claude to infer whether the provider received the request from the timeout text.

details.mechanismOrProperty: End-to-end architecture can combine deterministic checks, a guarded external action, exception review, and outcome attribution.

Persist a stable operation identity and reconcile the provider status after timeouts before retrying or reporting success.

Keep outcome, policy version, and reviewer/automation route tied to the case so later reversal and rework can be measured.

messages.text: An outcome without the decision context cannot show which release or evidence produced the recommendation.

Hiding failures removes the signal and leaves incomplete documents unowned.

options.text: Increase the model’s reasoning effort and retry each rejected document twice.
Record the failure, correction, retry result, and version; route unresolved cases to an owner.
Treat every operator edit as ground truth and immediately retrain on the full form text.
Suppress rejection messages so operators see only completed documents.

questions.prompt: An extraction workflow rejects 6% of documents because required fields are absent. messages.text: The final value is useful but does not reveal whether the extraction, checker, or human correction caused the difference.

Join extracted values, validation, human edits, final outcome, and release versions under one case ID.
Measure ERP acceptance as the final outcome, then sample operator corrections to investigate a field-level issue.
Ask operators to send a weekly free-text summary of the mistakes they remember.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Retain only approved field-level data and access controls; full screen recordings are not necessary to diagnose this field transition.
details.errorCorrection: The final record establishes what was posted but not whether the extraction or a later edit supplied it.

messages.text: The final record is authoritative for posting but cannot identify the pre-posting correction that caused the difference.

options.text: Use the rollout calendar to assign cases after the version-5 deployment date to version 5 unless a rollback was recorded.

Exclude this case from model evaluation while keeping it in a broader workflow outcome report.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An automatic retry would be appropriate only if the downstream contract guaranteed idempotent deduplication or a reliable status check.
details.errorCorrection: A missing response is not evidence that a non-idempotent write failed.

constraints: A timeout does not reveal whether the refund committed.

details.errorCorrection: Treat side-effect uncertainty as a state-machine problem with an external source of truth, not as a text classification problem.

messages.text: A new identity can create a second refund after the first request committed, and success of the last call does not prove the first state.

options.text: Retry the refund with a new request ID until one call returns success, then keep the last response.

questions.prompt: A payment service may time out after committing a refund. The provider accepts an application request ID and exposes a status lookup, while a duplicate refund is financially harmful. Which implementation should the architect choose?

constraints: The eventual outcome is delayed and may be affected by later releases.

details.scenarioApplication: For every claim, store the recommendation release, policy revision, adjuster action, and later resolution or recontact outcome, then compare matched cohorts.
details.transfer: For recommendations whose success appears later, define the outcome event and immutable decision lineage before claiming a model improvement.

messages.text: Aggregate volume and satisfaction cannot separate releases or show whether a specific recommendation led to the later outcome.
Re-running with today's prompt answers a different question and cannot replace the production decision and context that preceded the outcome.
Memory-based quarterly impressions are neither complete nor attributable to a release or case.

feedback.reason: Delayed outcomes only become useful feedback when they remain joined to the decision context that produced them. Version and reviewer identifiers prevent later releases from being mistaken for the original cause.

options.text: Correlate each recommendation with the case, source and policy versions, prompt/model release, reviewer action, and later resolution outcome before comparing versions.
Compare weekly recommendation volume and customer satisfaction without retaining which release produced each case.
Use the latest prompt to re-run old cases and treat its offline score as the production outcome regardless of the historical decision.
Ask reviewers to remember difficult cases and report a qualitative view at the end of each quarter.

questions.prompt: A claims recommender is judged by customer resolution that may arrive weeks after the recommendation. The service has multiple prompt and policy releases during that period. Which feedback-loop design yields attributable evidence?

constraints: The downstream service requires a typed payload and complete business fields.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Quarantine lowers straight-through throughput and requires a repair queue, but it prevents corrupted postings and gives the team evidence for extraction improvements.
details.errorCorrection: Place deterministic validation immediately before the external side effect and make the failure state observable instead of filling gaps silently.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The application owns schema and business validation at the tool boundary; Claude can extract and explain but cannot make an invalid payload safe by producing fluent text.
details.scenarioApplication: Reject malformed JSON, flag missing fields and invalid values, preserve the source and model response for correction, and post only validated records.
details.transfer: Use separate parse, field-completeness, business-rule, and authorization checks whenever an AI output drives a typed external operation.

messages.text: A prompt request does not validate the application payload or prevent an invalid response from reaching the ERP.
Refusal is not the only failure mode; parseable objects can still omit required fields or violate business rules.
Defaults can create false business data and turn missing evidence into an external mutation.

feedback.reason: Serialization and business validity are separate gates. A typed validator and quarantine keep malformed or incomplete model output from becoming an external ERP mutation.

options.text: Ask Claude in the system prompt to be more careful and post the next response if it parses as JSON.
Have a reviewer inspect only records that produce a model refusal while all parseable objects post automatically.
Wrap any missing field with a default value and send the record onward so the ERP queue remains full.
Parse against a typed schema, validate required fields and business rules, quarantine failures with evidence, and require correction or review before posting.

questions.prompt: An ERP posting workflow receives Claude's extraction, but malformed JSON and missing required fields occasionally reach the posting service. Which architecture should stop the defect at the correct boundary?

details.errorCorrection: That discards the gateway contract that proves no provider call occurred and can leave a valid refund unnecessarily unresolved.

details.scenarioApplication: Persist the rejection event, revalidate subject, approval, scope, and budget, retry once with the same idempotency key, and route any subsequent unknown result to status reconciliation.

messages.text: That discards the gateway contract that proves no provider call occurred and can leave a valid refund unnecessarily unresolved.
A bounded retry still requires a durable rejection record and current authorization and budget checks before the side effect is attempted.
A new key and repeated attempts can create duplicate refunds, and an unknown result must go to authoritative reconciliation rather than more blind retries.

feedback.reason: The service proof changes the side-effect state from unknown to not dispatched, so recovery can progress without blind repetition.

options.text: Treat every failure as an unknown side effect and wait for reconciliation before attempting any retry.
Retry immediately with the same idempotency key without persisting the rejection or rechecking approval, scope, and budget.
Record the rejection and retry once with the same key after current checks; reconcile any subsequent unknown outcome.
Generate a new idempotency key and retry repeatedly until the provider returns success, reconciling only if the final attempt times out.

questions.prompt:
A billing gateway returns an explicit REJECTED_BEFORE_DISPATCH for a refund request. No provider request ID exists, the gateway contract guarantees the provider was not called, and the user token, approval, and spend budget are still valid.

Which recovery action is safe for this proven pre-dispatch rejection?

constraints: Claude may prepare the request and citations, but the closure mutation is irreversible.

details.errorCorrection: A citation does not prove current authorization and post-action notification cannot prevent an irreversible closure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says agents need ground truth from the environment and can pause for human feedback at checkpoints. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The model may prepare work, but authorization and the final external mutation require a current deterministic check and human checkpoint.
details.scenarioApplication: Persist the request and evidence, run identity and retention checks, obtain the officer confirmation at the checkpoint, execute once through the closure service, and record the result.
details.transfer: Use measured evidence and the stated authority boundary to choose the least complex design that satisfies the workload's constraint; revisit the route when the counterfactual changes.

messages.text: A citation does not prove current authorization and post-action notification cannot prevent an irreversible closure.
The service checks do not replace the required officer confirmation before an irreversible external mutation.
Recording confirmation after the mutation provides no pre-action approval and cannot undo an irreversible closure.

feedback.reason: The stages give the model a useful preparation role while making the consequential action, approval, and outcome observable and replayable.

options.text: Let Claude close the account after it cites the retention policy, then notify compliance in the audit report.
Have the model submit the prepared request after deterministic checks and notify compliance to review the recorded decision.
Give the closure service an automated service-account approval, execute the mutation, and record the officer's confirmation after execution.
Prepare and persist evidence, run current identity and retention checks, require the officer checkpoint, execute once through the closure service, and record the result.

questions.prompt:
An account-closure assistant may prepare a closure request. Closure is irreversible, identity and retention checks are deterministic, and a compliance officer must confirm the evidence immediately before execution.

Which execution boundary should the architect implement for the irreversible closure?

constraints: The pipeline must validate and enrich before assignment.
An adjuster reviews the result and later outcomes must feed evaluation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The explicit stages add persistence and integration work, but they make failures diagnosable and prevent a polished response from being mistaken for an effective claims process.
details.errorCorrection: Do not stop at a model response or UI demo; connect each production handoff and feedback signal before selecting the implementation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Validation creates an admissible input contract, retrieval supplies policy context, structured model output supports routing, and review plus outcome records make later evaluation attributable.
details.scenarioApplication: For claims, retain claim and policy versions, queue decisions, adjuster edits, and eventual resolution so the team can measure routing quality and downstream rework.
details.transfer: For any AI workflow, map input, processing, output, reviewer action, and feedback artifact before optimizing a single model call.

messages.text: Direct generation skips input validation and loses the correction data needed to measure whether the queue recommendation helps.
A final summary cannot show where policy enrichment or assignment failed, and aggregate satisfaction is too remote to diagnose the pipeline.
Autonomous settlement crosses the review boundary and makes repeated tool calls a substitute for an observable end-to-end design.

feedback.reason: The design names every stage and closes the loop from input quality through human review to measured outcomes. It assigns language work to Claude while preserving typed validation and the adjuster decision.

options.text: Send the raw claim directly to Claude, display its queue suggestion, and let adjusters correct problems without recording the corrections.
Generate a final claim summary, store only that summary, and use aggregate satisfaction as the feedback signal.
Let an agent call policy and queue tools until it settles the claim, then bypass the adjuster when confidence is high.
Ingest and validate the claim, retrieve policy context, have Claude produce a typed enrichment and queue recommendation, obtain adjuster review, and link corrections and outcomes to evaluation.

questions.prompt: An insurer needs claim text validated, enriched with policy context, assigned to a queue, reviewed by an adjuster, and evaluated from the eventual outcome. Which architecture best makes that end-to-end loop explicit?

constraints: The external hold may have committed even when the caller times out.
The workflow needs a durable state trail and a bounded recovery path.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Recovery adds persistence and an operational queue, but it avoids duplicate financial controls and makes ambiguous outcomes visible.
details.errorCorrection: Do not infer an external side effect from a transport error or from model text; reconcile it against the effect system and preserve an uncertainty state.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The application owns the external effect and can use a provider status lookup or idempotent request identity, while the model can summarize state without defining exactly-once semantics.
details.scenarioApplication: Write the hold intent and correlation key durably, query the provider after timeout, record committed or absent status, and route unresolved results to operations.
details.transfer: For payments, access changes, or holds, design the durable intent, status reconciliation, retry bound, and human path before exposing a success state.

messages.text: A fixed-delay repeat still treats an unresolved side effect as safe to repeat without reconciliation, so it can duplicate a committed hold.
Conversation history is not a durable effect ledger and Claude cannot verify a provider-side hold from appearance alone.
Waiting without a deadline blocks recovery and still does not guarantee that the original response will return.
Without durable identity and reconciliation, the workflow cannot distinguish a committed hold from an absent one after timeout.
Without an explicit unknown and bounded handoff, unresolved effects become duplicate retries or misleading success states.

feedback.reason: A timeout is not evidence that the side effect failed. Durable identity and state support reconciliation; an explicit unknown state and bounded handoff prevent duplicate holds and false success.

options.text: Treat a timeout as unresolved and repeat the hold after a fixed delay without first checking provider status.
Persist a request identity and workflow state before the call, then reconcile the result through the provider's status operation before deciding whether another action is needed.
Keep the hold state only in the conversation transcript and ask the model whether the account appears held after reconnecting.
Represent the outcome as unknown, use a finite retry or reconciliation policy, and send unresolved cases to an operations queue rather than claiming success.
Wait indefinitely for the original HTTP response so the workflow never has to expose an uncertain state.

questions.prompt: A fraud workflow may place a temporary account hold, but a network timeout can occur after the external operation has committed. Which TWO design decisions make the uncertain side effect recoverable? Select TWO.

constraints: The handbook fits in the selected model's context.
The desired output is a grounded answer, not an external action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A simple pattern may not handle open-ended troubleshooting, but it is easier to evaluate and operate for this bounded use case.
details.errorCorrection: Start with the augmented LLM building block when retrieval, tools, or memory are enough and no dynamic process is required.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The handbook is an external knowledge augmentation; the answer cites the selected passage and can abstain when the source does not support it.
details.scenarioApplication: The manufacturer can update the handbook index without creating an agent loop for a question-answering task.
details.transfer: Use this pattern for manuals, FAQs, and stable internal knowledge where the response is the product and the source boundary is clear.

messages.text: The retrieval tool is useful, but exploratory agentic planning adds autonomy and a loop when the handbook already supports a bounded grounded response.
Classification and a second stage can be valid at larger scale, but the extra routing path adds latency without a stated category or ambiguity problem.
Separate research and writing agents duplicate the same source context and coordination work for a single evidence-grounded answer.

feedback.reason: Retrieval or supplied context augments a single LLM response and directly serves the grounded question. More autonomy would add complexity without a decision or action to coordinate.

options.text: An augmented LLM that receives or retrieves the handbook context and answers with a citation.
An agent with a read-only handbook retrieval tool that may explore follow-up questions before citing an answer.
A routing workflow that first classifies the question, then retrieves handbook context and renders a cited answer.
Two coordinated agents, one researching the handbook and one writing the answer, both reading the same source before responding.

questions.prompt: A small manufacturer has a 60-page, authoritative maintenance handbook. Technicians ask questions that can be answered from the handbook, and the application should cite the relevant passage. There is no need to take actions or plan multiple steps. Which pattern is the best fit?

constraints: The number and order of searches cannot be known before the investigation.
New evidence changes the next action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adaptive exploration can discover relevant evidence but has less predictable cost and latency, so explicit limits and review are part of the design.
details.errorCorrection: Diagnose whether uncertainty is about the next step itself; if it is, replace a rigid sequence with an evaluated, bounded loop rather than simply adding more fixed calls.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The agent observes intermediate findings, selects a next tool call, and writes checkpoints; limits on steps, time, and spend prevent an unbounded loop.
details.scenarioApplication: The research agent should record queries and sources, pursue newly relevant leads, and stop when coverage or budget criteria are met for lead review.
details.transfer: Use agentic control for open-ended investigation, planning, or discovery only when its adaptive benefit can be measured against a bounded stop condition.

messages.text: A fixed three-call limit cannot adapt when evidence requires a different number or order of searches.
Manual follow-up leaves the system unable to execute the evidence-dependent work and does not diagnose the pattern mismatch.
Searching every possibility wastes budget and still cannot decide which follow-up matters after a discovery.

feedback.reason: The next action is evidence-dependent, so a fixed chain cannot represent the work. A bounded agent can adapt while budgets, source records, and a stopping rule keep exploration operationally safe.

options.text: Encode a fixed sequence of three search calls and truncate any investigation that needs a fourth.
Use a static retrieval prompt and let the analyst manually perform every follow-up search outside the system.
Run all possible searches in parallel before seeing evidence, then concatenate the results for Claude.
Use a bounded agentic loop that chooses the next search from evidence, records sources, and stops on explicit budget or sufficiency criteria.

questions.prompt: A market-research assistant faces an unpredictable number of searches and follow-up paths; each discovery can change the next question. Which pattern addresses the actual failure of a fixed workflow?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Routing would omit two documents that the analyst asked to compare.
details.errorCorrection: Open-ended repetition adds no specified value or stopping criterion.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Parallelization can section independent subtasks and aggregate their results.

details.transfer: Use parallel work when subtasks are separable and the final aggregation rule is known.

Repeated autonomous searching is unnecessary because the documents are supplied and the task is bounded.

options.text: A serial prompt chain that makes each document summary depend on the prior summary.

options.text: Keep the fixed steps in a workflow; use bounded search only when policy evidence is missing.
