options.text: Create one agent and expose all four diagnostic schemas for every control so any failure can call any tool immediately.
Precheck and group failures by cause, assign bounded owners, discover only each selected schema, and split further only for contradictions.
Give one coordinator all four schemas and let it decide which cause to investigate after inspecting the entire case.
Run each of the 120 failing controls independently with full diagnostic context and merge the results manually.

questions.prompt:
A compliance audit has 1,200 controls. A deterministic precheck clears 1,080, while 120 failures cluster into eight causes. The request input budget is 16,000 tokens: current case evidence uses 10,000, and all four rare diagnostic tool schemas add 14,000, while the selected schema for one cause adds 3,000.

Which decomposition and tool-admission plan fits the clustered failures and 16,000-token budget?

constraints: The terminology table is a shared prerequisite.
Endpoint mappings are independent after it and all must pass one compatibility gate.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More task records and a final barrier add orchestration work, but they allow concurrency without losing consistent terminology or cross-endpoint validation.
details.errorCorrection: Split by meaningful business units and preserve shared prerequisites; arbitrary chunking or premature aggregation hides dependency errors.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A shared prerequisite artifact feeds isolated subtasks; an aggregate compatibility gate consumes all outputs and can identify the endpoint that failed.
details.scenarioApplication: Version the terminology table, assign one endpoint and correlation ID per worker, and run schema or compatibility checks before release.
details.transfer: For complex work, identify shared inputs, independent units, and integration gates before choosing task boundaries.

messages.text: One narrative obscures endpoint-level errors and makes the shared vocabulary and compatibility checks difficult to verify.
Token ranges do not correspond to endpoint ownership and can split terms or schemas without preserving the shared contract.
A compatibility gate that runs before all mappings arrive cannot validate the complete interface.

feedback.reason: The decomposition follows the dependency graph: establish common vocabulary, process independent endpoints, and validate the combined contract.

options.text: Give one agent the entire endpoint set and ask it to preserve terminology and compatibility in one final narrative.
Resolve the shared terminology contract first, decompose into isolated endpoint mapping tasks, then run the compatibility check over the collected results.
Split each endpoint into arbitrary token ranges and merge the partial mappings without a shared vocabulary artifact.
Run endpoint mapping and compatibility validation concurrently so the gate can finish before all mappings arrive.

questions.prompt: An API migration must map 80 endpoints. All mappings use one terminology table, then can be checked independently before a compatibility gate. Which decomposition is most useful?

constraints: Retention, access, and minimization have distinct evidence and checks.
The release owner needs complete, attributable results before deciding.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The gate can delay a release when one check is late or conflicting, but it prevents the owner from deciding on partial privacy evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Separate independent checks while making the integration requirement explicit; do not replace coverage with one broad narrative or unrelated approvals.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A decomposition contract assigns each reviewer an explicit dimension and shared identifiers; an aggregator checks presence, provenance, and contradictions before handoff.
details.scenarioApplication: Review the same data inventory under retention, access, and minimization rules, link findings to assets, and block release readiness until all reports pass the gate.
details.transfer: For composite governance decisions, decompose by criterion and require an evidence-complete aggregation before the accountable owner acts.

messages.text: A broad narrative hides omissions and gives the owner no reliable way to tell whether each privacy dimension was checked.
A classification label cannot establish current retention, access, and minimization behavior for every asset.
Independent readiness decisions create competing authority and do not ensure that all required findings reached the owner.
Without scoped dimension checks, evidence ownership and coverage cannot be audited or compared across the review.
Without a completeness and conflict gate, the release owner may act on a missing or contradictory privacy finding.

feedback.reason: The dimensions are distinct units, while the owner needs a complete combined decision. Scoped evidence and a final gate provide both independence and completeness.

options.text: Ask one reviewer to produce a broad privacy narrative and let the owner infer which checks it covered.
Assign one scoped check to each privacy dimension with a shared asset and policy context, then preserve a correlation ID for each result.
Run minimization only because retention and access can be assumed from the data classification label.
Let each reviewer decide release readiness independently so the owner can choose the most favorable conclusion.
Use a completeness and conflict gate that verifies all three findings before the release owner receives a decision packet.

questions.prompt: A privacy review must check retention, access, and data minimization independently, but every finding is required before one release owner decides. Which TWO decomposition choices are appropriate? Select TWO.

constraints: The opportunity depends on discovering new paths in a changing corpus.
Citations, budget limits, and human review are required before action.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The evaluated pilot costs more and may leave findings pending review, but it tests the transformational hypothesis without making exploration an uncontrolled action path.
details.errorCorrection: Match transformation claims to a measurable capability and preserve a review boundary for uncertain or consequential findings.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An agent can choose follow-up searches as findings change; budgets, source records, evaluation cases, and a human gate constrain the exploratory path.
details.scenarioApplication: Measure discovery recall, citation support, time, spend, and reviewer acceptance on representative research tasks before expanding the pilot.
details.transfer: For high-upside discovery, define the evidence, budget, and human decision boundary as part of the value case rather than as post-launch cleanup.

messages.text: A fixed path may be efficient but cannot adapt to the discovery-dependent work described and would publish without the required review.
Unrestricted exploration lacks a spending and evidence boundary and crosses the human action requirement.
Document count is an activity measure; it does not establish a useful discovery or supported conclusion.

feedback.reason: Open-ended discovery is where adaptive exploration can create transformational value, but the pilot needs evidence, stop conditions, and human ownership before action.

options.text: Use a fixed retrieval workflow and publish its first answer as the discovery result so cost and latency remain predictable.
Open the full corpus to an unrestricted agent and let it act on a novel finding without an evidence or spending boundary.
Pilot an evaluated agentic research path with bounded searches, source citations, cost tracking, and human review of the proposed conclusion.
Optimize only the number of documents searched and treat broad corpus coverage as transformation regardless of finding quality.

questions.prompt: A research group seeks potentially transformational discovery across a changing corpus. Exploration is open-ended and a human must review evidence before any conclusion is acted on. Which value-aligned design should be piloted?

constraints: Completion is high but does not reflect reviewer effort or outcome quality.
The current process can provide a baseline for resolution and handling time.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Richer measurement requires labeling and instrumentation, but it distinguishes a valuable draft from a fluent draft that adds work.
details.errorCorrection: Measure the business process end to end, including human correction, rather than optimizing a model-output or completion counter.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Resolution and acceptance capture usefulness, while handling time and rework capture productivity; segmentation shows where the assistant helps or burdens agents.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare accepted answers, resolution and repeat contacts, minutes per case, and edits with a matched baseline before changing prompts or models.
details.transfer: Whenever a product metric stays high while users still work around the system, add outcome and effort measures tied to the current process.

messages.text: Raising a proxy threshold does not address the unchanged handling time or reveal whether conversations actually resolve.
Generated volume can increase editing burden and says nothing about acceptance or customer outcome.
Rewriting identifies a possible defect but not whether a targeted prompt, route, or workflow change could recover value.

feedback.reason: Completion is a weak proxy when human rewriting consumes the supposed time benefit. The next diagnosis must measure the actual work and outcome against current practice.

options.text: Increase the completion target to 98% and treat the higher percentage as proof that the assistant creates productivity.
Measure resolution, accepted-answer rate, handling time, and rework against the current process, segmented by conversation type.
Count generated words and use longer answers as evidence that the assistant addresses more customer needs.
Replace the model immediately because any rewriting means the AI path has no business value.

questions.prompt: A dashboard reports that 92% of conversations completed, but agents spend the same time because they rewrite many answers before sending them. Which measurement diagnosis should guide the next change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Draft volume ignores whether reviewers can use the output without rework.
details.errorCorrection: Using the strongest route for all traffic may add cost where a simpler path is sufficient.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Model selection should be tested against use-case criteria and weighed by completed-task cost.
details.scenarioApplication: The legal slice has a material quality floor; token price alone does not prove it is met.
details.transfer: Compare cost per acceptable completed task and keep required quality and service constraints visible by slice.

messages.text: Lowest per-token price can still fail the legal clause requirement or create costly corrections.
Strongest-for-all assumes every workload needs the same capability and ignores the stated production cost.
A larger draft count is not business value if outputs require correction.

feedback.reason: The business outcome is an acceptable completed notice, not an inexpensive token or a large draft count. Segmenting routine and legal work can reveal whether one model meets each slice’s quality and cost needs.

options.text: Choose the model with the lowest price per token for every notice.
Compare cost per acceptable notice by type, including quality floors and reviewer time.
Choose the highest-quality model for every notice because reviewer time has no cost.
Measure total tokens and maximize the number of drafts, regardless of acceptance or correction work.

questions.prompt: A translation team pays per generated token, and a costly model returns excellent drafts. Reviewers find that routine notices require only simple rewrites, while a smaller set of legal notices needs nuanced clause preservation. Which value-aligned test should guide allocation?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Removing source evidence weakens the condition that makes the research result useful.
details.errorCorrection: A blended average can hide failures against the routine SLA.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success criteria can include separate quality and latency dimensions for different workload slices.
details.scenarioApplication: Only the condition with measured research value takes the slower route.
details.transfer: Use per-slice routing when a slower capability creates value only for an identifiable exception class.

messages.text: The measured improvement is limited to conflicts, so making every routine request wait adds latency without matching value.
The routine path still must meet its explicit 1.5-second requirement.
The conflict case needs evidence; removing the citation requirement evades the quality need.

feedback.reason: The valuable slower path applies only to an evidence conflict, while the ordinary path has a hard response contract. Routing preserves both service expectations and makes the exception state visible.

options.text: Keep routine answers within SLA; route conflicts to research with a pending state and separate measure.
Run research for every question and ask dispatchers to tolerate the latency because the research answers are better.
Set one average latency target across both paths so the slower conflict cases do not appear as outliers.
Remove the manual citation requirement from conflict cases to preserve the 1.5-second target.

questions.prompt: A dispatch assistant must return a usable answer within 1.5 seconds for routine questions. A high-quality research path takes 8 seconds and materially improves only cases where an asset record conflicts with the manual. What design best aligns the SLA and quality value?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tool count measures capability breadth, not business value or service outcomes.
details.errorCorrection: The predictable majority does not rule out a model for the distinct investigative task.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Simplicity is appropriate for predictable work; added agentic complexity needs evidence of value.
details.scenarioApplication: The exception slice is where the decision structure differs and should be measured separately.
details.transfer: Align architecture to the work distribution, then compare incremental value against the existing baseline.

messages.text: A single open-ended path imposes extra cost and variability on routine requests without evidence that they benefit.
The 8% evidence-dependent slice may benefit from a bounded investigation path.
More tools do not prove the service changed user outcomes.

feedback.reason: The case has a stable majority and a smaller workload with genuinely variable steps. A targeted pilot tests whether autonomy adds value for that slice without changing a routine path that already meets its service target.

options.text: Replace all cases with an open-ended agent to maximize the amount of work done by Claude.
Do not use Claude anywhere because most cases are predictable.
Measure the number of tools the agent can call as evidence of transformation.
Keep routine workflow; test investigation on the 8% exception slice.

questions.prompt: A product executive wants a “transformational agent” for a workflow. A study finds that 92% of requests follow the same three steps, while 8% require unplanned investigation; the current queue already meets its service target for routine requests. Which value proposal is strongest?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Final review alone is not an adequate plan when the missed field can cause irreversible loss.
details.errorCorrection: The case supports a targeted safeguard and evaluation, not a claim that all extraction is useless.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success measures need to reflect material task-specific risks, not just averages.
details.scenarioApplication: The rare deadline field needs its own requirement and an explicit uncertainty path.
details.transfer: Segment by consequence as well as frequency, and evaluate the full cost of controls.

messages.text: The 99% aggregate does not reveal the deadline-field recall or the consequence of its misses.
The observed weakness is concentrated in one field and can be addressed with a targeted gate.
Relying on discovery at final review does not prevent a missed statutory deadline.

feedback.reason: Aggregate accuracy hides a low-recall, high-consequence slice. The decision must protect deadline recall and include the human review cost when evaluating productivity.

options.text: Expand broadly because average accuracy and staff time both improved.
Stop all automation because one field is occasionally missed.
Require deadline-field recall; review uncertain cases and count that work.
Optimize extraction speed and let staff discover missed deadlines during final review.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An aggregate score can obscure which configuration meets the stated requirement and where it improves.
details.errorCorrection: A higher score on an optional slice does not establish that the compliant alternative is unsafe.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Cost and capability should be compared against the actual task requirements and workload slices.
details.scenarioApplication: The routine requirement is met at lower cost; the exception slice has no current quality floor.
details.transfer: Revisit routing when required outcomes, error consequences, or workload distribution change.

messages.text: Higher raw performance has no stated business value for this optional slice under the current contract.
The case says the routine path meets its floor, and the exception result is not currently required.
A blended score hides that both meet routine requirements while only one changes an optional slice.

feedback.reason: Both configurations meet the required routine floor, and the measured incremental gain applies to an explicitly optional slice. The lower-cost route satisfies the current contract; the decision should change if that slice becomes required or its volume/consequence changes.

options.text: Use the stronger configuration everywhere because a higher score is always more valuable.
Use the cheaper compliant route until exception need or volume changes.
Use the stronger configuration because its improvement proves the faster one is unsafe.
Average both configurations’ metrics and pick whichever has the better combined score.

questions.prompt: A service chooses between two Claude configurations for routine invoice extraction. On 10,000 representative invoices, both exceed the required field-accuracy floor; the faster configuration costs 40% less, while the stronger configuration improves a rare exception slice that the business has classified as optional for this workflow. What is the strongest decision?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Acceptance can be a useful diagnostic but does not replace the business metric named in the case.
details.errorCorrection: A faster initial reply does not establish a net reduction in staff time per resolved case.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Productivity must be measured across the complete work needed to resolve a case.
details.scenarioApplication: The pilot saves two minutes at first response but adds 3.5 minutes of correction and follow-up to the stated target.
details.transfer: Compare end-to-end time and outcome quality before treating a workflow pilot as productive.

messages.text: First-response time omits the added correction and follow-up effort in the stated target.
Acceptance is an activity or proxy and may not capture the staff time cost described.
The evidence does not show model capacity caused the rework or that a stronger model would eliminate it.

feedback.reason: The target is total staff time per resolved case. The 2-minute first response is offset by 3.5 minutes of correction and follow-up, so the pilot has not demonstrated the required productivity improvement.

options.text: Do not claim a productivity gain from first-response speed; measure total staff time and address the added correction work before expansion.
Expand because the first response is twice as fast.
Use answer acceptance instead of total time because it is easier to collect.
Route all cases to the strongest model to guarantee the correction work disappears.

questions.prompt: A contact-center pilot cuts average first-response time from 4 minutes to 2 minutes, but adds 3.5 minutes of average correction and follow-up work per case. Resolution rate is unchanged, and the productivity target is total staff time per resolved case. What conclusion follows?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A narrower document class could be evaluated if it has a distinct error profile and the contract permits that scope.
details.errorCorrection: Optimizing a weighted average without honoring a hard threshold can produce an unusable system.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value is constrained by explicit quality and service guardrails as well as efficiency.
details.scenarioApplication: The measured 1.1% error rate exceeds the 0.3% contractual maximum, even though unit cost falls.
details.transfer: Treat hard limits as feasibility constraints before optimizing cost, speed, or volume.

messages.text: A future correction budget does not change the stated quality ceiling or prove the economics after correction.
Customer reports are late and incomplete evidence for a known contractual error limit.
The contract sets a 0.3% maximum; an unrelated 2% threshold does not satisfy it.

feedback.reason: Cost and throughput gains do not compensate for missing a binding quality limit. The architecture must first meet the critical-field ceiling or define a permitted lower-risk subset.

options.text: Adopt it because the lower unit cost can fund later correction work.
Adopt it for all documents and let customers report mistakes.
Meet the critical-field floor first, then remeasure cost or narrow the eligible scope.
Compare only the total number of documents processed because the error rate is below 2%.

questions.prompt: A data-entry assistant lowers cost per document by 18%, but the pilot’s critical-field error rate rises from 0.2% to 1.1%. The contractual maximum is 0.3%; staff time and throughput improve. What is the decision?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the retry path is necessary for quality, the team may need to renegotiate latency or change the workflow; that tradeoff must be explicit.
details.errorCorrection: A lower average cannot demonstrate that a p95 SLA is met.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Performance value must be evaluated against the exact latency statistic and threshold promised to users.
details.scenarioApplication: The new mean improves, but p95 remains 0.7 seconds above the limit and a specific class accounts for repeated retries.
details.transfer: Report percentile metrics and slices that drive the tail, then evaluate targeted mitigations against quality and cost.

messages.text: The contract is p95, not mean latency; the reported percentile still fails.
A longer timeout can worsen the measured tail and does not address why retries occur.
The evidence identifies retries in one document class, not insufficient reasoning capability for all requests.

feedback.reason: The target is a tail percentile, and the measured p95 remains over its limit. Diagnose the retry-heavy slice rather than treating an improved mean as success.

options.text: Diagnose the retry-heavy slice; the measured p95 still misses the SLA.
It meets the SLA because the average is below 2 seconds.
Increase the timeout for all requests so the slow tail can finish successfully.
Switch every request to a more capable model, since the tail must be a reasoning problem.

questions.prompt: A recommendation service reduces mean latency from 3.1 seconds to 1.2 seconds. The business target is p95 under 2 seconds; the new p95 is 2.7 seconds because a small document class triggers repeated retries. Which value assessment is sound?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the review is needed only on high-risk cases, measure those cases separately and include their actual share.
details.errorCorrection: Multiplying gross savings by every query overstates value by ignoring the baseline mix and added labor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Business value compares the whole current and proposed workflow, weighted by actual workload and costs.
details.scenarioApplication: The 30-second gross saving can be overwhelmed by 45 seconds of review and should apply only to queries that previously incurred lookup effort.
details.transfer: Use net outcomes by relevant workload slice; do not substitute model speed or acceptance for business benefit.

messages.text: The gross saving ignores review effort and counts queries that had no lookup baseline.
Response latency alone does not include whether people spend less total time completing the work.
Acceptance is useful quality evidence but not a measure of net labor or service outcomes.

feedback.reason: The gross lookup reduction does not account for the new review step or queries that already required no lookup. A case-mix-aware end-to-end estimate is needed.

options.text: Compare net time by query type, including baseline work, review, escalations, and adoption.
Multiply the gross 30-second reduction by total weekly volume, then subtract review time from a small sample.
Measure model response latency because shorter responses are the direct source of productivity.
Report only the percentage of answers accepted by reviewers.

questions.prompt: An internal search assistant reduces average lookup time by 30 seconds, but the new workflow requires a reviewer to spend 45 seconds checking every answer. Search volume is 4,000 per week; 25% of queries currently need no human lookup. Which calculation is most useful for the business case?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a controlled route can meet the error floor and staff the review slice, a staged expansion may be justified with explicit monitoring.
details.errorCorrection: A half rollout still creates queue load and does not establish that the contractual quality floor is met.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Value optimization is constrained by quality floors and operational capacity; lower model cost alone is insufficient.
details.scenarioApplication: The review rate more than doubles while the team is at capacity, and the unresolved-error ceiling is a hard requirement.
details.transfer: Treat contractual floors and service capacity as constraints before optimizing cost.

messages.text: Inference savings do not establish total cost or compliance with the unresolved-error limit.
Reducing traffic does not make the known review-capacity gap disappear, and the answer offers no gate for the error limit.
Lower latency cannot by itself resolve capacity or routing correctness.

feedback.reason: The cost reduction cannot offset a breached service constraint or unstaffed review demand. Evaluate quality and operational capacity before expanding, then compare total cost.

options.text: Roll out because inference savings are certain while future labor costs are hard to estimate.
Limit rollout to half the traffic and monitor whether the new review queue stays manageable.
Gate rollout on staffed review capacity and the 0.5% error cap, then compare total cost.
Choose the lowest-latency model so more cases can move through review.

questions.prompt: A document-routing pilot lowers inference cost by 22%. It also increases manual review from 8% to 19%; the review team is already at capacity, and the contract caps unresolved routing errors at 0.5%. Which rollout decision follows the stated value constraints?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the owner changes the exception floor, document the revised risk decision before comparing costs.
details.errorCorrection: Applying a 4% weight to the floor turns a slice-level requirement into an aggregate that can hide misses.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Separate non-negotiable slice floors from workload-weighted cost and labor estimates.
details.scenarioApplication: A low-volume exception group still has an explicit 98% recall floor.
details.transfer: Use slice-specific quality gates and workload-aware economic analysis together.

messages.text: The scenario requires 98% exception recall; a review queue is not evidence that the model/system meets it.
Traffic share can weight aggregate workload but cannot relax the stated within-slice floor.
Average review time does not establish that the 98% recall constraint is met.

feedback.reason: The exception quality floor is a constraint, while costs and review load can be weighted by actual workload for business value. One aggregate should not erase a required slice minimum.

options.text: Prioritize routine cost because it dominates volume, then handle exception misses through the existing review queue.
Check the exception recall floor separately; estimate total cost and review labor using the real case mix.
Weight the 98% recall target by the 4% exception share when judging total-system recall.
Choose the route with lowest average review time, then monitor exception outcomes after launch.

questions.prompt: A route table from a two-week pilot shows model cost per case: routine $0.01, exception $0.03. Human review takes 20 seconds on 5% of routine cases and 4 minutes on 35% of exception cases. Exception volume is only 4%, but these cases have a 98% recall floor. Which evaluation statement is sound?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the statutory deadline applies only to a subset, define the routing trigger and measure false negatives as part of the system.
details.errorCorrection: Overall latency can hide a concentrated failure in a high-consequence segment.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Performance and quality service objectives may impose slice-specific hard constraints before cost optimization.
details.scenarioApplication: Route A breaches the urgent deadline that protects a statutory outcome.
details.transfer: Tie workload segmentation to business consequences and explicit service criteria.

messages.text: The mix average can hide the urgent-call breach tied to statutory deadlines.
Routine performance does not resolve the urgent slice with a statutory consequence.
The statutory consequence makes this more than an optional cost preference; the required service constraint must be established.

feedback.reason: The urgent slice has a consequence-bearing deadline. Its low volume does not make an average or cost comparison sufficient.

options.text: Use overall latency because it reflects the actual mix and gives one comparable deployment target.
Compare unit cost first because Route A meets the target for 99% of routine calls.
Check urgent-call volume and ask the owner whether a separate deadline target is worth the cost.
Treat the urgent SLA as its own gate; compare costs only among routes that meet it.

questions.prompt: A dispatch assistant has two candidate routes. Route A meets the 1-second p95 target for 99% of routine calls but breaches it on urgent calls; Route B meets it on both groups at higher cost. Urgent calls are 7% of traffic and failure can miss a statutory deadline. What should the architect compare?

constraints: The measured speed gain is paired with a material resolution regression.
The target resolution floor is 82% and slices can be evaluated before broad rollout.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Expansion pauses and analysis costs time, but it avoids scaling a fast workflow that drives repeat contacts and damages service value.
details.errorCorrection: Treat speed and outcome quality as a joint business constraint and use failure slices to target the smallest corrective change.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Segmented evaluation can locate failure classes such as policy gaps or unsafe confidence; routing, prompt, retrieval, or review changes can then be tested against both SLA pillars.
details.scenarioApplication: Hold broad rollout, compare resolution and handle time by intent and customer segment, and accept a revised path only when it clears the 82% floor without unacceptable effort.
details.transfer: When efficiency improves while outcome quality falls, keep both measures in the gate and diagnose the work slice before choosing rollout or redesign.

messages.text: Handle time alone ignores the resolution target and accepts a workflow that shifts effort into repeat contacts.
A full permanent rollback discards potentially recoverable value before identifying whether one slice or route causes the regression.
Changing the target hides a measured failure instead of bringing the service back to the agreed business floor.

feedback.reason: A faster interaction that fails to resolve the contact misses the service value target. The next step is a slice diagnosis and measured revision, not a single-metric rollout or an unscoped permanent rollback.

options.text: Keep the release because handle-time improvement is the clearest efficiency signal, and address repeat contacts after adoption grows.
Roll back every AI feature permanently because one aggregate outcome regressed without testing where the regression occurs.
Pause broad expansion, segment the resolution failures, and retest a scoped prompt, retrieval, or human route until the 82% floor and acceptable handling time are jointly met.
Raise the resolution target in the dashboard to match the observed result while continuing the same design.

questions.prompt: A contact-center assistant reduces average handle time by 18%, but first-contact resolution falls from 84% to 72% and repeat contacts increase. The target is at least 82% first-contact resolution. What decision should follow?

constraints: The current evidence covers acceptance but not operational or downstream value.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A longer pilot delays scale and requires outcome follow-up, but it protects the insurer from optimizing summaries that save no time or alter claim quality adversely.
details.errorCorrection: Do not turn early approval into a broad productivity claim; define the operational and downstream measures before increasing exposure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A pilot can connect summary versions to adjuster behavior, decision time, corrections, and later claim outcomes, producing a balanced value evaluation.
details.scenarioApplication: Instrument representative adjusters and claim slices, compare with current practice, and expand only if quality remains acceptable while time and downstream outcomes improve.
details.transfer: For AI features with indirect business effects, measure adoption, effort, corrections, and downstream outcomes before calling a pilot successful.

messages.text: Acceptance does not establish adoption, time-to-decision, correction burden, or downstream claim quality at scale.
Token cost is one constraint and cannot replace the quality and operational measures needed for the business decision.
Generation volume measures activity, not whether adjusters use the summaries or whether claims resolve better.

feedback.reason: Acceptance is useful but incomplete. The business case concerns adoption, time, correction burden, and claim outcomes, so expansion needs a measurement gate for those effects.

options.text: Extend the pilot with measures for adjuster adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream outcomes, then gate expansion on predefined thresholds.
Expand to every adjuster because acceptance of the summaries proves that the insurer will realize productivity value.
Stop measuring and select the model with the lowest token cost so the pilot cannot exceed budget.

questions.prompt: An insurer pilots Claude summaries for adjusters. Managers want broader deployment, but the pilot has only summary acceptance data; adoption, time-to-decision, correction rate, and downstream claim outcomes were not measured. What value decision is appropriate?

constraints: The efficient model scores 91% and the stronger model 98% on the same held-out exception set.

details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger model for the exception workload or route it to a validated stronger or human path, and retain the efficient model only where its measured quality clears the applicable floor.

messages.text: The efficient path misses the material-exception floor and shifts error cost into appeals without meeting the business outcome.

options.text: Use the efficient model for all appeals because its lower cost maximizes productivity.

questions.prompt:
A tax-appeal assistant must recall at least 97% of material exceptions. The efficient model reaches 91%, while a stronger model reaches 98% at four times the unit cost and remains under the asynchronous service deadline.

Which model allocation satisfies the material-exception quality requirement?

constraints: Both models were measured on the same routine and high-impact classes.

details.scenarioApplication: Document the agreed condition for each rounding rule, render it explicitly with the two sources, and require clarification when a request does not fit that condition.
details.transfer: Resolve conflicting trusted requirements with an explicit owner-approved rule before asking a model to apply them.

messages.text: Prompt position is not the agreed policy condition and can silently make one template dominate every request.
Semantic similarity does not establish which trusted authority controls a request that matches both templates.
A prior accepted price is not proof of the current request’s governing rounding rule.

feedback.reason: Two trusted instructions can still conflict. The prompt must express the owners’ governing rule rather than leave authority to ordering, similarity, or historical output.

options.text: Encode the agreed conditional precedence in labeled template sections and use an explicit clarification state for unmatched conflicts.
Place the finance template last, keep both versions unchanged, and use stable ordering as the conflict-resolution mechanism.
Provide examples for each template separately and choose whichever template the model judges semantically closer to the request.
Run one generation per template and select the price closest to the previous accepted transaction for the same customer.

questions.prompt: A pricing assistant receives two approved templates: one says to round to whole units and the other says to preserve cents. Both are current, but overlapping requests produce inconsistent results. Which prompt-contract change should follow agreement between the policy owners?

constraints: The template catalog is versioned.
Representative records can be used in render and output checks.
The failure begins with the variable-contract change.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If render checks showed correct variables and the error originated in untrusted content, authority or input handling would become the relevant diagnosis instead.
details.errorCorrection: Postprocessing, retries, and additional examples can mask symptoms while the mismatched input variable remains unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends establishing clear success criteria and empirical tests before improving a prompt; versioning and render checks here are scenario-authored controls for the changed template contract.
details.scenarioApplication: Update all references consistently, render representative records, test for unresolved variables, and release only a version that satisfies the contract.
details.transfer: Treat changes to prompt variables as versioned interface changes with executable render checks.

messages.text: A postprocessor may not know the intended missing value or field mapping; it does not repair the broken render contract.
Generation variability is not the demonstrated cause, and a brace-free result could still contain an invented due date.
New examples cannot reliably compensate for an old schema that still binds the wrong variable name.

feedback.reason: The regression aligns with a template-variable contract change. Repairing and testing that contract is more direct than treating unresolved placeholders as generation variance.

options.text: Normalize unresolved placeholders in a postprocessor and keep the deployed template, monitoring how often the repair is applied.
Lower generation variability and retry emails containing braces, accepting the first output whose format check passes.
Add more completed email examples using the new variable and leave the old variable schema in place until the next catalog release.
Align the template, variable schema, and examples in one version, run representative render checks, and reject or roll back a failing release.

questions.prompt: A customer-email template renames {due_date} to {payment_due_date}. After deployment, some generated emails contain the old literal placeholder. The surrounding instructions are unchanged. Which repair targets the observed failure?

constraints: A field-to-source-span check is available.
A specialist can review an escalation.
The schema and citation allowlist checks have already passed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If each field came from a validated typed policy record through deterministic mapping, that mapping could establish support without a separate model entailment check.
details.errorCorrection: Analyst review, a stale supporting citation, and self-confidence do not repair the mismatch between the current governing evidence and the generated claim.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends structuring long document context and asking Claude to ground responses in relevant document passages; the field-to-span gate and escalation are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare the amount and decision with their current supporting spans, expose the unsupported field, and route the case for clarification or review rather than publishing a confident approval.
details.transfer: Validate what structured fields mean and what supports them, not just whether they parse or contain an approved source identifier.

messages.text: The proposed handoff still presents an unsupported value as a completed result despite the known evidence mismatch.
A stale passage can explain where the number came from but cannot authorize it under the current policy.
The model’s confidence is not evidence that P17 contains or permits the stated limit.

feedback.reason: Structural validity and an approved citation ID do not establish that the cited current policy supports the claim. The unsupported amount and approval cannot be passed as a grounded policy result.

options.text: Pass the result because its types and source ID are valid, and ask the analyst to verify the numeric value during ordinary review.
Check material fields against current evidence, mark the unsupported limit unknown, and abstain or escalate; retain separate action-authorization checks.
Replace the citation with P12 so the number has a matching span, while retaining P17 as the governing policy for the approval decision.
Ask the same model to confirm its confidence in the limit and pass results above the application’s confidence threshold.

questions.prompt: A claims assistant returns schema-valid JSON with decision="approve" and limit=5000, citing approved policy P17. The cited P17 passage requires manager approval but contains no 5,000 limit; that amount appears only in stale P12 evidence. What should happen before the result is sent to the analyst?

constraints: P17 is the current governing revision and explicitly supports the 5,000 limit.
Manager approval A88, account scope, and field-level evidence spans are valid.
P12 is stale and must not override the current policy record; final credit execution remains separately authorized.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If P17 omitted the limit or A88 were missing or the account scope invalid, return to the sibling decision: mark the unsupported field unknown and abstain or escalate.
details.errorCorrection: The older P12 passage is not the governing revision, while current P17 and A88 support the result; abstention would discard valid evidence without resolving the actual authority order.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends structuring long document context and asking Claude to ground responses in relevant document passages; the field-to-span gate and escalation are scenario controls. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The current governing evidence and approval record support every material field, so the assistant should produce a grounded ready-for-analyst result while retaining separate execution authorization.
details.scenarioApplication: Parse the schema, verify the decision and limit against the current P17 span and approval A88, include those references in the analyst handoff, mark the result grounded and ready for analyst review, and leave any final credit execution behind the service authorization gate.
details.transfer: Use measured slice quality, service limits, and authority boundaries together; choose the least complex route that clears every stated floor and revisit it when the evidence changes.

messages.text: The scenario identifies P17 as governing and A88 as valid; treating the stale passage as coequal creates an unnecessary block instead of grounding the handoff in current evidence.
A valid shape does not prove the material decision or limit; the handoff must bind fields to the current P17 span and A88.
Choosing stale policy over the current governing revision creates an unnecessary escalation and fails to use the valid current evidence.

feedback.reason: The evidence state changes from unsupported stale text to complete current support; grounding requires delivery with references, not abstention simply because an older conflicting passage exists.

options.text: Pause the handoff, treat P12 and P17 as coequal sources, and ask an owner to choose the applicable limit before proceeding.
Ground every field in current P17 and approval A88, hand off for review, and leave execution behind service authorization.
Return the JSON fields without policy and approval citations because schema validity is sufficient for analyst review.
Apply the older P12 limit conservatively and escalate the claim even though P17 and A88 support the requested result.

questions.prompt:
A claims assistant returns {decision: approve, limit: 5000} in the required JSON schema and cites policy revision P17. The current P17 passage explicitly supports a 5,000 limit, records the required manager approval, and the account scope is valid; a stale P12 passage is also present but is not the governing revision.

How should the assistant handle the apparently conflicting evidence?

constraints: Prompt version 7 raises correct refusals to 97% but lowers JSON validity to 96.8%.

The template can be revised, replayed, canaried, and rolled back with refusal behavior retained.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If revised version 8 reaches 99.2% validity with at least 96% correct refusals, canary it; if not, keep version 6 and escalate the unresolved safety requirement.
details.errorCorrection: Invalid records breach the production contract and make downstream handling unsafe; unchanged latency does not make malformed decisions acceptable.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends establishing clear success criteria and empirical tests before improving a prompt; versioning and render checks here are scenario-authored controls for the changed template contract. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The safer refusal behavior is valuable, but the prompt contract cannot ship below the output validity floor; revise the contract and guardrail together with observable outcomes.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the refusal requirement, revise the schema/template examples so risk_reason is emitted only under the documented condition, replay the cases, and canary only a version that clears 99% validity while retaining the refusal gain.
details.transfer: Use measured slice quality, service limits, and authority boundaries together; choose the least complex route that clears every stated floor and revisit it when the evidence changes.

messages.text: Invalid records breach the production contract and make downstream handling unsafe; unchanged latency does not make malformed decisions acceptable.
That protects validity by discarding the measured safety improvement; the contract should be repaired and tested instead of choosing between the two goals.
A retry layer does not repair the conditional schema that causes invalid output and can hide a versioned contract defect while remaining below the 99% floor.

feedback.reason: The conflicting safety and contract metrics require a versioned prompt decision plus field-level observability rather than choosing one aggregate metric.

options.text: Ship version 7 because correct refusals improved, then let downstream parsers handle the 3.2% invalid records.
Revert immediately to version 6 and remove the refusal rule so the prior validity score is preserved.
Retain the refusal rule, repair the conditional schema, replay, and canary only a version meeting 99% validity while retaining the measured refusal improvement.
Keep version 7 unchanged and add a parser retry after each invalid response, using the retry result as the new contract.

questions.prompt:
Prompt version 7 adds a conditional refusal rule and a risk_reason field to a claims assistant. On a 10,000-case replay, JSON validity falls from 99.6% to 96.8%, correct refusals rise from 93% to 97%, p95 is unchanged, and the production floor is 99% valid output.

Which change should be made before any production canary?

constraints: Ticket text and policy passages have different authority.
The specialist sends the final reply.
The receiving application needs a machine-checkable handoff state.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If all required evidence were guaranteed upstream, the prompt could have a simpler output contract; the stated missing-policy case requires an explicit alternate state.
details.errorCorrection: Examples and review can complement the design, but do not replace source authority or a machine-readable abstention path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends clear, explicit instructions and descriptive XML tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and inputs.
details.scenarioApplication: Separate instructions, policy, and ticket data; specify the workflow; require either an evidence-grounded draft or a structured escalation with the missing requirement.
details.transfer: Represent known failure states in the prompt and output contract instead of requiring a complete answer for every input.

messages.text: Closest-example matching can transfer a reply across different policies, and a free-form uncertainty note does not provide the required handoff state.
Chronology obscures authority, while a mandatory reply pressures the model to complete an answer even when the policy is absent.
Two helpful-looking answers can share unsupported policy assumptions; agreement is not evidence that the supplied policy supports the reply.

feedback.reason: The prompt needs both an authority structure and an explicit output state for missing evidence. A fluent reply, a valid shape, or model agreement does not establish policy support.

options.text: Define the role and sequence, separate ticket and policy content, and require a structured draft-or-escalate result tied to the available evidence.
Provide several polished reply examples and let the assistant select the closest example, returning a prose note when a policy match looks uncertain.
Merge policy and ticket into one chronological conversation, then require valid JSON containing a summary and a mandatory completed reply.
Ask a second model to review the draft for helpfulness and use agreement between the two models as the signal that policy support is sufficient.

questions.prompt: A support assistant must summarize a ticket, use the supplied policy to draft a reply, and hand it to a specialist. If policy evidence is missing, the handoff must identify that state instead of proposing a policy answer. Which prompt design best supports this workflow?

constraints: The role, workflow, and output structure are shared.
Regional variables are validated before insertion.
The receiving workflow can request clarification.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A region with a genuinely different workflow may need a distinct template; changing data alone does not justify duplicating the shared contract.
details.errorCorrection: Prompt copies can drift, estimated fields can be mistaken for shipment facts, and a permissive string schema does not identify why a value is absent.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends explicit instructions, desired output formats, and constraints so Claude does not have to infer the team's workflow.
details.scenarioApplication: Render one common template with validated regional data and require the structured output to identify any fields that block completion.
details.transfer: Separate stable behavioral rules from request variables, and encode missing information as a state the receiving workflow can act on.

messages.text: Periodic reconciliation does not prevent shared rules from diverging between copies and gives up the stated common-template advantage.
An estimate label does not satisfy the requirement to expose missing fields rather than supply invented shipment values.
A uniform type can be convenient, but without explicit missingness the receiver cannot distinguish an absent value from an ordinary string.
The common template preserves one version of the shared instructions while allowing validated regional variation.
The structured missing-data path preserves factual integrity and gives the operator an actionable clarification request.

feedback.reason: Reusable governing instructions avoid drift, while an explicit missing-data state preserves the difference between observed shipment facts and absent information.

options.text: Maintain separate complete prompt copies for every region and reconcile their shared instructions during periodic release reviews.
Fill missing values from the nearest complete shipment example, then label the entire result as an estimate for the operator.
Keep the shared role, workflow, and output rules in a reusable template with explicit validated regional variables.
Return every required field as a string so missing values and completed values fit one schema without a separate state.
Define a structured missing-data result that identifies absent fields and routes clarification instead of inventing them.

questions.prompt: A logistics assistant uses the same workflow across regions, with regional shipment data supplied at request time. Missing shipment fields must be visible to the operator rather than filled from likely patterns. Select TWO prompt-contract choices that support reuse and correctness.

constraints: The task involves multi-step comparison.
A deterministic calculator can verify numerical results.
The customer-facing response has a bounded format.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Simple extraction may not benefit from extra reasoning. Use it where the measured task requires multi-step comparison and preserve an independently checkable output.
details.errorCorrection: A convincing derivation, a brief answer, or sample agreement does not establish arithmetic correctness or satisfy the required separation of internal work and final explanation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic's prompting guide treats thinking as a controllable capability for complex tasks and emphasizes explicit output guidance.
details.scenarioApplication: Configure supported reasoning for the comparison, specify the final assumptions and justification fields, and check the numerical projection with the deterministic calculator.
details.transfer: Specify the final explanatory contract separately from the model’s reasoning support, and validate calculations with an appropriate external check.

messages.text: Visible internal consistency can still contain a shared arithmetic or assumption error and exceeds the requested customer-facing format.
A short output does not show that the necessary constraint comparison occurred, and brevity is not a correctness metric.
Multiple samples can share the same error; choosing a common value does not replace the available deterministic calculation check.

feedback.reason: Reasoning support and customer-facing explanation are different concerns. The model can perform the needed analysis while the application exposes a bounded result and verifies arithmetic independently.

options.text: Ask for a complete visible derivation and accept numerical outputs when every intermediate line appears internally consistent.
Use a short answer-only prompt for all cases and treat brevity as evidence that the model avoided unnecessary reasoning.
Run several answer-only samples and publish the most common projection together with one sampled explanation.
Use suitable thinking support, request assumptions and a concise final justification, and verify the calculations independently before display.

questions.prompt: An assistant must compare planning constraints and calculate a projection. Customers need the assumptions and a concise justification, not an internal reasoning transcript. Which prompting and validation approach fits the requirement?

constraints: Ordinary-message performance must be preserved.
The edge cases contain several different wordings for the same decision boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If failures came from missing or contradictory policy rules rather than interpretation, clarify the rules before selecting examples.
details.errorCorrection: One exhaustive example can overfit wording, repeated policy may not resolve contextual ambiguity, and keyword rules remove the very distinction being tested.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends relevant, diverse, structured examples and says a few well-crafted examples can improve accuracy and consistency.
details.scenarioApplication: Choose representative pairs that distinguish quoting from endorsing abuse and contextual uses of terms, delimit them as examples, and compare the revised prompt on held-out cases.
details.transfer: Use few-shot examples to illustrate a known ambiguous boundary, and keep regression evidence outside the examples.

messages.text: An example containing every term does not supply varied near-miss boundaries, and imitation of explanation style is not label correctness.
The aggregate can hide the same rare failures, while repetition alone does not demonstrate how context changes the label.
A term-level rule would treat quotation and reclaimed usage like direct abuse, reproducing the contextual error instead of repairing it.

feedback.reason: The failures involve how context changes the meaning of similar words. Contrastive verified examples teach that boundary, while mixed-slice evaluation checks that the repair does not harm ordinary decisions.

options.text: Add a small diverse set of tagged contrastive examples and evaluate both the difficult and ordinary slices.
Add a single comprehensive example containing all sensitive terms, then measure whether the model reproduces its explanation style.
Increase the repetition of the general moderation policy and use the existing overall accuracy score as the acceptance test.
Add a keyword prefilter that assigns every message containing the troublesome terms to the restrictive label before the model sees context.

questions.prompt: A moderation classifier performs well on ordinary messages but reverses labels on sarcasm, quoted abuse, and reclaimed terms. The team has verified labels for these edge cases. Which prompt change best targets the failure?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Training examples cannot provide an unbiased held-out evaluation.
details.errorCorrection: The validated output contract is part of the task and should remain stable.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompting should be guided by success criteria and empirical tests.
details.scenarioApplication: Examples can help but should be relevant and diverse; they are not universally beneficial.
details.transfer: Use additional examples when they address a measured confusion and verify the change on untouched cases.

messages.text: Example count alone does not guarantee improvement and may consume context or introduce unintended patterns.
Changing to free-form output violates the established classification contract.
Reusing training cases for evaluation overstates generalization.

feedback.reason: The current prompt already clears the measured requirements, so examples add context and potential overfitting without a demonstrated benefit. A prompt change should answer a specific observed failure.

options.text: Add all 40 examples because more in-context examples always improve classification.
Keep zero-shot until evaluation identifies a gap examples could address.
Replace the labels with free-form explanations so the model can decide what each invoice means.
Add examples from the training set to the evaluation cases so the new prompt appears more accurate.

questions.prompt: A classifier maps routine invoices into three fixed labels. The output schema is clear, and a representative zero-shot evaluation meets the accuracy and latency targets on every required slice. A team proposes adding 40 examples because examples often improve prompts. What should the architect do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A model switch may help, but it does not address the identified prompt ambiguity by itself.
details.errorCorrection: An internal reasoning transcript is not required to improve or validate the output field.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Examples are useful when they mirror a real distinction and vary enough to avoid accidental patterns.
details.scenarioApplication: The examples should contrast the two meanings that the current prompt confuses.
details.transfer: Use examples for a demonstrated edge-case boundary and preserve held-out evaluation for generalization.

messages.text: A broad caution does not define how to encode the two different states.
Requesting internal reasoning is not a substitute for a clear output distinction and test.
The failure mechanism is already localized; first test a targeted prompt repair before attributing it to model capability.

feedback.reason: The failure is a specific semantic distinction, so contrasting examples and an explicit representation can target it. Replaying ordinary cases checks that the change did not create a new confusion.

options.text: Add verified contrasts for the two labels; retest edge and ordinary notes.
Add a long general instruction to be careful with every clinical fact.
Ask Claude to provide its full internal reasoning for every note so clinicians can inspect it.
Change to a larger model without updating the prompt or evaluation.

questions.prompt: A medical summarizer must distinguish “not documented” from “no symptom.” The model performs well on ordinary notes but confuses the two on a held-out set. Which prompt change is most targeted?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Free-form labels would break the fixed schema instead of improving the classifier.
details.errorCorrection: Internal reasoning text is not part of the label contract and does not directly test the identified gap.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Examples are useful when they address a demonstrated confusion and preserve the required output format.
details.scenarioApplication: Repeating examples from already working classes does not supply information about the new class.
details.transfer: Target prompt changes to the measured error category and replay the full relevant test set.

messages.text: More repetitions of examples from correctly handled classes do not teach the new boundary.
The issue is coverage of a class, not lack of a reasoning transcript.
Invented free-form labels make the output less comparable and violate the contract.

feedback.reason: The observed gap concerns a new class and its boundary, so examples should target those distinctions. Evaluation must remain held out and include the original classes to detect regressions.

options.text: Duplicate both old examples many times so the model pays more attention to the established classes.
Add a chain-of-thought request for every classification even though the output contract is only a label.
Replace the schema with free text so the model can invent a label for ambiguous cases.
Add reviewed examples for the new class and its boundary; test untouched cases across all classes.

questions.prompt: A support classifier’s prompt includes two examples, but its held-out errors cluster around a new third class introduced last month. The current classes and schema are clear; no confusion remains between the original two. What prompt change is most justified?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Examples should address an observed failure; the prompt already meets this requirement.
details.errorCorrection: A confidence score does not identify which contract text supports the answer.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt for observable checks and user-facing rationale rather than a private chain-of-thought transcript.
details.scenarioApplication: The full internal transcript is unnecessary and is not the requested output.
details.transfer: Align explanation depth with the consumer’s verification need and test the visible result.

messages.text: The task asks for an auditable concise explanation; a full internal trace is neither necessary nor the output contract.

Unneeded examples add context without a demonstrated improvement.

options.text: Require a complete hidden reasoning transcript before producing any answer.
Replace contract citations with a confidence score so the response is shorter.
Ask for a concise conclusion, clause citation, and assumptions; test answer and citation accuracy.
Add demonstrations even though the current prompt already produces the requested clause and assumptions reliably.

questions.prompt: A support assistant must answer from a supplied contract and the operator asks for a one-sentence explanation with the clause number and assumptions. A proposed prompt instead requests every internal reasoning step. Which prompt target better meets the task?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The existing label schema remains part of the requirement; free-form output does not test the corrected boundary.
details.errorCorrection: Contrastive examples using the phrase across labels can separate the actual intent cues from the phrase itself.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Few-shot examples should demonstrate the decision boundary rather than correlate labels with incidental wording.
details.scenarioApplication: The held-out error shows the positive examples taught a phrase-based shortcut that also appears in negative cases.
details.transfer: Vary example wording and evaluate on untouched examples so a prompt does not memorize one surface cue.

messages.text: Repeating the correlated examples strengthens the accidental cue instead of correcting it.
Free text changes the task output and does not establish whether the classification boundary improved.
A reasoning transcript does not replace representative contrastive data and held-out evaluation.

feedback.reason: The examples have taught a spurious lexical shortcut. Contrastive examples should separate the intent from the phrase’s presence, and untouched cases should test whether the model learned the actual boundary.

options.text: Repeat the positive examples containing the phrase so the model recognizes it more strongly.
Remove the output schema and let Claude explain the phrase’s meaning in free text.
Add varied contrastive examples that include the phrase in both labels and vary the surrounding intent cues; keep an untouched test set for the same boundary.
Ask for a full private reasoning transcript on every classification.

questions.prompt: A few-shot classifier reaches 95% on held-out support intents, but error review shows it learned a phrase that appears only in positive examples; the phrase also occurs in negative examples in production. Which prompt change is most targeted?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Changing examples and reasoning together would prevent attribution of any resulting quality change.
details.errorCorrection: Longer responses and latency do not establish more careful or more accurate classification.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt complexity should be retained only when it improves a measured task requirement.
details.scenarioApplication: The zero-shot baseline already clears every quality slice, while the added instruction breaches the 500 ms SLA without a measured gain.
details.transfer: Use more involved reasoning where evaluation demonstrates value and the workload can meet its service contract.

messages.text: Longer latency or output does not establish more accurate classification.
Changing two prompt elements at once would obscure which change affected results.
The SLA is an explicit requirement and should not be relaxed without an authorized business decision.

feedback.reason: The added reasoning instruction has no measured quality benefit and violates the service latency contract. The simpler prompt already meets the required evaluation targets.

options.text: Keep the reasoning instruction because longer answers indicate more careful classification.
Add examples and reasoning together so any improvement is easier to attribute.
Relax the SLA to preserve the more sophisticated prompt.
Keep the zero-shot prompt and omit the added reasoning instruction for this workload; reserve more involved reasoning for tasks where evaluation shows it improves a required outcome.

questions.prompt: A low-risk ticket classifier meets every held-out quality target with a direct zero-shot prompt. Adding a “think step by step” instruction raises p95 latency by 70% and changes no required error slice. The application has a 500 ms SLA. What should the architect ship?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the extraction itself were wrong, improve or review extraction separately; the case says the amounts are already correct.
details.errorCorrection: More reasoning text or demonstrations can still produce a plausible incorrect sum and do not replace an exact check.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt technique should address a model-controllable behavior; exact arithmetic and threshold comparisons are better owned by deterministic computation when the values are already extracted.
details.scenarioApplication: The amounts are correct but the sum is wrong, so the application can compute the total and compare it with the ledger before the model writes an audit note.
details.transfer: Locate whether the error is in understanding, transformation, or computation, then assign each step to the control that can verify it.

messages.text: The assistant already explains its arithmetic, and an internally consistent trace can still contain a wrong total.
Examples do not make repeated exact addition a reliable model responsibility when deterministic code can compute it.
The observed defect is arithmetic, not a demonstrated capability gap; a model change without validation leaves the same failure path.

feedback.reason: The replay isolates arithmetic, not extraction, as the failure. A longer private reasoning trace does not make exact totals authoritative; calculate and validate them deterministically, then ask the model only for the concise explanation.

options.text: Ask for a longer chain of thought, then accept the total whenever the explanation looks consistent.
Sum and compare amounts with deterministic application logic; prompt for a concise note based on the validated result.
Add examples of manually summed receipts while keeping the model responsible for all arithmetic.
Switch every expense request to a stronger model and keep the same unvalidated calculation path.

questions.prompt: An expense assistant extracts every line-item amount correctly, but in 7% of replays its total differs from the ledger by $12. It already explains each arithmetic step; the output needs the verified total and a short audit note. Which change best targets the observed failure?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If another trusted field reliably determines locale, include it and evaluate the resulting prompt; absent that field, preserve ambiguity.
details.errorCorrection: Adding examples that silently pick a convention teaches a guess, not a supported boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Prompt engineering can express a defined transformation but cannot create missing authoritative information.
details.scenarioApplication: An ambiguous numeric date needs a locale source or an explicit unknown/error result before a demonstration can teach the correct conversion.
details.transfer: Resolve data and policy assumptions before using examples to teach model behavior.

messages.text: Demonstrations cannot safely resolve an ambiguity the application has not defined.
Nearby names may not determine the date convention and can turn missing input into an unsupported guess.
Free text changes the output contract but does not provide the missing locale rule.

feedback.reason: The input itself is ambiguous when locale metadata is absent. First define whether locale is supplied by an authoritative field or whether the result must remain unresolved; examples can only reinforce that rule afterward.

options.text: Add many examples that map every ambiguous date to one preferred interpretation.
Define locale authority and missing-locale behavior before testing examples.
Ask Claude to infer the locale from nearby names and return its best guess.
Change the extraction to free text so the model can explain its uncertainty.

questions.prompt: A zero-shot extraction prompt misses the same date normalization rule in 11% of cases. The expected format is clear, but examples in the draft prompt all use ISO dates; failures occur on ambiguous `03/04/26` values where region metadata is sometimes absent. What should the team resolve before adding demonstrations?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If labels disagree on negated phrases, resolve the labeling rule before encoding examples.
details.errorCorrection: Rare examples are useful only when labels are reliable and their feature is relevant to a demonstrated error.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Few-shot examples should target observed decision errors and be evaluated on held-out representative cases.
details.scenarioApplication: Frequency-weighted selection would overrepresent a segment that already dominates the prompt and misses the negation confusion.
details.transfer: Use a small set to clarify the boundary, not to mirror the raw frequency distribution blindly.

messages.text: The dominant wording is already overrepresented and does not target the known failure.
Unverified unusual examples can teach an incorrect rule and do not specifically address negation.
One example per class may fail to show how negation changes otherwise similar cases.

feedback.reason: The error pattern is tied to negation and segment shift, so contrastive verified examples directly expose that decision boundary. Held-out segment results check whether the change generalizes.

options.text: Choose the four most frequent cases so examples reflect the dominant production segment.
Choose four examples with the most unusual wording, regardless of whether their labels are verified.
Use one clear example per class, then check negation cases in the next evaluation cycle.
Use verified negation contrasts; measure held-out results by the affected segments.

questions.prompt: A classifier has 20,000 labeled cases, but 70% repeat near-identical wording from one customer segment. Errors cluster on negation used by two other segments. The team has room for four examples in the prompt. Which demonstration strategy is strongest?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the task requires an internal rationale, follow the product’s supported rationale policy; it does not replace correcting examples and testing labels.
details.errorCorrection: More examples of one side can reinforce the conflation rather than teach the distinction.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Examples should encode the intended label boundary, and evaluation should test both sides of that boundary.
details.scenarioApplication: Explicit denial is affirmative evidence of absence; a missing statement is an evidence gap.
details.transfer: When two labels differ by evidence status, construct matched contrastive tests.

messages.text: More single-sided examples do not distinguish explicit denial from missing evidence.
Removing demonstrations does not establish that the model learned the required distinction.
Reasoning text cannot repair an incorrect label definition and may make unsupported inferences sound persuasive.

feedback.reason: The two labels have different evidence meanings. Contrastive cases isolate the distinction and a targeted evaluation can detect whether each state is handled correctly.
