messages.text: The definitions consume negligible context and every request needs them, so discovery adds avoidable latency and complexity.
This creates the measured second-round latency even though all five tools are universal and already fit comfortably in context.
Replacing typed definitions removes contract clarity and does not improve authorization; invocation enforcement must remain independent of prompt exposure.

feedback.reason: The context and latency evidence reverses the large-inventory default: eager core plus deferred tail has no tail to defer here.

options.text: Use a discovery mechanism first and defer every tool because eager capability exposure is always harmful.
Eagerly load the five governed typed tools and retain invocation authorization; defer discovery until the inventory changes.
Expose only search and fetch initially, then discover update, notify, and close for each route that needs them.
Flatten the five definitions into prose and let the model choose calls without typed schemas, using the server only for transport.

questions.prompt:
A small internal assistant has five tools: search, fetch, update, notify, and close. All five are used by every request path, their typed definitions total 1% of context, and the server can enforce authorization at invocation.

Which tool-surface strategy is proportionate to this small, universal inventory?

constraints: Wrong-tool selection rose from 0.5% to 4.2% after twelve tools were added, while transport p95 stayed stable.
Two tools have similar names but different tenant filters.
The application can version the inventory and trace tool, parameters, authorization, and outcome.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If traces show the errors come from a single malformed backend response rather than selection, repair that contract and keep the tool surface unchanged.
details.errorCorrection: The defect is wrong selection and parameters, not transport latency; extra visibility and randomness can increase the ambiguity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that tools with similar names can lead to wrong tool selection and incorrect parameters. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The capability surface needs schema clarity and observable selection outcomes; latency alone cannot identify or repair the new tool-choice failure.
details.scenarioApplication: Split overlapping capabilities into canonical tools with distinct required filters, version the inventory, and trace the selected tool, parameters, authorization, and result before expanding the catalog.
details.transfer: When selection errors rise after a catalog change, trace inventory version, chosen operation, and parameters before repairing ambiguous contracts; healthy transport is not selection evidence.

messages.text: The defect is wrong selection and parameters, not transport latency; extra visibility and randomness can increase ambiguity.
An optional filter hides a material tenant distinction and can make an incorrect scope look valid instead of requiring the correct typed field.
Descriptions may help, but without canonical required fields, versioning, and selection traces the observed choice and parameter failure cannot be diagnosed.

feedback.reason: The decision addresses both capability bloat and the evidence needed to determine whether the repair works.

options.text: Keep all tools visible and tune model temperature because the transport p95 metric is healthy.
Merge the similar tools behind one broad tool with an optional tenant filter so the model has fewer names to choose from.
Split overlapping tools with required filters, version the inventory, and trace selection, authorization, parameters, and outcomes.
Add aliases and longer descriptions to the existing catalog, but keep only final-answer logging because selection traces add overhead.

questions.prompt:
After a catalog release adds twelve tools, wrong-tool selection rises from 0.5% to 4.2% while transport p95 stays unchanged. Two tools have similar names but different tenant filters, and traces record only the final answer, not the selected tool or inventory version.

Which catalog repair makes tool selection observable and less ambiguous?

constraints: Supplier search, contract retrieval, and summarization are the high-use path.
Rare governed capabilities must remain available without occupying the initial context.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Discovery adds one step for rare requests, but it preserves the long tail while reducing initial context pressure and wrong-tool selection.
details.errorCorrection: Treat tool descriptions as part of the context budget and capability boundary rather than exposing every operation merely because it exists.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A curated initial inventory keeps high-use tool contracts visible while tool search or another controlled discovery mechanism loads detailed rare capabilities only when relevant.
details.scenarioApplication: The assistant can search suppliers, retrieve the selected contract, and summarize it directly; an approved discovery path handles uncommon export or mutation workflows.
details.transfer: For a large tool catalog, measure use and selection quality, keep the narrow high-use surface eager, and discover governed long-tail tools on demand.

messages.text: Loading all definitions recreates the context bloat and leaves similar or rare capabilities competing with the three required tools.
Removing capabilities turns a context problem into an unsupported manual process and loses legitimate procurement workflows.
A universal schema hides distinct contracts behind optional parameters and can increase invalid combinations and selection errors.

feedback.reason: The common workflow needs precise schemas immediately; rare capabilities can be discovered when their governed use is actually selected. This reduces context and selection ambiguity without deleting valid behavior.

options.text: Expose all twenty tools at startup so Claude can choose among every procurement capability without a discovery step.
Keep the three precise read tools available for this workflow and defer rare governed tools to an explicit discovery path.
Remove every tool except a text generator and have procurement staff perform supplier and contract lookups outside the assistant.
Expose only one universal procurement tool with optional parameters so the model sees fewer names while retaining every operation.

questions.prompt: A procurement assistant has twenty available tools, but its current workflow only searches suppliers, retrieves one contract, and summarizes it. Tool descriptions consume much of the initial context. Which configuration is the best first release?

constraints: Tool visibility must follow the validated requesting tenant and user.
High-use authorized reads should be immediate, while rare governed capabilities remain discoverable.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tenant-scoped discovery adds filtering and invocation checks, yet it retains rare business behavior without exposing unauthorized schemas or actions.
details.errorCorrection: Separate context optimization from authorization: defer capabilities by use, but never let a model-visible catalog grant access.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Tenant and user identity scope the catalog and discovery results, while the server rechecks current permission at invocation before executing a tool.
details.scenarioApplication: Expose the municipality's three core reads, discover regional forms and exports only for that tenant, and reject a stale or cross-tenant request at the server boundary.
details.transfer: In multi-tenant catalogs, curate the eager set by validated access and usage, then enforce the same scope again at execution.

messages.text: A global eager catalog consumes context and exposes irrelevant or unauthorized capability descriptions to every municipality.
Frequency alone is not a reason to delete valid regional behavior; discovery can preserve it without eager context cost.
Prompt wording is not an authorization boundary and can be bypassed by a manipulated or stale request.
Without an eager authorized core, the common path is either bloated with irrelevant tools or lacks its precise read contracts.
Without tenant-scoped discovery and an invocation recheck, rare tools can leak across municipalities or execute after permissions change.

feedback.reason: The common capability surface can be curated per tenant, but rare tools should remain available through controlled discovery. Discovery and execution both need tenant-aware authorization; visibility alone is insufficient.

options.text: Load all 80 definitions for every municipality so the model can discover regional differences from the catalog.
Keep the authorized high-use reads eager and defer rare regional tools so ordinary requests retain their precise contracts without the full catalog.
Delete rare regional tools from the catalog because their low frequency makes their maintenance cost disproportionate.
Show every tool to the model but rely on municipality names in the prompt to prevent cross-tenant calls.
Scope discovery results by validated tenant and user, and recheck the current operation scope at invocation before executing a discovered regional form or export.

questions.prompt: A building-permit platform serves three municipalities through one catalog of 80 tools. Each municipality authorizes a different subset; three core reads dominate, while regional forms and exports are rare. Which TWO configuration decisions preserve capability and authorization? Select TWO.

constraints: The server is currently a local child process connected over stdio.
If the integration changes to HTTP, its HTTP resource authorization requirements apply even to a local listener.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local process controls require host hardening and careful launch configuration, but they avoid an inapplicable protocol exchange while still protecting the database.
details.errorCorrection: Match the credential and threat control to the actual transport instead of mechanically applying a remote protocol to a local process.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Process ownership, environment permissions, and workstation isolation protect local stdio credentials. For the protected HTTP endpoint in this scenario, enforce authorization at the resource boundary and validate the token and required scopes under the implemented MCP authorization profile. Running the listener on loopback does not waive the application access-control requirements.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep secrets out of model-visible metadata, restrict the child process environment and files, and apply HTTP authorization when the integration changes from stdio to HTTP.
details.transfer: For integrations, identify who can reach the boundary and choose process, network, or protocol authorization controls accordingly.

messages.text: An HTTP exchange is not the stdio transport boundary and adds no useful resource-server binding inside a local message stream.
Local execution does not eliminate threats from a compromised process, environment, or workstation and cannot justify removing controls.
Secrets in tool descriptions become model-visible metadata and are not a safe credential mechanism.

feedback.reason: The protocol boundary differs by transport. Stdio is protected through the process and environment, while HTTP exposure introduces a resource-server authorization boundary; sensitive data still needs local controls.

options.text: Protect stdio credentials with process, environment, and workstation controls; if this sensitive database is exposed over HTTP, enforce its implemented MCP authorization profile at the resource boundary, including on loopback.
Run a bearer-token exchange through the stdio stream for every local call, even though the child process is not an HTTP resource server.
Assume the local child process is trusted and disable credential checks while the workstation and process environment remain otherwise unrestricted.
Place the local database password in the tool schema so Claude can supply it to the child process when a sensitive query is requested.

questions.prompt: A developer runs a local MCP server as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation. A reviewer proposes applying HTTP bearer-token authorization to every message because the local database is sensitive. Which boundary-specific control is correct?

constraints: The code flow must bind an exact destination and the response to its initiating session.
The client needs protection against authorization-code interception.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The checks require registration and per-request state, but they reduce redirect abuse, response injection, and intercepted-code reuse.
details.errorCorrection: Diagnose authorization as destination, session, and code binding rather than relying on domain ownership or transport confidentiality alone.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Exact URI comparison constrains the redirect, state links the response to the initiating browser transaction, and PKCE binds the authorization code to the verifier held by the client.
details.scenarioApplication: Register the precise callback, generate and validate state per authorization request, and require a code challenge and verifier on the token exchange.
details.transfer: For browser authorization flows, make the redirect exact and bind both the response and code exchange to the initiating client transaction.

messages.text: A domain wildcard still permits an unregistered destination, a fragment does not replace state, and TLS does not bind the code to this client.
Manual copy-paste removes a controlled callback but does not establish a secure redirect or code-binding protocol.
Checking the account after redemption is too late to prevent redirect or authorization-code mix-up.

feedback.reason: A broad redirect accepts destinations the client did not register, missing state allows response mix-up, and missing PKCE leaves a public client code vulnerable to interception. The three controls address distinct bindings.

options.text: Keep a company-domain redirect wildcard, deliver the code through the browser fragment, and rely on TLS and the signed-in account to identify the initiating client.
Remove the callback registration and ask the user to paste the authorization code into the client, treating manual possession as the session binding.
Register one broad callback and compare the account after redemption, without validating a per-request state value or a code verifier.
Require exact pre-registered redirect URIs, validate state for the initiating session, and use PKCE to bind the code exchange to the client.

questions.prompt: A web client starts an MCP authorization flow. The authorization server accepts any redirect URI under the company domain, and the client sends neither state nor PKCE. What should the security diagnosis require?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A service mesh identity or signed internal assertion can provide the trusted propagation mechanism.
details.errorCorrection: Prompt rules cannot protect headers; hostnames alone do not authenticate message contents; model comparison is not identity proof.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The gateway, downstream API, and caller principal are distinct trust boundaries. The scenario supplies the forged-header behavior; the source informs the HTTP authorization boundary, while the downstream service must bind identity to validated credentials rather than accept a caller-selected subject.
details.scenarioApplication: Strip caller-supplied identity headers and propagate a trusted, verifiable principal context.
details.transfer: Protect identity context across every hop that performs authorization.

messages.text: Prompt instructions cannot prevent a caller from forging the identity header.
A hostname does not authenticate the identity value carried in a request.
Comparing a display name in a conversation does not establish an authenticated subject.

feedback.reason: The caller currently controls the identity assertion that the downstream service trusts. The gateway must overwrite or cryptographically bind that context across the service boundary.

options.text: Ask the model to compare the subject name with the conversation before each call.
Keep the header and add a prompt rule telling Claude not to change it.
Trust the header only when the request originates from the public gateway hostname.
Build trusted principal context from validated credentials; block spoofed headers and verify it downstream.

questions.prompt: A gateway validates an access token but forwards user-supplied X-Subject headers to a downstream service, which trusts the header. What must be corrected?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the workflow is intentionally service-to-service rather than user-delegated, the service identity still needs a narrowly scoped payroll permission and an explicit audit link to the initiating user where policy requires it.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat issuer validity as permission to reuse a token across audiences, trust a target header, or silently replace the user with a broader service identity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The MCP authorization specification binds access tokens to their intended resource server and requires the resource server to validate authorization. The cross-service forwarding behavior is supplied by the scenario.
details.scenarioApplication: Use an explicit delegated-token or token-exchange design for the payroll audience, constrain it to the required payroll scope, and have payroll reject a token intended only for the gateway.
details.transfer: At each HTTP resource boundary, verify that the credential names that resource and authorizes that operation.

messages.text: The prompt names two resource audiences; signature and issuer validation alone do not grant permission for the payroll resource.
A caller-selected routing header is not an authorization credential and leaves the token audience unchanged.
Replacing the user with a service account changes the authorization model and could broaden access; any service identity must be explicitly scoped and auditable.

feedback.reason: A token is intended for its resource audience; a valid signature alone does not make it portable to a different payroll service. Obtain a credential for that resource and validate its scope at the receiving boundary.

options.text: Accept the token at both services because a valid issuer and signature make its permissions portable across internal resource servers.
Obtain a payroll-audience token with delegated scopes; payroll validates audience and operation permission.
Replace audience validation with a caller-supplied `X-Target-Service` header so the same token can be routed dynamically.
Remove the user token at the gateway and authorize every payroll action under the gateway service account.

questions.prompt: A user presents an access token to an MCP gateway. The gateway validates it, then forwards the same token to a payroll service whose resource identifier is a different audience. The payroll service currently accepts it because the signature and issuer are valid. What should be corrected?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If approval is withdrawn, expired or covers a different amount, do not release the artifact; report the actual unavailable state.
details.errorCorrection: A user’s natural-language self-approval and a valid scope are not substitutes for a separate authority record.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Authentication scopes and application approval are separate authorization predicates; satisfying one does not satisfy the other.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the job pending or reject it until the finance approver’s signed/validated approval covers this amount, then recheck the user’s current scope and the approval at release.
details.transfer: Evaluate identity, operation scope and required human approval as distinct checks at the side-effect boundary.

messages.text: The operation has a separate required approval state that is not satisfied by the caller’s own message.
The model cannot manufacture the required approval record or serve as the designated approver.
Post-execution cancellation cannot reliably undo exposure of a sensitive payroll artifact.

feedback.reason: The token permits the operation type, but the high-value export also requires an independent approval that is still pending. Enforce both conditions before producing the artifact.

options.text: Execute because the token includes payroll.export and the user explicitly approved in chat.
Wait for designated finance approval, then recheck scope and approved amount at execution.
Expose the export but ask Claude to decide whether the finance approver would probably agree.
Run the export and allow the finance approver to cancel the downloaded file afterward.

questions.prompt: A payroll user’s token includes payroll.export, but policy requires approval from a separate finance approver for exports above $50,000. The user requests a $75,000 export and says “I approve” in chat; the server-side approval record is still pending. What should the tool boundary do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the exact original intent is executed unchanged and its approval remains current, the supplied approval may be sufficient; a changed payee requires the separately approved intent.
details.errorCorrection: An approval flag without binding to the operation can be reused for a materially different effect.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Authentication establishes a principal; application authorization must also cover the requested operation and resource at the enforcement boundary. The specific grants in this case are supplied premises.
details.scenarioApplication: Version or fingerprint the executable intent, match the approval to Vendor B and $8,000, and expose pending status until the required approver authorizes it.
details.transfer: Bind consequential approval to the actual operation, not merely to a job name or unchanged amount.

messages.text: The policy binds approval to payee as well as amount; unchanged exposure does not authorize a different recipient.
Silently changing the requested operation produces a different payment and a false completion report instead of resolving the approval mismatch.
The model is not the authorized finance approver and cannot manufacture approval for the revised intent.

feedback.reason: The approval is valid for the original operation but does not cover the changed payee. Current requester permission does not replace the required intent-specific approval.

options.text: Execute the corrected intent because payment.create is valid and the amount stays within the signed payment’s financial exposure.
Execute to Vendor A by silently restoring the original payee, then report that the corrected request completed successfully.
Ask the model to assess whether Vendor B is equivalent, and accept its explanation as the link to the existing approval.
Keep the changed intent pending until approval is bound to its exact payee and amount; preserve the prior intent’s status separately.

questions.prompt: A finance approver signs a payment intent for $8,000 to Vendor A. Before execution, a model-generated correction changes the payee to Vendor B while preserving the amount. The requester still has payment.create, and the approval service reports the original intent as approved. Policy requires approval of the exact payee and amount. What should the server do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If an authorized payroll workflow requires bank details, expose them only through that separately authorized path and its appropriate logging policy.
details.errorCorrection: Hiding a value on screen does not prevent disclosure through tool context or logs.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Authentication establishes a principal; application authorization must also cover the requested operation and resource at the enforcement boundary. The specific grants in this case are supplied premises.
details.scenarioApplication: Resolve authorized fields at the API response boundary and return only job grade and other permitted fields to the assistant’s downstream consumers.
details.transfer: Check the scope of the returned data as well as the scope of the requested object.

messages.text: Prompt instructions do not undo disclosure of the forbidden field into model context and troubleshooting records.
Encryption protects storage access but does not grant this caller permission to expose bank details to the assistant or logging path.
The policy permits job-grade access; a field-aware response can serve that request without disclosing the restricted field.

feedback.reason: Record access and field access are different grants in this case. UI masking happens after the prohibited data has entered model context and logs.

options.text: Filter restricted fields before the tool response reaches the model and logs, using the verified caller’s field permissions.
Retain the full response for troubleshooting and require the assistant’s system prompt to omit the bank-account field from its answer.
Keep UI masking and encrypt the full log at rest; record-level access can remain the sole authorization decision.
Reject all employee-record reads until every field is public, including the job-grade information that policy already permits.

questions.prompt: A benefits assistant may show an employee’s public job grade but not their bank account. The API authorizes access to the employee record, sends all fields into the model and logs the full tool response, then the UI hides bank_account. Which boundary should change?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A permission cache may remain useful if its scope, versioning and invalidation satisfy the actual revocation contract; this case does not justify banning all caches.
details.errorCorrection: Do not diagnose a stale server grant as prompt memory or equate token validity with a current export permission.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Authentication establishes a principal; application authorization must also cover the requested operation and resource at the enforcement boundary. The specific grants in this case are supplied premises.
details.scenarioApplication: Trace policy version and invalidation to the export check, then test requests immediately after revocation against the one-second requirement.
details.transfer: Use traces to locate stale authority and verify the repair against the promised revocation window.

messages.text: The trace locates the stale allow in the server authorization cache, not in model memory.
The stated revocation requirement is stricter than token expiry; signature validity does not satisfy the current permission decision.
Unrelated rendering and public-schema caches do not cause this permission failure; repair and verify the authorization decision path.

feedback.reason: The identity check succeeds, but the cached grant violates the supplied revocation deadline. The repair must restore current permission enforcement at execution.

options.text: Shorten the model’s conversation window so it cannot remember the earlier export grant, while leaving the authorization cache unchanged.
Expire the user’s token at its ordinary end of life; a valid signature should remain sufficient until that time.
Use current policy state at execution, or a versioned, invalidated decision cache that demonstrably meets the one-second revocation contract.
Disable every cache in the export pipeline, including document rendering and immutable public schemas, before testing another export.

questions.prompt: An export service promises that role revocation blocks new exports within one second. At 10:00:00 a grant is revoked; at 10:00:02 a new request passes token validation and uses an allow decision cached by role name for ten minutes. The live policy service already returns deny. Which repair addresses the demonstrated gap?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a separately authorized system job initiates reconciliation, apply its system grants; do not silently substitute those grants for interactive requests.
details.errorCorrection: A valid service credential is not proof that the initiating user may access every resource reachable through it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Authentication establishes a principal; application authorization must also cover the requested operation and resource at the enforcement boundary. The specific grants in this case are supplied premises.
details.scenarioApplication: Carry the verified interactive principal and tenant scope to the invoice boundary, check B-17 against U’s grants, and retain a separate authenticated reconciliation caller.
details.transfer: Separate system authority from delegated user authority when one backend credential serves different workflows.

messages.text: The nightly job has its own legitimate authority; tying it to an arbitrary interactive user breaks that contract rather than enforcing delegated user requests.
Conversation state and model behavior cannot replace enforcement of the verified user’s resource permissions by the API.
An audit can support investigation, but the unauthorized invoice has already been disclosed when the read is merely recorded.

feedback.reason: The backend credential enables a legitimate system workflow but must not expand an interactive user’s authority. Enforce the user-bound resource decision on the interactive path.

options.text: Remove the service account’s cross-tenant grant, and make nightly reconciliation obtain permission from whichever user last opened the assistant.
Bind interactive calls to verified user and tenant authority; keep the separately authorized reconciliation path explicit.
Require the model to compare the requested tenant with its conversation history before calling the existing service-account path.
Keep the service-account check and add an invoice-access audit so owners can reverse unauthorized reads after they are discovered.

questions.prompt: An invoice assistant runs user requests through a backend service account that also performs authorized nightly reconciliation. A trace shows user U, allowed to view only Tenant A, requesting invoice B-17 from Tenant B. The gateway verifies U’s identity, but the invoice API checks only the service account’s cross-tenant grant. Which repair preserves both workflows?

constraints: Operation visibility should reflect current scopes.
The server must recheck scope and approval before any export or mutation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Per-user catalogs and invocation checks require refresh and policy plumbing, but they make least privilege visible and enforceable.
details.errorCorrection: Use capability visibility as a convenience and server authorization as the security control; never treat a user request or model plan as a scope grant.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Access-token scopes map to operation permissions; server checks run at invocation so a visible or stale model plan cannot bypass current authorization.
details.scenarioApplication: Expose the read tool for this user, keep export and adjustment unavailable, and reject any attempted call unless the current credential and approval satisfy the operation.
details.transfer: For tool catalogs, filter discovery by scope and reauthorize every consequential call against current identity and policy.

messages.text: Prompt instructions can be bypassed and do not prevent the model from requesting a visible export or adjustment.
Hiding names without server rejection leaves the operation callable and makes a plausible reason an authority substitute.
A model prediction cannot grant a missing scope or provide the approval required for a payroll mutation.

feedback.reason: A logged-in identity alone does not grant every payroll operation. Discovery should reduce accidental exposure, but the resource server remains the authority for current scope and high-impact approval.

options.text: Show read, export, and adjustment tools but add a system instruction that Claude should call export or adjustment only after the user explicitly asks.
Hide export and adjustment in the catalog UI, but let the server accept a hidden call when Claude supplies a business justification in its arguments.
Expose only tools allowed by the current scope, require server-side scope and approval checks for export or adjustment, and reject unauthorized requests.
Grant payroll.export temporarily when a model confidence or task-completion prediction indicates that a payroll file would be useful.

questions.prompt: A payroll tool catalog exposes read, export, and adjustment operations. The user has payroll.read but not payroll.export or payroll.adjust, while the model can still see and request all three. Which enforcement design is correct?

constraints: Authorization may change between discovery and invocation.
The current subject, credential validity, and export scope must be checked at the resource boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A late rejection can waste planning work and require the agent to report an unavailable state, but it prevents execution under revoked authority.
details.errorCorrection: Close the time-of-check/time-of-use gap at invocation instead of trusting an earlier catalog snapshot.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The server validates a current credential, audience, expiry, and operation scope atomically or immediately before the side effect; an audit record explains the rejection.
details.scenarioApplication: Mark the queued handle stale, revalidate or refresh as needed, reject the export after role revocation, and record the attempted operation and subject.
details.transfer: For long-running plans, reauthorize every consequential operation at execution and make revoked or expired capabilities explicit.

messages.text: A cached catalog can outlive role changes and would turn a previously valid plan into an unauthorized export.
Post-production confirmation cannot undo a payroll disclosure and is not an authorization check.
A daily refresh leaves a long revocation window and still trusts stale operation handles.

feedback.reason: Discovery is a capability hint, not a durable grant. Revocation before invocation must take effect at the current resource boundary, before the export is produced.

options.text: Validate the current credential and scope immediately before execution, reject the stale export handle if authorization is gone, and audit the operation and subject.
Trust the discovery result and execute the queued export because the role and token were valid when the agent planned the operation.
Execute the export first and request user confirmation after the payroll file has been generated, so an analyst can cancel future requests.
Refresh the catalog once per day and allow all handles discovered before the refresh to run during the remaining interval.

questions.prompt: A long-running agent discovers a payroll export while the user is authorized, but the role is revoked before the queued invocation reaches the server. What should happen at execution?

constraints: The endpoint now serves six remote clients, bearer tokens, separate tenants, and user sessions.
Process and environment controls protected the old local child process only.
Issuer, audience, expiry, resource, scope, redirect, and invocation checks are available.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the server returns to a local child process with no remote exposure, use process and environment controls again, while keeping application authorization for sensitive operations.
details.errorCorrection: Remote clients are outside the protected process, so environment controls cannot bind a bearer token to its resource, tenant, or scope.
details.mechanismOrProperty: MCP's HTTP authorization requirements differ from stdio, where environment and process controls protect credentials. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: The transport boundary has changed, so local process controls no longer suffice; remote HTTP authorization and resource-server enforcement are required.
details.scenarioApplication: Use MCP HTTP authorization for the shared endpoint, validate issuer, audience, expiry, resource, and scopes at the resource server, and keep tenant binding and invocation checks independent of model arguments.
details.transfer: Reassess identity and resource authorization when moving from a local process boundary to shared protected HTTP; local environment trust does not identify remote tenants.

messages.text: Remote clients are outside the protected process, so environment controls cannot bind a bearer token to its resource, tenant, or scope.
Model-supplied arguments are not an authorization boundary; the resource server must validate the token and enforce tenant and operation scope.
Gateway authentication alone does not establish the resource, tenant, or invocation scope at the resource server for each operation.

feedback.reason: The same logical tools require a different authorization strategy once they cross from local process isolation to a remote shared resource.

options.text: Keep stdio environment controls because the server code and tool names did not change.
Pass the bearer token as a model argument and let the model select the tenant operation before the server executes it.
Terminate tokens at a shared gateway and trust the MCP server to execute any operation named by an authenticated client.
Use MCP HTTP authorization and explicitly validate issuer, audience, expiry, resource, and scopes at the resource server, independent of model arguments.

questions.prompt:
A local MCP server currently runs as a child process over stdio on a locked workstation. The same server is moved behind a shared HTTP endpoint for six remote clients, each with separate tenant scopes and user sessions.

Which authorization design fits the move from local stdio to shared remote HTTP?

constraints: The token expires during generation and the user's role is revoked before the download artifact is released.
The export state is resumable and can be bound to subject, resource, and scope.
The download is consequential and must be audited at completion.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If reauthorization succeeds with the same intended resource and scope, resume from the checkpoint; if it fails, retain the job as unavailable and do not expose the artifact.
details.errorCorrection: The token is expired and the role revoked before a consequential release; discovery-time authority cannot authorize a later artifact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The resource server must validate that the token is intended for it and must not forward a received token upstream to another resource server. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Authorization must be checked at each release boundary; a token valid at discovery cannot authorize a later artifact after expiry or revocation.
details.scenarioApplication: Persist the resumable job, stop release when the token or role is stale, reauthorize and recheck subject, resource, and scope before continuing, and publish only after the current authorization and audit record succeeds.
details.transfer: Bind resumable jobs to subject, resource, and scope, then reauthorize before releasing a durable artifact when permissions may have changed.

messages.text: Discovery-time authority cannot authorize a later artifact after token expiry and role revocation; logging after delivery is too late.
Starting over loses resumable state and audit continuity; reauthorization should preserve the intended resource and requester linkage.
A role check alone does not revalidate subject, resource, and scope for the artifact; all current authorization fields must pass before release.

feedback.reason: The case integrates token lifecycle with durable workflow state so a safe pause is explicit and resumable.

options.text: Pause release, persist the job, reauthorize, recheck subject, resource, and scope, then publish only with current authorization and audit.
Continue with the original token because its scope was valid when the tool was discovered, then log the expiry after delivery.
Delete the expired job and start a new export under the current session without linking it to the original requester or checkpoint.
Resume after checking only that the current role is present, leaving the original token and resource binding unchanged.

questions.prompt:

Raise the route deadline for the affected retry cases only, then compare their completion rate with the original route.
Allow the tool to coerce rejected arguments into its nearest valid schema, then monitor whether final-answer p95 falls below target.

questions.prompt: A release comparison shows model p95 fell from 3.2s to 2.0s. The attached call trace also shows schema-rejection retries rose from 0.4% to 3.7%; the task’s final validated answer p95 is 4.8s and the route limit is 4.0s. What should the release owner conclude?

constraints: The four lookups are independent, but the citation verifier depends on all of them.
The production target is 2.5 seconds p95, with errors and citation correctness measured under load.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Concurrency adds rate-limit and partial-failure handling, but it attacks the measured serialized bottleneck without weakening the citation dependency.
details.errorCorrection: Distinguish average from tail behavior and independent from dependent stages before moving work off the critical path.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent calls run concurrently and aggregate programmatically; the dependent verifier consumes the aggregate after a barrier, with concurrency limits protecting the backend.
details.scenarioApplication: Load-test the fanout at production concurrency, record per-call and aggregate failures, and accept the route only if citation quality and p95 satisfy the contract.
details.transfer: Parallelize proven independent calls, keep dependent checks behind an evidence barrier, and validate the complete path under real load.

messages.text: Verification before all lookups can miss the decisive policy clause and make a fast but unsupported citation.
The 3.8-second production tail violates the relevant service behavior even when the average is acceptable.
A fully parallel verifier lacks required evidence, and selecting the fastest result trades correctness for an unvalidated latency number.

feedback.reason: Only the lookup fanout is independent. A bounded concurrent stage can reduce the critical path while the verifier still waits for complete evidence and the service measures its production tail.

options.text: Start the verifier after the first lookup and have it infer the remaining policy evidence, then report the fast path as valid if the average stays below two seconds.
Optimize the 1.6-second average and keep the serialized fan-out, accepting a production p95 above the target because most requests finish sooner.
Run the four independent lookups concurrently with bounded concurrency, aggregate their results, invoke the verifier after the evidence barrier, and load-test p95, errors, and citation correctness.
Run lookup and verification calls concurrently and select the quickest completed verifier result even when it lacks one of the required policy responses.

questions.prompt: A claims request fans out to four independent policy lookups. Average latency is 1.6 seconds, but production p95 reaches 3.8 seconds because the integration serializes the lookups before a dependent citation verifier. Which redesign is justified?

constraints: Retry count and fallback behavior are part of the critical path.
Evidence may be absent when the deadline expires, so the user needs an explicit route or abstention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some requests will abstain or reach operations, but the service avoids an unbounded tail and makes missing evidence visible.
details.errorCorrection: Treat retries and fallback as product behavior in the latency and accuracy contract rather than hiding them from measurement.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A deadline and finite retry apply to an idempotent lookup; preserved artifacts can be reused, and an unavailable evidence state prevents the model from presenting unsupported certainty.
details.scenarioApplication: Benchmark one retry and the fallback or abstention path under timeout load, recording p95, citation support, and operations volume.
details.transfer: For retrieval stages, bound recovery, preserve evidence when available, and choose an explicit unavailable state when the correctness budget expires.

messages.text: Two retries already violate the observed tail, and an unvalidated fallback can meet speed by returning unsupported citations.
Removing retrieval abandons the authoritative evidence and does not create a safe answer path merely because it is fast.
Unbounded retries hide failures and measuring only successes gives no valid production tail or availability contract.

feedback.reason: Two retries create the measured tail, while the fallback is unvalidated. A bounded policy makes latency and evidence behavior explicit and evaluates both before rollout.

options.text: Retain both retries for availability, and when they expire return the fallback answer with its ordinary citation field without measuring whether the source supports it.

Set a per-stage deadline with at most one bounded retry for the idempotent lookup, preserve any retrieved artifact, and route or abstain when the evidence budget expires while measuring p95 and citation accuracy.
Remove the retrieval stage when the deadline is tight and let a fast model produce an answer from its trained knowledge, recording the response as a successful low-latency fallback.
Retry until retrieval succeeds and report latency only for successful calls, using the hidden tail as an operational reliability concern rather than a user contract.

questions.prompt: A retrieval tool is usually available within 800 ms, but transient timeouts trigger two full retries; p95 becomes 6.2 seconds and the fallback answer's citation accuracy is unmeasured. Which recovery policy should be tested?

constraints: The synchronous interface accepts only complete validated JSON within 1 second; it cannot parse partial deltas.
As an alternative to the synchronous interface, the approved asynchronous interface permits a 1-second acknowledgment and a 4-second complete validated callback.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The ledger receives its result later and needs callback state, but it never acts on partial or unvalidated JSON.
details.errorCorrection: Design delivery around the consumer's completion semantics, not perceived first-token speed or a deadline renegotiation that the scenario does not permit.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Streaming emits incremental events while SDK accumulation produces a complete message; the ledger contract requires the latter, so asynchronous delivery separates acceptance from validated completion.
details.scenarioApplication: Acknowledge the job, validate JSON and citations, deliver the complete callback by four seconds, and expose callback failure for operations rather than forwarding partial deltas.
details.transfer: When a downstream contract requires complete output, use a supported asynchronous acknowledgment path unless measured final completion fits the synchronous deadline.

messages.text: The ledger cannot parse partial deltas, and early bytes do not produce a complete validated result by its one-second requirement.
A fragment is not a valid complete payload and patching after rejection cannot satisfy the ledger's atomic input contract.
Changing the stated synchronous deadline is not an available design and would still expose a 2.4-second completion to a one-second consumer.

feedback.reason: First-byte latency does not satisfy a consumer that needs one complete validated payload within one second. The supplied asynchronous contract provides the appropriate acknowledgment and completion boundary.

options.text: Use the approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge acceptance within 1 second, then deliver the complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds; keep deltas out of the complete-payload parser.
Enable streaming and forward incremental deltas to the ledger, asking its parser to assemble a complete object once enough fields have arrived.
Send the first JSON-looking fragment synchronously and patch missing fields with a later callback if the ledger rejects or cannot parse the fragment.
Increase the synchronous deadline to the measured 2.4 seconds so the final validator can finish, even though the ledger contract specifies one second.

questions.prompt: A policy service emits text deltas after 180 ms, but final validated JSON with a citation check arrives at 2.4 seconds. A claims ledger offers two approved interfaces: synchronous delivery of one complete JSON payload within 1 second, or an approved asynchronous contract: acknowledge within 1 second and deliver complete validated JSON by callback within 4 seconds. Which delivery path satisfies the ledger?

constraints: The high-consequence field requires 98% accuracy; the efficient route measures 94% and the stronger route 98.5%.
The stronger route measures 3.4 seconds p95 against a 5-second asynchronous deadline.
A human queue can handle a small unresolved remainder, and cost still requires validation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the stronger route exceeded the deadline under production load, use a smaller targeted escalation or a reviewed asynchronous workflow rather than accepting 94%.
details.errorCorrection: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.
details.mechanismOrProperty: For complex accuracy-sensitive work, Anthropic recommends starting capability-first, then evaluating and optimizing efficiency. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Quality is the hard constraint for this workload and latency remains feasible, so the efficient-first route must reverse.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the stronger route for the consequence-bearing extraction, validate its end-to-end p95 and cost, and retain a human or explicit unavailable path for unresolved cases.
details.transfer: Reject routes below a hard field-quality floor even when faster; evaluate the qualifying route against its actual completion deadline and unresolved-case path.

messages.text: The held-out result already shows a four-point quality shortfall on a hard field, so waiting for incidents knowingly violates the floor.
The stronger route is feasible, but end-to-end p95 and cost still need validation before an unbounded production rollout.
A human path is needed for unresolved cases, but rejecting all feasible model assistance ignores the measured stronger route and its deadline.

feedback.reason: The quality floor and feasible deadline outweigh the efficiency advantage on this slice.

options.text: Use the efficient route because it is faster and escalate only after an incident demonstrates a problem.
Use the stronger route, validate end-to-end p95 and cost, and retain human or unavailable handling for unresolved cases.
Use the stronger route for every request and approve it immediately because its held-out accuracy clears the floor.
Send every document to the human queue and skip model evaluation because the field is consequential.

questions.prompt:
A tax-document extractor must maintain 98% accuracy on a high-consequence field and has a 5-second asynchronous deadline. The efficient route is 1.1 seconds p95 and 94%; the stronger route is 3.4 seconds p95 and 98.5% at higher cost.

Which model route meets the hard accuracy and deadline requirements?

constraints: Sequential execution measures 2.4 seconds p95 and $0.04; bounded parallel execution measures 1.5 seconds and $0.08 on the same mix.
Both routes meet the 2.5-second p95 and 96% quality floor; the average cost budget is $0.05.
Premium cases are 15% of traffic and value the 0.9-second saving at $0.20 versus $0.01 for ordinary cases; premium-only cost averages $0.046.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If bounded parallel p95 rose above 2.5 seconds under production load, remove it from the affected slice and use the explicit sequential or asynchronous contract; if premium value fell below the incremental cost, serialize that slice.
details.errorCorrection: Global parallelism costs $0.08 on average and breaches the $0.05 budget, while global serialization gives up the premium benefit despite room for the $0.046 segmented route.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Independent subtasks can run in parallel and be aggregated programmatically; bounded concurrency and load-tested tail behavior are application constraints supplied by this scenario. The scenario's mechanism is governed by this decisive constraint: Global parallelism passes p95 but exceeds the average cost budget. Premium-only parallelism produces a $0.046 average cost and captures value exceeding its extra cost on that slice.
details.scenarioApplication: Use bounded parallel checks for premium cases where the $0.20 value exceeds the incremental cost, use the sequential route for ordinary cases, and monitor p95, spend, and accepted quality by slice.
details.transfer: Use bounded parallelism on the segment where measured latency value exceeds its incremental cost, while checking quality and the weighted global spend.

messages.text: Global parallelism costs $0.08 on average and breaches the $0.05 budget despite passing latency.
Global serialization stays within budget but gives up a premium benefit whose measured value exceeds the incremental cost.
Volume does not establish value; the premium slice and complete-mix budget determine the bounded route.

feedback.reason: The same-unit latency measurements and hard p95 budget show both routes are feasible; business value and cost, not an infeasible default, determine where parallelism belongs.

options.text: Parallelize every request because it saves 0.9 seconds under the tested p95.
Serialize every request because parallel calls cost more than sequential calls.
Parallelize bounded checks only for premium cases, serialize ordinary cases, and monitor value, p95, spend, and quality by slice.
Choose parallelism from traffic volume alone, sending the largest slice to parallel checks without comparing slice value and average cost.

questions.prompt:
A support workflow can run three independent model checks in parallel. On the same request mix, sequential execution has a measured 2.4-second p95 and costs $0.04 per case; parallel execution has a measured 1.5-second p95 and costs $0.08. The hard service p95 budget is 2.5 seconds, and premium cases are 15% of traffic.

Which concurrency policy captures the premium value without breaching the global budget?

constraints: The service has a 3-second p95 target and a 95% critical-field quality floor.
A quality-based escalation path may be used only after measuring the combined end-to-end behavior.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A selective upgrade adds routing complexity and occasional higher latency, but it can improve difficult claims without violating the routine service target.
details.errorCorrection: Treat accuracy, latency, and cost as a joint configuration decision and measure added calls instead of reasoning from isolated model benchmarks.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A workload router can use confidence or a validated slice to invoke the stronger model; the acceptance gate measures both critical-field quality and the full p95 and cost.
details.scenarioApplication: Benchmark representative and edge claims, retain the efficient default, and accept escalation only if the routed path meets the 3-second and quality floors under load.
details.transfer: Choose the simplest measured configuration that clears the task floor, then test targeted complexity only where its incremental value is demonstrated.

messages.text: The stronger model misses the stated p95 target for every claim, so its accuracy advantage cannot justify a universal default without a new contract.

feedback.reason: The efficient candidate meets the latency target and has a measured quality baseline; a targeted stronger path may recover hard cases, but its route must be evaluated end to end rather than assumed.

options.text: Use the stronger model for all claims, accepting the 4.8-second p95 as the price of its two-point accuracy gain and revisiting the SLA later.
Use the efficient candidate as the default after holdout validation, then test confidence-based escalation to the stronger model with end-to-end p95, quality, and cost measurement.
Add an unmeasured second validation call to the efficient model and infer that its 2.1-second model time leaves enough room for the full path.
Route every low-confidence claim to the stronger model using an unvalidated threshold, then judge the design from its average latency rather than the tail.

questions.prompt: An insurance intake service must extract twelve fields within a 3-second p95 target. An efficient model reaches 2.1 seconds and 95% critical-field accuracy; a stronger model reaches 4.8 seconds and 97%. Which configuration should be evaluated first?

constraints: Synthesis and citation quality have an acceptance floor.
Cost can be optimized after the accepted outcome is measured.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Capability-first evaluation may spend more initially, but it prevents cheap unsupported summaries and makes later savings defensible.
details.errorCorrection: Use the absence of an interactive SLA to optimize efficiency deliberately, not to skip the quality and evidence checks that make the batch useful.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A representative report set evaluates synthesis and citation, while cost and throughput measurements show whether a lower-cost route preserves the accepted outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Review reports before distribution, compare candidate model or staged paths, and promote a cheaper default only after its citation and synthesis floors hold.
details.transfer: For offline workloads, establish the accepted outcome first, then optimize model tier or staging against quality, evidence, and spend.

messages.text: Immediate cheapest selection can distribute unsupported summaries and removes the quality gate that defines batch value.
No interactive SLA does not make quality or spend irrelevant; a permanent strongest model may waste budget without an outcome comparison.

Without a representative quality and citation baseline, cost comparisons cannot show whether a configuration preserves the accepted outcome.
Without a conditional quality gate, a cheaper route can become the default while its summaries or citations fall below the required floor.

feedback.reason: Batch removes an interactive latency constraint but does not remove quality or spend trade-offs. A measured baseline and conditional efficiency test protect the distribution gate.

options.text: Choose the lowest-cost model immediately and treat citation review as an optional editorial step after distribution.
Measure synthesis quality and citation support on representative reports, then compare total spend and throughput for candidate configurations.
Choose the strongest model permanently because batch work has no interactive latency requirement.
Optimize document count processed per night and infer summary quality from whether every report received an output.
Test a lower-cost model or staged route only when its measured summaries and citations continue to meet the accepted outcome floor.

questions.prompt: A research team produces nightly summaries of 500 long scientific reports. There is no interactive latency SLA, but synthesis quality, citation support, and total spend are reviewed before distribution. Which TWO configuration principles fit the batch workload? Select TWO.

constraints: Operational metadata must support latency and tool diagnosis.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some incidents require an approved content sample and may remain partly unresolved, but default logging does not expose protected data unnecessarily.
details.errorCorrection: Treat privacy as a telemetry boundary with explicit sampling and retention, not as a reason to erase the execution graph.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Run and span IDs, timings, configuration, tool names, status, and redacted outcome fields reveal causal behavior; content samples are separately authorized and time-limited.
details.scenarioApplication: Trace a triage run and its tool calls by ID, redact patient fields, restrict any incident sample to approved investigators, and delete it on the defined schedule.
details.transfer: For sensitive AI systems, preserve stage-level operational evidence by default and gate content capture with purpose, access, and retention controls.

messages.text: Indefinite raw capture violates minimization and retention boundaries and creates a larger breach surface than the diagnosis requires.
Suppressing traces removes the timing and tool evidence needed to diagnose production failures.
Model name and count cannot explain a slow span or wrong tool, and memory-based reconstruction is incomplete.

feedback.reason: The default must retain enough signal to locate slow or wrong stages without creating an unrestricted patient transcript. Metadata-first tracing with controlled samples balances diagnosis and minimization.

options.text: Log every patient prompt, retrieved passage, and tool result indefinitely so investigators can reconstruct any run without requesting special access.
Disable tracing by default and retain only monthly uptime and volume, avoiding protected content at the cost of stage-level diagnosis.
Keep correlated metadata and redacted outcomes by default, and capture sampled content only under explicit access, purpose, and retention controls.
Store model name and request count, then ask clinicians to describe the slow or wrong tool run from memory during the incident review.

details.errorCorrection: Do not treat a provider finish event as proof of end-user delivery or persistence.

details.scenarioApplication: Instrument stage transitions with shared operation and attempt identifiers, outcome timestamps, and bounded metadata.

options.text: Give every worker the parent’s single request ID and omit worker identifiers.
Link worker and parent attempts with task, source, and merge identifiers.
Use only each provider request ID because it is globally unique.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not collect raw sensitive payloads when metadata answers the diagnostic question.
details.errorCorrection: Increasing ordinary head sampling may still miss very rare outcomes.

messages.text: This is unnecessarily broad and retains content that is not needed to understand authorization failures.

feedback.reason: Rare high-value failures may need targeted capture in addition to statistically representative traffic sampling. Add a privacy-bounded denial event with the decision reason category and relevant operation dimensions.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not retry a consequential action with a new identity to escape duplicate detection; reconcile through the service’s idempotency or status contract.
details.errorCorrection: Dispatch, durable commit, and duplicate denial are separate events; a later denial cannot undo the first commit or make the retry a second success.

details.scenarioApplication: Link both attempts to the same operation identifier; show the first commit as operation success and the later duplicate denial as an attempt-level event.

messages.text: The later denial does not undo the already committed first attempt; a new ID could repeat the side effect.
Dispatch alone is not commit evidence, and suppressing the retry hides a relevant duplicate-attempt outcome.

options.text: Keep the operation marked failed because its latest attempt was denied, then ask the caller to retry with a new operation ID if it still needs the action.

Mark success at the first dispatch and collapse later attempts into that result, since the retry denial did not change the durable state.
Treat the retry as a second successful operation because its request was accepted, while keeping the first timeout as a separate trace failure.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep version metadata separate from conversation content; do not broaden content retention to solve an attribution gap.
details.errorCorrection: More examples, operator guesses, or a joint rollback do not attribute the regression; link each quality outcome to both independently changed artifacts.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Causal diagnosis depends on observing the independently changing artifacts that produced an outcome.

details.errorCorrection: Browser total and model time alone do not identify the intervening path.

messages.text: Total time shows the user impact but cannot isolate queue wait from downstream processing.

feedback.reason: Asynchronous boundaries need trace-context propagation and stage timing to attribute latency. Link the worker span to the enqueueing request and report queue wait separately from execution stages.

details.errorCorrection: Do not infer user-visible completion from the provider’s stop reason or first-token signal.

details.errorCorrection: A shared request ID alone merges the retries; payload logging adds privacy exposure, while suppressing attempts removes the failure path.

details.scenarioApplication: Preserve the operation ID across retries but give each attempt its own span, status, and terminal marker, then link the accepted result to its attempt.

feedback.reason: A logical operation and its retries are different trace scopes. Attempt-level correlation shows where each provisional and terminal event came from without requiring raw customer content.

options.text: Log each full prompt and event body so the duplicated records can be compared later.

Suppress all retry events and retain only the final HTTP status to keep dashboards concise.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Sampling improves the number of observed executions but does not fix a missing correlation contract.

messages.text: Content retention is broader than needed and citations alone do not link each worker attempt and merge outcome to the parent.

options.text: Carry a parent operation ID through each worker task and record task, attempt, source reference, and merge outcome links.

details.errorCorrection: A fixed tool order rejects valid solutions, prose does not prove repository state, and shared production trials contaminate evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends clean isolated trials, outcome-based grading, deterministic checks where possible, and calibrated judgment for nuanced dimensions.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the repair in an isolated checkout, execute security and regression checks, and send the diff and rubric to a calibrated reviewer.
details.transfer: Grade required outcomes and safety boundaries, then add independent judgment only for dimensions deterministic checks cannot observe.

messages.text: A valid repair can use a different sequence, so sequence identity would be a brittle proxy.
An explanation can claim a fix without changing the vulnerable artifact.
Shared state contaminates trials and risks changing production during evaluation.
Deterministic checks verify the concrete security and regression contract.
A calibrated independent review can assess nuanced quality without turning one path into the requirement.

feedback.reason: Artifact checks prove the known security contract, while calibrated review covers nuanced behavior without requiring one brittle implementation path.

options.text: Grade the changed repository with deterministic security and regression checks, including static analysis.
Require the agent to use one recorded tool order even when the resulting artifact is equivalent.
Score the final explanation only and infer that the repository changed correctly.
Run all trials in the shared production checkout so the patch is realistic.
Use a calibrated rubric or fresh review for interaction and code-quality dimensions that automated checks cannot decide.

questions.prompt: A code-review agent repairs a vulnerable authentication handler in an isolated repository, and valid implementations may use different tool sequences. Select TWO grading controls.

constraints: The task and grader disagree about the required path.
A reference implementation can test the harness contract.
Valid agent outputs were observed at another path.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the reference solution passed and the task contract were explicit, a 0% result would justify investigating model behavior or tool access.
details.errorCorrection: A larger model or manual impressions cannot repair a contradictory contract, and removing the path requirement makes the evaluation unfaithful.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic warns that ambiguous specifications create evaluation noise and recommends a reference solution to verify task and grader configuration.
details.scenarioApplication: Correct the declared path or grader expectation, run the reference migration, and only then compare model results.
details.transfer: Validate the evaluator’s own contract with a known-good result before interpreting a model score.

messages.text: Model size cannot resolve an unstated or contradictory file-path contract.
Removing a real output requirement hides the harness defect instead of fixing it.
Anecdotal impressions cannot establish whether the automated task and grader agree.

feedback.reason: The score is uninterpretable until task and grader agree and a known working solution passes the harness.

options.text: Switch to a larger model so it may infer the grader’s hidden path.
Remove the path assertion so the current score improves.
Align task and grader; make the reference solution pass, then rerun.
Average the 0% result with manual impressions from the engineers who ran the trials.

questions.prompt: A coding-agent evaluation reports 0% pass across 100 migration trials because the task omits the required file path while the grader expects one exact path. A known working solution can be placed at the grader’s path. What should happen first?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A separate holdout can be periodically refreshed or access-controlled so repeated tuning does not turn it into another development set.
details.errorCorrection: Avoid both extremes: do not discard useful regression fixtures, and do not treat them as independent generalization evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An evaluation set’s interpretation depends on its relationship to prompt examples and tuning data; fixture reuse is not universally invalid, but it limits what a score establishes.
details.scenarioApplication: Label the 24-case score as development/regression evidence and construct a disjoint holdout with representative claims, layouts, and source provenance.
details.transfer: Match each dataset’s use and independence boundary to the claim made from its score.

messages.text: Known fixtures can still detect regressions on their intended examples; they simply cannot stand in for independent generalization evidence.
Synthetic origin does not make cases independent once the exact examples are included in the prompt.
Paraphrased descendants can carry the same answers and patterns, so they do not automatically create an independent evaluation set.

feedback.reason: These fixtures still serve a valid known-case regression purpose, but their direct reuse in the prompt contaminates a claim about unseen-case performance. Maintain the regression suite and evaluate a separate, provenance-checked holdout.

options.text: Keep reused fixtures for regression; use unseen, independently sourced cases to support generalization claims.
Delete the regression suite because any fixture that appears in a prompt is unusable for future testing.
Keep reporting the 100% as holdout accuracy because the prompts are synthetic rather than production text.
Generate paraphrases from the same 24 cases and call them a holdout without checking whether they preserve the same cues.

questions.prompt: A team uses 24 public synthetic cases both as few-shot prompt examples and as a continuous regression suite. Those cases catch formatting breaks after a prompt edit, but product leaders now cite the 100% score as evidence of performance on unseen claims. What is the correct interpretation and next evaluation step?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: After calibration, use automated or single-reviewer grading for clearer cases and retain double review where judgments remain consequential or ambiguous.
details.errorCorrection: Seniority, averaging, or a larger aggregate does not establish that reviewers share the intended boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Human review is a measurement process; agreement should be assessed on the dimensions that matter, not only as a global percentage.
details.scenarioApplication: Create examples for mixed source support and partial completion, double-score those cases blind, record why disagreements resolve one way, and report agreement by category.
details.transfer: Locate disagreement clusters, refine the rubric at that boundary, and verify calibration before expanding grader use.

messages.text: Discarding the disagreements hides a systematic rubric boundary and prevents the team from knowing whether the lead is applying it consistently.
An average can conceal a categorical disagreement about evidence or partial completion rather than resolve its meaning.
More cases do not correct an ambiguous category boundary; they may simply dilute the problematic slice in the aggregate.

feedback.reason: Agreement is high overall but fails on a consequential, identifiable slice. Improve the rubric and adjudication record for that slice before using the score as a stable grader.

options.text: Use the lead reviewer’s labels as ground truth and discard the independent ratings.
Average the numeric scores from both reviewers and treat the mean as an adjudicated label.
Adjudicate disagreement, report uncertain outcomes, and test a revised rubric on held-out mixed cases.
Add more cases until the overall 92% agreement rises, leaving the rubric unchanged.

questions.prompt: Two trained reviewers independently grade 80 long-form assistant answers with the same rubric. They agree on 92% overall, but disagree on 31% of answers involving mixed evidence and partial completion; a lead reviewer currently resolves every disagreement without recording a reason. What should the evaluation team improve first?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automated entailment checks are themselves imperfect, so report their validated scope and retain sampling on difficult claims.
details.errorCorrection: A citation string can be well-formed yet irrelevant; swapping all checks for one broad judge may hide both kinds of defects.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evaluation needs a grader for each assertion; syntactic validity and factual support are different outcomes.
details.scenarioApplication: Bind claim spans to retrieved passages where feasible, evaluate the support relation, and send ambiguous cases to a calibrated reviewer while retaining JSON/schema tests.
details.transfer: List what each grader actually observes, then add coverage for high-impact assertions it misses.

messages.text: Removing known deterministic checks loses useful coverage, and one opaque score may reproduce the same citation blind spot.
Citation length does not establish that the cited span supports the claim.
Document membership alone does not prove that the cited passage entails the answer.

feedback.reason: The grader currently tests citation presence and output shape, not evidence support. Keep the deterministic format checks and add a distinct support assertion with calibrated review where entailment is not mechanically decidable.

options.text: Audit whether cited passages support each claim; citation presence alone does not establish correctness.
Replace the structural grader with a single LLM judge that returns pass or fail for the whole answer.
Require longer citations so at least one sentence is likely to contain the right evidence.
Treat a non-empty source ID as sufficient because the model has already selected a retrieved document.

questions.prompt: A customer-support evaluation’s deterministic grader checks valid JSON, required field names, and whether every response has a non-empty citation string. A release scores 100%, but reviewers find citations that point to unrelated passages. Which harness change best addresses the blind spot?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The added sample does not imply equal deployment volumes; weights should follow a documented production population and be revisited when it shifts.
details.errorCorrection: Neither a simple presence check nor a weighted average resolves the small-slice evidence gap.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A dataset should reflect its intended population while still exposing subgroups whose errors carry distinct risk.
details.scenarioApplication: Collect additional Japanese examples across relevant tasks, preserve English and Spanish coverage, publish per-language estimates with uncertainty, and separately show a production-weighted overall result.
details.transfer: Report both representative overall performance and the slices whose failures the aggregate could conceal.

messages.text: Presence alone does not make the sample representative, and five Japanese cases cannot establish its error rate reliably.
A weighted aggregate can reflect traffic mix but can still hide the severe Japanese failure and its uncertainty.
Equal counts may help estimate slices but do not represent production weighting, and removing common cases discards relevant behavior.

feedback.reason: The current sample is dominated beyond the production mix and under-samples the language with the observed severe error. Expand and label the strata, report slice uncertainty, and keep an aggregate from masking a consequential slice.

options.text: Keep the current overall score because the evaluation contains all three languages.
Sample to the production language mix and separately evaluate the underrepresented high-risk language.
Weight Japanese to 10% and report only the weighted average so the slice has the same influence as in production.
Add many Japanese cases and remove English cases until all language counts are equal, then report only the unweighted mean.

questions.prompt: A production assistant is used 70% in English, 20% in Spanish, and 10% in Japanese. The current 100-case evaluation is 95% English and reports a 94% overall score; Japanese has only five cases and one severe unsupported answer. What should the next dataset and report do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a group is too small to estimate reliably, add cases or report uncertainty instead of silently dropping it.
details.errorCorrection: Do not equate refusal with failure or omit refusals and partial outputs from the report.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A task and grader must define how abstention and partial evidence contribute to outcomes; the denominator should match the eligible request population.
details.scenarioApplication: Label evidence sufficiency, grade supported answers on the answerable group, appropriate refusals on the unanswerable group, and qualification on partial-evidence cases; show all three results and the overall decision rule.
details.transfer: Make every valid completion mode observable in the grader and denominator.

messages.text: This excludes two required behaviors and can hide unsupported answers or inappropriate refusals.
