That incorrectly penalizes appropriate refusals when evidence is absent and does not distinguish partial support.
Removing those cases abandons explicit product requirements and biases the evaluation toward fully answerable requests.

feedback.reason: The policy defines valid behavior for answerable, unanswerable and partially supported requests. Excluding two groups makes the 98% result incomplete; score each declared outcome and publish the category breakdown.

options.text: Accuracy on the 120 answered requests only, since refusals and partial answers do not contain a factual claim.
Report answerable, unanswerable and partial cases separately against their appropriate outcomes.
One overall pass rate that counts all refusals and partial answers as failures.
Remove the unanswerable and partial-evidence cases so the remaining task is easier to grade.

questions.prompt: A document assistant is tested on 200 requests: 120 have sufficient evidence, 40 are deliberately unanswerable, and 40 have only partial evidence. The report shows 98% accuracy after excluding refusals and partial responses from its denominator. Product policy requires supported answers, appropriate refusals, and explicit qualification when evidence is incomplete. What should the harness measure?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the release owner revises the policy threshold, evaluate that as an explicit new criterion with its own decision record.
details.errorCorrection: Do not substitute a large relative lift for the stated minimum or lower the threshold after observing results.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evaluation reports should retain both absolute criteria and comparative deltas; a gain over a weak baseline does not prove an acceptable outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Report the +13-point change and the 91% absolute score separately, then check each required slice against the no-more-than-2-point regression rule.
details.transfer: Use comparative deltas to understand improvement and absolute gates to decide whether the result is fit for use.

messages.text: A relative improvement does not satisfy the 93% absolute pass condition.
The contract includes a slice-regression bound, which must be checked and cannot be waived by the aggregate gain.
Changing the release criterion after seeing the result would redefine success rather than evaluate against the existing contract.

feedback.reason: The candidate improves substantially over baseline but remains below the absolute 93% gate. Relative change and release readiness answer different questions.

options.text: Release the new model because its 13-point improvement is large.
Release only to the overall cohort because every individual slice is less important than the gain.
Require the absolute gate; report relative gain separately as a secondary comparison.
Lower the threshold to the prior model’s 79% so the comparison reflects the baseline.

questions.prompt: A new model raises the evaluation score from 78% to 91% on a 300-case suite. The release contract requires at least 93% absolute pass and no more than a 2-point regression on any required slice. The prior model scores 79% on the same suite. What does the evaluation support?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keep structural assertions deterministic where possible and use the calibrated grader only for dimensions that need judgment.
details.errorCorrection: Do not assume unchanged topic means unchanged grading validity, and do not replace evidence checks with fluency/style penalties.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Model-based graders are flexible but need calibration for the actual task and outcome dimensions they score.
details.scenarioApplication: Build blinded labels for complete answers, partial evidence, appropriate refusal and citation support; compare grader decisions and inspect disagreements before using it in a release decision.
details.transfer: Revalidate a grader when the task shape or outcome population changes.

messages.text: The task and outcome distribution changed, and the observed blind spot shows the old calibration does not cover the new behavior.
Style or confidence language is not a reliable substitute for evidence support, partial completion or appropriate refusal.
That omits newly required outcomes and would make the release comparison incomplete.

feedback.reason: The grader’s calibration set covered a narrower answer shape, and the spot check identifies a blind spot in newly added outcomes. Validate it on representative expert-labeled cases before relying on the scores.

options.text: Keep the grader because the model and answer domain are unchanged.
Calibrate the grader on refusal, partial-answer and citation outcomes before comparing systems.
Add a stricter confidence-word penalty so the grader rejects any answer that sounds uncertain.
Use the grader only on the easiest complete answers and exclude all partial/refusal cases from the comparison.

questions.prompt: An LLM grader was calibrated on short, complete support answers. The product now accepts multi-turn cases with partial evidence, refusals, and citations; a spot check finds that the grader rewards fluent unsupported guesses in this new set. What should happen before using its scores for the next release comparison?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A group-disjoint set may have fewer examples and wider uncertainty; collect additional suppliers rather than silently returning to a row split.
details.errorCorrection: More rows from the same groups or a different invoice number do not create an independent new-supplier test.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evaluation independence follows the unit that can share answer cues or layout structure; row-level randomization can leak across correlated documents.
details.scenarioApplication: Partition by supplier and template family, inspect monthly revision lineage for near-duplicates, and report the current split as within-known-group performance.
details.transfer: Choose split boundaries that isolate the source of generalization the score is meant to support.

messages.text: The holdout still shares supplier and layout groups with tuning, so more rows mainly increase precision for the wrong population.
Changing invoice numbers does not prevent shared supplier templates and revision cues from crossing the split.
Removing training groups after seeing the existing score changes the evaluation and still requires a fresh, group-aware run.

feedback.reason: The row-level split tests new invoices from known supplier and template families, not generalization to new suppliers. Preserve it for that narrower purpose and build a group-disjoint evaluation for the claim leaders want to make.

options.text: Keep the random split and increase the number of rows, since each invoice is a separate example.
Keep random-split regression; add a supplier-disjoint holdout for new-supplier generalization.
Move only the newest invoice from each supplier to holdout; shared template families do not affect generalization if invoice numbers differ.
Remove all repeated suppliers from training and report the current holdout score without rerunning it.

questions.prompt: A claims extractor is tuned on 600 invoice rows from 12 suppliers. The random 20% holdout contains different invoices, but every supplier and document-template family appears in both tuning and holdout; several suppliers reuse near-identical layouts across monthly revisions. The team wants to claim performance on new suppliers. What should the next evaluation do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Adjudicate representative cases, test the revised rubric on held-out examples, then rerun both candidates under the same definitions.
details.errorCorrection: Neither all refusals nor all answers are automatically correct.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Evaluation criteria should reflect supported task outcomes and label definitions.
details.scenarioApplication: Tuning against the scored refusal cases risks adapting to the test set rather than validating general behavior.
details.transfer: Keep evaluator version and denominator consistent for comparisons.

messages.text: A separate table still leaves the primary comparison unable to distinguish unsafe abstention from a missed supported handoff.
This treats two different workflow outcomes alike and leaves the handoff contract outside the candidate comparison.
Reusing evaluation examples for tuning and comparison leaks the test into development even if the held-back subset is smaller.

feedback.reason: The evaluator collapsed distinct outcomes into one label. A calibrated rubric must distinguish safe refusal, correct handoff, and avoidable failure before it can compare systems.

options.text: Keep the old answer-rate measure as the primary headline, but add a separate refusal and handoff table so the new rubric does not interrupt the trend.
Define and adjudicate answerable, unsafe, and handoff outcomes; test the rubric on a held-out set before comparing candidates.
Score a refusal as correct when the request is unsafe, and score a handoff as neutral until the receiving team reports an outcome.
Use the newly observed refusal cases for prompt tuning, then reserve a smaller random subset of the same cases to compare the revised score.

questions.prompt: An evaluator update turns every refusal into a failure. Reviewers find that some cases are genuinely unsafe to answer, while others require a supported handoff; the candidate’s answer rate rises but the new score falls. What is the best next evaluation step?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Preserve separate correctness and safety outcomes so one does not mask the other.
details.errorCorrection: Disabling the block would increase risk and is unnecessary for scoring the attempt.
details.mechanismOrProperty: An outcome-only grader misses unsafe intermediate behavior when a policy control blocks the attempted action.
details.scenarioApplication: The test should record whether disallowed tools were attempted, not only whether side effects completed.
details.transfer: Evaluate the complete tool-using trajectory when the task includes side-effect boundaries.

messages.text: A separate count does not prevent a prohibited attempt from receiving a passing safety grade.
The attempted deletion crossed the prohibited boundary even though the environment prevented its effect.
Removing the control allows a real destructive action; evaluation should detect the attempted call while preserving the safeguard.

feedback.reason: The final text hides a prohibited action attempt. The evaluation must score the action trace as well as answer correctness.

options.text: Keep the run passed because the control blocked the deletion; add a separate counter showing how often the agent proposes a prohibited mutation.
Keep final-answer grading and add a tool-use penalty only when a prohibited call returns data or changes state.
Add trace-based safety criteria that fail prohibited mutation attempts, even when the environment blocks them and the final answer is correct.
Use a reversible sandbox without the blocking stub, then restore the test data after the run to observe the agent’s actual behavior.

questions.prompt: A billing-agent test ends with the correct read-only report. The tool trace shows it first attempted `delete_customer`; a policy stub blocked the call. The evaluator grades only the final text and marks the run passed. What should change?

constraints: Fixture origin can be traced and near-duplicates removed.
A reference solution can verify the task and grader before a split is frozen.
The holdout must represent unseen layouts.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: With no tuning and complete production representation, a separate holdout would add less evidence, though a reference check would remain useful.
details.errorCorrection: Duplicating tuned templates and postponing unseen cases inflate evidence without testing generalization; wording similarity is not the extraction contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a known working reference solution to verify task and grader configuration; provenance, deduplication, and holdout separation are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Freeze a deduplicated holdout after checking its source and layout distribution, run the reference, and publish holdout results separately from tuning results.
details.transfer: Protect evaluation evidence from tuning leakage and validate the frozen split before using it to compare systems.

messages.text: Copies increase volume but preserve the same tuning leakage.
A tuning score cannot estimate unseen-layout behavior.
Surface wording is not a reliable proxy for extracted fields or claim state.

feedback.reason: Tuned examples cannot be the sole evidence for generalization; an independent, traceable holdout tests unseen layouts and a valid task/grader contract.

options.text: Add more copies of tuned templates so the 100% score has a larger sample.
Use a provenance-tracked, deduplicated holdout and validate a reference before scoring it.
Use the tuning score as the release baseline and add unseen layouts only after deployment.
Replace deterministic field checks with a judge that rewards similar wording to the tuned examples.

questions.prompt: A claims extractor scores 100% after prompt tuning, but tuning and scored fixtures share templates and the suite has no provenance or frozen holdout. Production contains unseen document layouts. Which evaluation change is best?

constraints: Trial-level tool responses, transcripts, and outcomes are retained.
The harness can identify whether external state differed.
The team needs stability evidence rather than a best-run headline.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If runs and tools were deterministic and the reference passed, one clean trial per case could be sufficient for this harness.
details.errorCorrection: A best run, untraceable average, or removal of the external dependency discards the production behavior being evaluated.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic defines evaluations through tasks, trials, graders, transcripts, outcomes, and a harness, supporting explicit evidence across each trial.
details.scenarioApplication: Repeat each case under recorded lookup conditions, retain transcripts, classify failures, and report a distribution rather than the most favorable aggregate.
details.transfer: When outcomes vary, preserve trial-level evidence and report variance and causes instead of compressing them into a lucky score.

messages.text: A favorable run confuses a sample with stable capability and omits the observed variance.
Averages without state evidence cannot explain which failures were external or model-driven.
Removing a production dependency changes the evaluated contract rather than diagnosing it.

feedback.reason: The run variance is itself evidence; repeated isolated trials and retained state reveal whether failures come from stochastic behavior or external conditions.

options.text: Publish the 9/10 run as the baseline and rerun only after users report failures.
Average the best and worst runs without retaining the tool responses.
Repeat isolated trials and report distributions with retained transcripts and tool state.
Disable the external lookup and report the deterministic score as production capability while documenting the changed environment.

questions.prompt: A tool-using agent passes 9 of 10 trials on one run, then ranges from 5 to 9 on repeated runs because an external lookup is variable. What should the harness report?

constraints: Option order can be randomized in the harness.
Human labels and judge rationales can be retained for calibration.
Objective assertions can use deterministic checks.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every assertion had a deterministic checker and no model judgment were used, presentation order would not affect evaluation.
details.errorCorrection: Reproducibility of a biased order, shortening answers, or preserving the favored position does not test the intended code behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends deterministic graders where possible and human review for validation and calibration; order and verbosity probes are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Randomize option order, compare judge labels with calibrated human labels, retain rationales, and route material disagreement for review.
details.transfer: Validate an evaluator for bias against the target outcome before trusting its aggregate scores.

messages.text: A repeatable position or verbosity bias remains a validity problem.
Editing answers to fit a biased judge changes the candidates instead of fixing the evaluator.
Consistently favoring one position makes the order confound permanent.

feedback.reason: A stable score can still be systematically biased by position and verbosity, so the judge needs controlled presentation and calibration against the intended outcome.

options.text: Keep the judge because its average score remains stable across repeated runs and the current presentation order is consistent for every candidate.
Shorten every candidate answer until the verbosity effect disappears.
Put the preferred answer first consistently so the judge’s ranking is reproducible.
Randomize order, calibrate judge labels against human review, and use deterministic checks for objective claims.

questions.prompt: A model judge rates the same code explanations higher when they are longer and when the preferred answer is listed first; calibrated human reviewers disagree. What should the team change first?

constraints: The transcript records the denied destructive call and its real target.
The final report and allowed read path pass their outcome checks.
The contract treats an unauthorized attempt as a safety failure.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the first call were an allowed read_customer operation producing the same report, the varied sequence could pass within the authorized action set.
details.errorCorrection: A denial is not evidence of respectful tool choice, intent is not observable proof, and requiring one read sequence confuses safety with path identity.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic lists tool-call verification among code-based graders, supports binary or hybrid scoring, and cautions that rigidly requiring one valid path is brittle; the prohibition is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Mark the safety gate failed, preserve the transcript and report-test result, and allow authorized read-only variations among otherwise compliant trials.
details.transfer: When a task prohibits an action, grade attempted actions as a separate gate even if a downstream control blocks the effect.

messages.text: A downstream denial prevents state change but does not make the attempted delete compliant.
Intent cannot override the recorded action and explicit prohibition.
The contract prohibits the action itself; exact path matching is unnecessary for authorized reads.

feedback.reason: The attempted destructive action violates an explicit safety gate even though downstream policy prevented state change; report correctness can remain a separate dimension.

options.text: Fail for the unauthorized destructive attempt; record separate credit for the correct report.
Pass because the policy server blocked the delete and the report is exact.
Pass if a reviewer believes the agent intended to test authorization.
Require the exact read-query sequence and ignore the denied call because sequence is the only objective evidence.

questions.prompt: A coding agent must produce a correct read-only billing report. It first calls delete_customer with a real ID; the policy server denies the call. It then uses an allowed read query and returns the exact report, and all report tests pass. The contract prohibits attempting destructive actions. What result is correct?

constraints: The tool-safety cases, ordinary cases, tool-call traces, and independent evaluator are available; the destructive behavior is governed by a separate guardrail.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the evaluation already contained a provenance-tracked, balanced high-impact slice with independent traces and passing safety gates, the ordinary aggregate could be combined with it for release.
details.errorCorrection: Production monitoring would discover a high-blast-radius failure after release, and aggregate accuracy hides the missing trigger/refusal behavior. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends testing cases where a behavior should occur and where it should not to avoid one-sided optimization. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Expand or hold out a risk-stratified set with both allowed and refused destructive-action cases, grade tool traces deterministically, and block the release until the safety slice passes its own gate.
details.transfer: Give rare consequential behaviors their own balanced tests and release boundary instead of letting volume hide them.

messages.text: Production monitoring would discover a high-blast-radius failure only after release.
More ordinary cases cannot compensate for missing positive and negative coverage of the dangerous behavior.
A holistic score does not supply deterministic evidence that the tool was allowed or refused under the right condition.
Required control: Add a risk-stratified safety slice with balanced cases where the destructive action is allowed and where it must be refused.
Required control: Grade tool traces deterministically and block release until the high-impact safety slice passes its own gate.

feedback.reason: Expand or hold out a risk-stratified set with both allowed and refused destructive-action cases, grade tool traces deterministically, and block the release until the safety slice passes its own gate. The decisive constraint is A rare high-impact behavior needs balanced positive and negative cases before the aggregate can support release; ordinary-case volume cannot compensate for missing safety coverage.

options.text: Ship because the 99% aggregate and ordinary-case tool traces pass, then monitor destructive attempts in production.
Add more ordinary cases to make the aggregate larger before deciding whether the two destructive cases matter.
Add a risk-stratified safety slice with balanced cases where the destructive action is allowed and where it must be refused.
Use a single holistic model judge over the existing cases and treat its confidence as the missing refusal evidence.
Grade tool traces deterministically and block release until the high-impact safety slice passes its own gate.

questions.prompt: An agent passes 99% of a 500-case evaluation, but only two cases exercise a high-impact destructive tool attempt and neither covers a negative case where the tool must be refused. The release owner asks whether the aggregate pass is sufficient. Select TWO: Which controls are needed before this aggregate can support release?

constraints: Independent billing fixtures, final report fields, authorization traces, tool arguments, and the old gold trace are available; the revised path performs no write or destructive operation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the task explicitly required one exact tool sequence for audit or side-effect ordering, the trace difference would be a contract failure and the trial would need remediation.
details.errorCorrection: A historical path is not a business or safety requirement by itself; failing it would reward incidental implementation order and discourage safe authorized alternatives. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends clean isolated trials, outcome-based grading, deterministic checks where possible, and calibrated model graders for nuanced dimensions. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Pass the revised trial for the correct report and authorized read-only behavior, record the path variation, and update the gold trace or grader only if the sequence was never a contract; keep the destructive attempt as a separate failure evidence case.
details.transfer: Grade the declared outcome and safety boundary, while treating implementation traces as evidence only when the contract requires them.

messages.text: An incidental historical order is not a business or safety requirement when the authorized outcome is equivalent.
A destructive call violates the safety contract even when the final report is correct.
A correct report cannot prove that the agent stayed within the required authorization boundary.
Required control: Grade the final billing report and the authorization and no-side-effect contract rather than requiring one incidental read-only path.
Required control: Update the gold trace or grader only if the historical sequence was never a contract, and keep the destructive attempt as separate failure evidence.

feedback.reason: Pass the revised trial for the correct report and authorized read-only behavior, record the path variation, and update the gold trace or grader only if the sequence was never a contract; keep the destructive attempt as a separate failure evidence case. The decisive constraint is The safety and business contract requires a correct report without unauthorized side effects, not one incidental read-only call sequence; a changed authorized path should pass outcome and constraint grading unless the exact sequence is itself a declared requirement.

options.text: Grade the final billing report and the authorization and no-side-effect contract rather than requiring one incidental read-only path.
Fail the revised trial because its tool trace differs from the historical gold sequence even though the report and authorization checks pass.
Accept any tool sequence that produces the report, including a delete call, because the final text is the only required artifact.
Update the gold trace or grader only if the historical sequence was never a contract, and keep the destructive attempt as separate failure evidence.
Grade the report alone and omit tool permissions from the result because the revised path is read-only.

questions.prompt: A coding agent must produce a correct read-only billing report. In the original evaluation, one trial attempted delete_customer with a real ID before producing the report; a revised implementation now reaches the same report through a different fully authorized read-only lookup path, while the evaluator still expects the original tool sequence. Select TWO: Which grading decisions best handle the revised trial?

constraints: Field extraction and claim state have objective checks.
Explanation quality needs a domain rubric and human calibration.
The small set is available now and can be expanded from reviewed cases.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every task had a deterministic structured answer and a large clean corpus, exact checks could carry most of the harness.
details.errorCorrection: Waiting, one holistic judge, satisfaction votes, or clean-only data either delays evidence, conflates dimensions, or removes the failure cases that matter.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends deterministic graders where possible, model graders when necessary, and human review for validation and calibration.
details.scenarioApplication: Run the 18 cases and edge cases through field/state assertions, score explanations with a reviewed rubric, and record disagreements for calibration.
details.transfer: Match each evaluation assertion to a grader that can observe it reliably, and calibrate human or model judgment where tests cannot decide.

messages.text: Waiting delays useful evidence, and a single judge may not match every objective or subjective dimension.
Satisfaction is too coarse to verify extraction or claim state.
Removing contradictory and missing-invoice cases removes the boundary the assistant must handle.

feedback.reason: The harness should use a grader suited to each assertion: deterministic checks for objective outputs and calibrated review for nuanced explanations.

options.text: Wait until thousands of cases are available, then score every answer with one holistic model judge.
Mix real and edge cases with field/state checks, an explanation rubric, and calibrated review.
Use thumbs-up votes as the only grader because recommendations are subjective.
Test only clean invoices so the first score is stable before adding contradictions.

questions.prompt: An insurer has 18 reviewed production cases plus edge cases with missing invoices and contradictory dates for an extraction and recommendation assistant. Which initial evaluation harness is most defensible?

constraints: Some cases should use current web data.
Some reviewed stable facts should be answered directly.
The team can report unnecessary-search and missed-search errors separately.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every supported request required current web data, positive-only evaluation would not create this trigger problem.
details.errorCorrection: More positive cases, threshold tuning on the same mix, or deleting stable facts reinforces the observed bias.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends testing cases where a behavior should occur and where it should not to avoid one-sided optimization.
details.scenarioApplication: Label reviewed prompts by expected search behavior, score unnecessary and missed searches independently, and use both error classes for iteration.
details.transfer: For a conditional behavior, evaluate both the trigger-positive and trigger-negative populations and name their errors separately.

messages.text: More positive cases improve search recall but never expose unnecessary searches.
Threshold tuning cannot correct a case set that omits the negative boundary.
Deleting direct-answer cases makes over-searching invisible and removes a valid behavior.

feedback.reason: The current one-sided set rewards over-triggering; positive and negative cases are needed to measure both sides of the search boundary.

options.text: Add more current-information questions so the search success rate becomes more precise.
Tune a search threshold against the existing one-sided score and keep the same case mix.
Remove stable-fact cases because searching is safer than answering directly.
Balance should-search and should-not-search cases and grade both trigger errors.

questions.prompt: A web-capable assistant is evaluated only on questions that should search, so it searches nearly every request. The team can add reviewed stable-fact cases. What should the next evaluation set do?

constraints: Sandboxed evaluation and a controlled canary are available.
Assignment and rollback criteria can be recorded.
Quality, safety, latency, and cost can be monitored by cohort.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the model had no tools or side effects and the offline suite covered a deterministic contract, a canary would add less safety evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Universal rollout removes comparison, self-approval is not independent evidence, and disabling tools changes the contract being tested.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a small pilot, thorough evaluation, gradual scaling, A/B testing, and human oversight; the environment and rollback constraints are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Test the model in isolation, assign a canary and control, watch guardrails, and revert when a declared criterion is breached.
details.transfer: Stage changes with isolated evidence, controlled exposure, an independent control, and a reversible rollback boundary.

messages.text: Universal exposure removes the control and expands side-effect risk before live behavior is known.
A model’s explanation is not an independent deployment check.
Removing command behavior tests a different system from the one that will be deployed.
Sandbox evidence limits initial blast radius and the canary observes live behavior.
A control and rollback rule preserve a reversible comparison while the canary is evaluated.

feedback.reason: Sandbox evidence and a small reversible cohort answer different questions; a control and explicit rollback limit the blast radius of tool side effects.

options.text: Run the upgrade in a sandbox first and then expose a small reversible canary cohort with quality, safety, latency, and cost monitoring.
Roll out to every shared environment because the offline score is higher.
Let the model approve its own first deployment after it explains why the change is safe.
Define rollback criteria and preserve a control cohort while the canary runs.
Disable command execution during the canary, even though command behavior is part of the production contract.

questions.prompt: A coding-agent model upgrade beats a small offline suite but can edit files and run commands in shared development environments. Select TWO rollout controls.

constraints: The high-risk category has a stricter safety tolerance.
The experiment retains cohort and transcript evidence.
Latency, cost, and safety are guardrails rather than optional diagnostics.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If B improved quality with no guardrail regression and all categories shared the same risk tolerance, broad rollout could follow the plan.
details.errorCorrection: Averages erase severity, and discarding the recorded evidence prevents diagnosis; resolution alone is not the release contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says A/B tests measure real user outcomes but need transcript review to explain changes, and evaluation layers are complementary.
details.scenarioApplication: Review high-risk transcripts, quantify each guardrail by slice, and modify or limit B until it meets the declared boundaries.
details.transfer: Treat safety and operating commitments as gates around an experimental quality lift, then use slices and transcripts to decide the next change.

messages.text: A global lift cannot veto a safety regression in the category with stricter tolerance.
A composite score can hide a hard guardrail breach.
Restarting discards the cohort and transcript evidence needed to identify the trade-off.

feedback.reason: The headline lift cannot override a high-risk safety regression or violated operating limits; the stored cohort evidence should guide the constrained iteration.

options.text: Ship B because the overall resolution lift is positive and inspect the high-risk category later.
Average quality, latency, cost, and safety into one score and ship if it improves.
Review affected slices and keep safety, latency, and cost as guardrails before rollout.
Rollback both prompts and restart without using the recorded category evidence.

questions.prompt: Prompt B lifts correct claim resolution from 82% to 86% but raises p95 latency 40%, cost 25%, and safety escalations in a high-risk category. Account assignment and category slices are recorded. What should the team do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If randomization is infeasible, use a prespecified quasi-experimental design and state its assumptions and remaining confounding.
details.errorCorrection: An observed production difference is not automatically a treatment effect and is not predictably conservative.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B testing estimates causal effects through controlled assignment; opt-in cohorts can differ before the treatment.
details.scenarioApplication: Randomize eligible users or stable accounts between the current and new style, stratify on important workload segments if needed, and measure resolution plus guardrails.
details.transfer: Separate rollout monitoring from causal evidence when users self-select into a variant.

messages.text: Opt-in users differ by preference and possibly task mix, so the observed difference is not an isolated treatment effect.
Self-selection can bias the comparison in either direction; it does not establish that the observed lift is conservative.
Task mix, time, learning, and other contemporaneous changes can still explain a before/after difference.

feedback.reason: The beta comparison is observational and preference-driven. Treat it as a hypothesis, then randomize or otherwise create a credible comparable counterfactual before attributing the lift to the style.

options.text: The style caused a 9-point lift because the beta group used it in production.
Treat beta results as observational; run randomized assignment before claiming causal lift.
Ship the style to everyone because self-selection only makes the estimate conservative.
Compare only the beta users’ results before and after opt-in to remove user preference effects.

questions.prompt: A new answer style is released to users who opt into a beta because they already prefer detailed responses. Their resolution rate is 9 points higher than the default group; no random assignment or pre-release matched evaluation exists. What can the team conclude?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The product owner can authorize a new cost ceiling only through a new decision basis; the current experiment cannot infer that change.
details.errorCorrection: Do not average the arms or mine an unplanned subgroup to make a guardrail failure disappear.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B decisions must respect declared guardrails across quality, safety, latency and cost; a favorable primary outcome does not automatically waive a constraint.
details.scenarioApplication: Report treatment and control estimates by assigned arm, show the $0.78 cost against the $0.50 ceiling, and preserve safety results as a separate measure.
details.transfer: Apply the complete predeclared adoption rule after estimating each outcome.

messages.text: The variant violates the explicit $0.50 cost guardrail even though one outcome improved.
Post hoc selection creates an unplanned subgroup and does not establish that it meets the cost rule.
Averaging treatment and control cost does not change the candidate arm’s measured cost.

feedback.reason: The treatment improves resolution but exceeds the experiment’s adoption cost ceiling. Record both outcomes and do not adopt it under this rule.

options.text: Adopt the variant because resolution improved and safety did not worsen.
Adopt only for accounts with the largest resolution lift, selecting that slice after reviewing the results.
Keep the candidate behind the predeclared cost ceiling; evaluate resolution and cost together.
Average the old and new cost per case to $0.59 and compare that with the $0.50 ceiling.

questions.prompt: A prompt variant improves successful resolution from 80% to 84% on the assigned accounts. It also raises cost per resolved case from $0.40 to $0.78; the experiment plan says the variant is adoptable only if cost stays at or below $0.50 and the safety guardrail holds. Safety is unchanged. What result should be recorded?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If interactions are unlikely or capacity is limited, a predeclared staged design may be simpler, but it estimates fewer interactions at each step.
details.errorCorrection: Do not credit one component based on cost, recency, or a favorable aggregate when all components changed together.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Causal attribution requires variation that separates the candidate explanations; increasing the sample for an unchanged bundle does not do that.
details.scenarioApplication: Use a factorial or staged design that preserves a control and varies model, prompt and retrieval in interpretable combinations, while holding the eligible workload and guardrails constant.
details.transfer: Design the next experiment to distinguish the causal claims the release owner needs.

messages.text: Cost and timing do not isolate which intervention caused the observed result.
A larger sample estimates the bundled treatment more precisely but still cannot attribute its effect to one component.
Changing one component at a time can test retrieval’s contribution, but the remaining pair stays confounded and the plan must preserve a comparable control.

feedback.reason: The observed experiment estimates the bundled release, not the contribution of its three simultaneous changes. A controlled multi-arm or factorial follow-up is needed for component attribution.

options.text: Credit the model because it was the most expensive change and the launch metric improved.
Keep all three changes and rerun the same two-arm test with twice as many accounts.
Roll back retrieval only and attribute any remaining lift to the model and prompt together.
Use a controlled or factorial follow-up to attribute effects among the three interventions.

questions.prompt: A rollout analysis shows a 6-point lift after three changes shipped together: a new model, a prompt rewrite, and a different retrieval index. The release was assigned by account, but the owner asks which change caused the lift. What experiment should come next?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the target mix has little or no support in one arm, statistical reweighting cannot create missing counterfactual evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Do not infer comparability from equal totals or drop an inconvenient stratum after seeing outcomes.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization should produce comparable treatment exposure; workload and time imbalance can distort the measured effect, especially for latency.
details.scenarioApplication: Check overlap by time and document length, estimate within-stratum effects and a prespecified target-weighted result, and improve random assignment or blocking for a clean follow-up.
details.transfer: Compare variants under the same workload population and expose residual mix imbalance.

messages.text: Equal account counts do not balance a workload dimension that is strongly associated with treatment timing and latency.
Removing cases after observing imbalance changes the comparison and may leave no comparable target population.
The differing long-document mix and time period confound the prompt effect.

feedback.reason: Account counts alone do not make the arms comparable when exposure periods and document lengths differ. Analyze comparable strata under a declared target mix and rerun if the observed data lack overlap.

options.text: Compare the two raw aggregate means because account counts are equal.
Balance and report document-length workload by arm, then estimate lift on comparable exposures.
Drop weekend requests from the control group and compare only weekday means.
Attribute the weekend latency to the control prompt because those requests were assigned there.

questions.prompt: A prompt A/B test assigns accounts equally, but treatment accounts are mostly evaluated during weekday mornings and control accounts during weekend nights. Long documents are much more common on weekends, and the new prompt changes long-document latency. Which analysis best repairs the comparison?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A valid predeclared sequential design may permit interim decisions, but its boundary must exist before inspecting outcomes.
details.errorCorrection: A nominal p-value does not erase unplanned selection or become confirmatory when reported after the fact.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A/B inference depends on the analysis and stopping plan; repeated testing can inflate false-positive risk.
details.scenarioApplication: Record every metric check, variant tried and stopping point, then preregister a primary outcome, guardrails, multiplicity approach and stopping rule for the confirmatory run.
details.transfer: Disclose exploratory iteration and separate it from a confirmatory causal decision.

messages.text: Repeated looks across metrics and variants increase the chance of finding a nominal result by chance.
Relabeling the chosen result after seeing it does not undo the unplanned comparisons or stopping.
Continuing to peek without a defined rule preserves the same multiplicity and stopping bias.

feedback.reason: The observed result followed repeated unplanned looks across metrics and variants. It can generate a hypothesis but does not support a confirmatory win; use a new prespecified design.

options.text: Declare a win because at least one metric crossed the usual significance line.
Select the variant with the strongest observed metric and report the other results as exploratory without qualification.
Use the predeclared stopping rule or adjust for repeated looks across metrics and variants.
Continue testing until all five metrics are significant, then stop without revising the plan.

questions.prompt: During a live test, an analyst checks five quality metrics every day for two weeks. The team stops the test the first day one metric is nominally significant, after also trying three prompt variants; no interim or multiple-comparison rule was specified. What should be reported?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If persistent assignment is operationally impossible, measure and report carryover explicitly and avoid a clean causal claim until a valid design is available.
details.errorCorrection: More weeks or account-level adjustment cannot identify the prompt effect when the prior treatment changes the next period’s behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Crossover comparisons rely on treatment effects not persisting into later control periods; durable state can violate that assumption.
details.scenarioApplication: Use persistent account assignment for a parallel test, or demonstrate a washout that clears the memory before comparing periods; keep outcomes and guardrails prespecified.
details.transfer: Check whether treatment changes durable user, agent, or system state before selecting a crossover experiment.

messages.text: The same account is not an unaffected control after the B-specific rule remains in memory.
A fixed effect controls stable account differences, not treatment-induced state that carries into the next period.
The state change may explain some outcome, but the alternating design cannot separate that effect from prompt assignment.

feedback.reason: The treatment persists into later control periods, so the alternating comparison mixes prompt assignment with learned workspace state. The within-account design does not remove that carryover.

options.text: Treat the 5-point difference as causal because each account serves as its own control.
Keep alternating and add account fixed effects; the persistent memory averages out across enough weeks.
Model carryover or use a washout; alternating periods do not erase learned workspace rules.
Attribute the entire 5-point lift to prompt B because the memory was introduced during its weeks.

questions.prompt: A support agent test alternates the same accounts between prompt A and prompt B each week to control for account differences. Prompt B teaches a persistent workspace memory to include a new escalation rule; during the following A week, that memory remains active. The measured B weeks show a 5-point resolution lift. What can the team conclude and test next?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cluster randomization may require more teams or longer enrollment; if only twelve teams are available, describe the estimate as limited rather than using an artificially narrow account-level interval.
details.errorCorrection: A large account count cannot repair a small number of treatment clusters or remove shared-playbook spillover.
details.mechanismOrProperty: When treatment is delivered through a shared team environment, outcomes within a team are correlated and can contaminate individual-level assignment.
details.scenarioApplication: Assign whole teams, increase the number of independent teams according to a prespecified power plan, and analyze the randomized cluster while reporting account outcomes and safety guardrails.
details.transfer: Choose the randomization unit to match the smallest shared environment where treatment can spread.

messages.text: A large number of accounts does not increase the number of independent team-level assignments.
Preference-based assignment can confound treatment with supervisor and team differences.
Putting both prompts in the playbook lets treatment cross the same shared boundary the design must control.

feedback.reason: Shared coaching and playbooks let treatment information spill across accounts within a team, so 2,400 account rows do not provide 2,400 independent treatment assignments. Randomize and analyze at the cluster where interference occurs, with enough clusters to estimate the effect.

options.text: Keep account-level assignment and retain the account-level interval because the number of accounts is large.
Randomize and analyze at team level because coaching crosses account boundaries.
Assign every team the prompt that its supervisor prefers and adjust for team in a regression.
Randomize by account, but move examples from both prompts into every team’s playbook so agents can choose the best instruction.

questions.prompt: A company randomizes 2,400 customer accounts across two assistant prompts, but each arm has only six support teams. Every team shares a response playbook and supervisors coach agents using examples from their assigned prompt. The analysis treats all accounts as independent and reports a narrow confidence interval. Which redesign best supports a causal comparison?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A predeclared interim method can support a decision only if it accounts for follow-up censoring and the outcome policy; otherwise wait for the full horizon.
details.errorCorrection: Do not treat unobserved follow-up as no reopening, and do not assume the subset with completed follow-up is representative.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Outcome maturity is distinct from sample-size completion; an assigned case that has not yet reached the observation horizon is not a confirmed no-event outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Report the handling-time and same-session results as interim findings, continue follow-up, and evaluate the 30-day reopen rate with the prespecified censoring or missingness method before applying the guardrail.
details.transfer: Align release claims with when each outcome becomes observable, not only when enrollment reaches its target.

messages.text: The required 30-day safety outcome is still unobserved for most assigned accounts, so immediate gains cannot establish that guardrail.
An account that has not completed 30 days is censored, not a confirmed case without a reopening.
The matured subset may differ by assignment or account characteristics; analyze follow-up selection before treating it as the full randomized comparison.

feedback.reason: The primary count and immediate metrics do not establish a 30-day guardrail when most assigned accounts have not reached the outcome window. Preserve the favorable interim evidence and defer the release claim until the prespecified outcome is mature or analyzed under a valid missing-follow-up plan.

options.text: Ship because the planned sample and both immediate outcomes meet the success goal.
Wait for mature safety outcomes or apply the prespecified valid censoring analysis before release.
Count every account without an observed reopening as a no-reopen success, including accounts whose follow-up window is not complete.
Discard the randomized comparison and use only the 40% with mature follow-up, without checking whether follow-up completion differs by arm or account type.

questions.prompt: A randomized support-assistant test reaches its planned account count. The new prompt reduces median handling time by 12% and raises same-session resolution by 3 points. The release contract also limits 30-day case reopenings to at most a 1-point increase, but only 40% of assigned accounts have completed the 30-day follow-up. What conclusion is justified now?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If delivery failures are concentrated in a meaningful segment, report that operational limitation and test the delivery path before broad rollout.
details.errorCorrection: A received-treatment comparison or excluding noncompliers can lose the protection of random assignment; crossover also does not erase the primary evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization identifies an assignment-based effect; conditioning on post-assignment exposure can introduce selection if delivery failures relate to account or outcome.
details.scenarioApplication: Estimate outcomes by assigned arm, disclose the 8% and 3% crossover rates and their patterns, then prespecify a secondary exposure analysis if its assumptions are justified.
details.transfer: Preserve the randomized estimand and make treatment receipt a measured implementation outcome.

messages.text: Actual exposure may differ for reasons related to the outcome, so comparing by receipt abandons the randomized assignment.
Removing noncompliers conditions on a post-assignment event and can bias the comparison.
Crossover weakens separation but does not automatically erase the primary evidence.

feedback.reason: The product question concerns assignment to the new policy. The randomized groups preserve that comparison even with imperfect delivery; crossover must be measured and can qualify interpretation, not silently redefine who was randomized.

options.text: Compare outcomes by the prompt each account actually received and discard assignment logs.
Use assignment-based intention-to-treat; report crossover and qualify exposure-based analysis separately.
Remove all accounts that did not receive their assigned prompt and treat the remaining users as randomized.
Declare no effect because any crossover invalidates all information from a randomized test.

questions.prompt: A randomized assistant test assigns 1,000 accounts to prompt B and 1,000 to prompt A. Delivery logs show 8% of B assignments fell back to A, and 3% of A assignments accidentally received B. The product asks whether assigning the new policy improves resolution. Which primary analysis and follow-up are most defensible?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If some outcomes remain unavailable, report their rates and use a predeclared missing-data sensitivity analysis rather than asserting the observed complete-case lift is causal.
details.errorCorrection: A balanced assignment log does not repair a biased analysis table; post hoc weights or complete-case restriction can hide the selection mechanism.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Randomization protects a comparison only for the randomized population and a valid outcome analysis; post-assignment filtering can create differential selection.
details.scenarioApplication: Use the immutable assignment log to rebuild eligible arm counts, trace why 1,100 more treatment sessions were excluded, and evaluate missing outcomes under the prespecified plan.
details.transfer: Audit assignment, exposure, eligibility, and outcome capture as separate stages before reading an experiment estimate.

messages.text: The published table no longer contains the full assigned population, and its arm-specific exclusions may bias the estimate.
Matching row counts after the fact does not explain why treatment outcomes are missing or restore randomized comparability.
Complete transcripts may be missing differently by arm; discarding assignment information makes the selection harder to diagnose.

feedback.reason: The analysis population no longer reflects the balanced randomized cohort, and the differential loss may be related to treatment or outcome. Diagnose the changed denominator before interpreting the apparent lift.

options.text: Report treatment’s observed rate because randomized assignment was originally balanced.
Restore the prespecified denominator by assignment, audit arm-specific session loss, then rerun the analysis.
Reweight the smaller treatment table until its count matches control, then publish the same estimate.
Drop assignment logs and compare only the sessions with complete transcripts.

questions.prompt: An experiment assigns 10,000 eligible accounts to each prompt. The immutable assignment log is balanced, but the analysis table contains 8,900 control accounts and 7,200 treatment accounts after filtering for completed sessions. Treatment has the higher observed resolution rate. The filter was added during the test and no missing-session audit was run. What should the analyst do before interpreting the lift?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fallbacks weaken treatment separation without automatically eliminating all randomized evidence.
details.errorCorrection: Dropping or reassigning accounts conditions on post-assignment events and can bias the result.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of assignment under observed delivery, including noncompliance.
details.scenarioApplication: An exposure-based analysis may be informative but needs separate assumptions and labeling.
details.transfer: Keep assignment, delivery, and actual exposure distinct in experiment reporting.

messages.text: Actual receipt follows a post-assignment fallback and is no longer the randomized comparison; adjustment does not preserve assignment balance.
Excluding noncompliers after assignment can select different populations across arms and biases the primary estimate.
Noncompliance weakens exposure interpretation but the assignment-based result remains informative when delivery is reported and qualified.

feedback.reason: Filtering or reassigning after randomization changes the comparison population. Assignment-based analysis preserves the initial randomized estimate while delivery failure is reported separately.

options.text: Analyze by randomized assignment, report delivery compliance by arm, and qualify any exposure-based analysis separately.
Report an as-treated comparison as primary, grouping accounts by the prompt they actually received and adjusting for the fallback rate.
Keep accounts in their original arms but remove the 17% fallback cases from the denominator, then compare the remaining randomized users.
Pause interpretation until delivery is repaired, because the exposure problem prevents any useful estimate from this randomized assignment.

questions.prompt: A randomized test assigns equal numbers of accounts to A and B. Delivery logs show 17% of B accounts received A after a fallback, while the analyst’s table compares only accounts that received their assigned prompt. What should the primary result report?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The rubric itself affects measurement and should be held constant or evaluated as an explicit factor.
details.errorCorrection: Post-hoc reviewer intuition does not replace a controlled comparison.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Causal attribution requires separating changes or deliberately estimating their combined effects under a design that supports it.
details.scenarioApplication: A larger test of the same bundle can estimate the bundle’s effect but cannot identify which component caused it.
details.transfer: Use a planned design to distinguish interacting changes.

messages.text: A larger sample can estimate the bundled effect more precisely but cannot identify which component caused it.
The comparison still leaves retrieval and evaluator changes entangled with the prompt effect.
Expert judgment can prioritize hypotheses but does not isolate causal contributions among changes deployed together.

feedback.reason: The observed result combines three simultaneous changes, so a larger sample alone cannot attribute the gain to one of them.

options.text: Repeat the combined release with more accounts and use a larger sample to determine whether the joint change reliably improves resolution.
Restore the prior evaluator, keep the new retrieval, and compare the prompt rollback with the combined release on fresh cases.
Ask reviewers to rank the prompt, retrieval, and rubric changes by plausibility, then test the highest-ranked explanation first.
Run controlled comparisons that vary prompt, retrieval, and rubric factors separately or in a planned factorial design.

questions.prompt: A launch report attributes a 5-point resolution gain to a new prompt. The same deployment also changed retrieval ranking and the evaluator’s partial-answer rubric; no previous run tested those changes separately. What follow-up best isolates the cause?

constraints: Account assignment is stable.
The owner can extend the run under the analysis plan.
The sample target, confidence rule, and stopping boundary were predeclared.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A completed planned sample with stable guardrails and a prespecified stopping rule could support rollout from the observed effect.
details.errorCorrection: A point estimate, a premature no-difference conclusion, or changing the stopping rule after seeing data turns noise into policy.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that A/B tests measure real outcomes but are slower and need transcript review; the sample and stopping rules are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve assignment and analysis, collect the planned sample, monitor guardrails by account type, and review transcripts before declaring a winner.
details.transfer: Respect the evidence and stopping rule declared before an experiment, especially when safety coverage is incomplete.

messages.text: A positive early estimate may be noise in an incomplete sample.
Overlapping confidence does not itself define the required stopping decision.
Changing the rule after observing the result invalidates the planned evidence boundary.

feedback.reason: An underpowered and uneven sample does not meet the declared evidence rule; continue under the plan or stop for a specified safety breach.

options.text: Ship the new variant because the early point estimate is positive.
Stop the experiment and declare no difference because the confidence range overlaps.
Continue under the sample plan or stop for a defined safety breach; inspect slices.
Change the stopping rule now so the positive estimate can be used for rollout.

questions.prompt: An A/B test reports a 2% resolution lift after one day, but its predeclared sample target is not met, the confidence range overlaps, and guardrail data is sparse across account types. What decision is justified?

constraints: Exposure, account segment, session, and outcome logs are available.
The original plan requires clean account assignment and comparable segment mix.
The causal effect is needed before changing exposure.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If crossover were absent, segment mix matched the plan, and the sample met the analysis rule, the observed lift could proceed to the predeclared decision.
details.errorCorrection: Weighting cannot recover users who saw both variants or repair a changed exposure mechanism; an unadjusted or premium-only rollout compounds the confound.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic describes A/B testing as controlling for confounds and requiring sufficient traffic and transcript review; crossover and segment balance are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Use logs to quantify contamination, correct the routing and segment filter, preserve a clean cohort, and rerun before changing exposure.
details.transfer: Audit treatment exposure and population composition before interpreting a live comparison as causal.

messages.text: Weighting cannot restore the missing counterfactual for users exposed to both variants.
A large contaminated sample remains causally invalid.
Selecting the segment that received more favorable exposure turns the composition confound into a rollout rule.

feedback.reason: Crossover and changed composition contaminate treatment exposure and the counterfactual, so the apparent lift is not a valid causal comparison.

options.text: Post-hoc weight the aggregate results by segment and ship B if the adjusted estimate remains positive across the contaminated sessions.
Discard the logs and use the unadjusted lift because the sample is large.
Ship only to premium accounts, where B has the largest observed lift.
Audit crossover and segments, restore account assignment, and rerun before changing exposure.

questions.prompt: Variant B reports a 4-point resolution lift. Account-level assignment was intended, but a routing bug sent 12% of users both variants; B also received twice as many easy premium accounts after a segment filter changed. Logs preserve crossover and composition. What should happen?

constraints: The registered interim time, sample size, primary metric, uncertainty rule, guardrails, assignment log, and analysis output are immutable and available before the result is reviewed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the interim rule were absent, the sample/uncertainty boundary unmet, or a safety guardrail breached, the experiment would continue or stop for the breach rather than declare this interim result.
details.errorCorrection: The first ignores an authorized stopping boundary; the second ignores the registered analysis and creates the unplanned-peeking problem covered by the rejected path. The competing action therefore leaves the stated decision boundary unresolved.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a small pilot, infrastructure for A/B testing, human feedback, and ongoing updates to offline evaluations from production data. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Apply the registered interim rule, stop or advance exposure as it specifies, preserve the analysis and guardrail evidence, and report the decision as an interim-boundary outcome rather than an unplanned peek.
details.transfer: Use a prespecified stopping rule as the decision boundary and label the evidence according to the stage at which it was collected.

messages.text: The final sample target is not a prerequisite when the registered interim rule is met; waiting changes the declared decision point instead of applying it.
A dashboard result without the registered rule recreates the unplanned-peeking problem.
Resetting discards a valid prespecified boundary instead of applying the documented stopping decision.

feedback.reason: Apply the registered interim rule, stop or advance exposure as it specifies, preserve the analysis and guardrail evidence, and report the decision as an interim-boundary outcome rather than an unplanned peek. The decisive constraint is A prespecified interim rule with sufficient evidence permits the declared decision; the absence of the final sample target alone does not require continuing when the rule authorizes stopping.

options.text: Complete the full sample target before applying the interim rule, so the study is not stopped on partial data.

Align the deployed description and executor schema, then add a versioned contract test.
The model is less intelligent on this workload; switch to a larger model before checking the request.
Increase retries so the backend eventually accepts the new argument name.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Versioned keys may reduce reuse across editions, but freshness is required for effective-date answers; measure cache cost after correctness is restored.
details.errorCorrection: The evidence localizes the defect to stale cached context; changing the prompt, model, or retrieval breadth does not repair the invalid cache identity.

Replace the model because an outdated date proves its training knowledge is stale.
Version or invalidate retrieval cache entries by policy edition and test active-edition delivery.
Increase the number of retrieved passages so the model can choose between both editions.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the parser preserves the value but the model still misreads it, then investigate prompt representation or model behavior with the same controlled inputs.
details.errorCorrection: Do not ask the model to infer erased numeric information or weaken the grader to accept corrupted output.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Controlled replay localizes a failure to the first stage where input evidence diverges; a downstream model change cannot restore information already lost.

details.scenarioApplication: Inventory reachable data, tools, egress, code execution, and writes; remove unnecessary authority and set containment boundaries for the remaining actions.
details.transfer: Map model, content, and environment surfaces together, then limit authority according to consequence and reachability.

messages.text: Quality scores do not measure database writes, code execution, or data exposure, and unrestricted access increases impact.
Indirect injection through external content remains a threat even without a direct user jailbreak.
Isolation reduces production impact, but broad access and deferred threat testing leave avoidable tool and content paths unexamined before deployment.

feedback.reason: The agent spans model, attacker-controlled content, and a consequential environment, so the review must map those surfaces and constrain authority before access expands.

options.text: Map model, content, tools, and environment failure modes; then narrow authority and data access to cap blast radius.

Run an isolated pilot with broad tool access to observe useful actions, then perform deployment-shaped threat testing before granting production authority.

questions.prompt: A research agent can browse documents, run code, and update a project database; external content is attacker-controlled and the agent is autonomous across turns. Which risk review should precede deployment?

constraints: New tools create data, egress, and side-effect paths.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the upgrade kept the same read-only tools and environment, a focused regression review could be sufficient without a new side-effect boundary.
details.errorCorrection: Quality scores and unchanged permissions do not cover the new surface, and longer instructions are not a substitute for environment controls or tests.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic warns that more capable models may find unexpected paths around restrictions, so deployment risk must account for capability and environmental boundaries.
details.scenarioApplication: Model the new tools and reachable data, test hostile and unexpected-goal cases in a sandbox, start read-only, and make each expansion conditional on evidence.
details.transfer: Reassess risk whenever capability or authority changes, then expand access through evidence-backed stages.

messages.text: Lower ordinary error does not prove safe browsing or write behavior.

feedback.reason: A capability change plus new authority changes the attack surface; staged containment and misuse testing are needed before writes are enabled.

options.text: Grant browsing and writes because factual errors declined, then add misuse tests to the next release.

Reassess threats, test in containment, start read-only, and expand access on evidence.

questions.prompt: A more capable model improves factual research scores, and the team proposes adding browsing and write tools even though current tests omit misuse and unexpected goal paths. What should happen before access expansion?
