details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends defining measurable, use-case-relevant criteria before iterating on prompts or implementation. The case-specific population, thresholds, roles, and authority limits are supplied by this scenario rather than by the provider documentation.
details.scenarioApplication: Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a revisit trigger, hand the bounded requirements to design, and reopen only if new evidence crosses the trigger.
details.transfer: Close a discovery phase with evidence, ownership, residual uncertainty, and a trigger that tells the team when to reopen it.

messages.text: Collecting more suggestions before setting an exit boundary adds noise once representative requirements and acceptance evidence are complete.
An undocumented handoff loses the authority and acceptance record that should govern design.
Indefinite discovery has no owner-controlled exit and delays design without changing the authorized brief.

feedback.reason: Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a revisit trigger, hand the bounded requirements to design, and reopen only if new evidence crosses the trigger. The decisive constraint is Once representative requirements and acceptance evidence are complete, discovery needs an owned exit decision; indefinite collection adds noise and delays design without changing the authorized problem brief.

options.text: Continue interviews to collect additional suggestions before setting an evidence boundary or handing requirements to design.
Move to design immediately without recording that discovery is complete or preserving the unresolved-question log.
Close discovery with the evidence-backed brief, record residual questions and a trigger, hand requirements to design, and reopen only on new evidence.
Keep discovery open indefinitely so future suggestions cannot be rejected as late.

questions.prompt: Discovery has covered each affected role, observed the current workflow, resolved authority, and produced measurable acceptance criteria. New interview requests repeat already answered questions, and no high-impact unresolved requirement remains, but the team keeps discovery open without an exit decision. What should the team do now that discovery evidence is complete?

constraints: The current workflow and exceptions can be observed.
Privacy is a hard boundary.
Backlog reduction needs a measurable outcome.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If users, workflow, target, and access rules were already documented and only a model migration remained, a solution comparison could be next.
details.errorCorrection: Model ranking and a future-state diagram assume a solution, while a field list omits workflow ownership and success evidence; a post-demo definition is too late.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic advises defining success criteria before prompt iteration and tying them to the application’s actual user needs; the problem brief structure is scenario reasoning.
details.scenarioApplication: Document each group’s advising decision, current exception path, protected records, backlog measure, and acceptance test before comparing models or architectures.
details.transfer: Resolve the problem, users, workflow, data boundary, and acceptance measure before choosing an AI solution.

messages.text: A one-group pilot can supply evidence, but it leaves the other groups’ needs and exceptions unresolved before solution selection.
Mapping fields and steps without agreed outcomes lets the agent define acceptance during the pilot instead of clarifying the problem first.
A benchmark-led choice tests capability before the university has established its own workflow, exception, and backlog evidence.

feedback.reason: The problem is still underspecified, so discovery must connect user groups and workflow evidence to the outcome, data boundary, and measurable acceptance before solution choice.

options.text: Start with one user group, pilot its current workflow, and use backlog and privacy results to shape requirements for the other groups.
Map the email and spreadsheet steps plus protected fields, then choose an agent whose pilot will discover user-group acceptance.
Write a structured problem brief connecting each user group and workflow evidence to outcome, access, data, and acceptance criteria.
Compare public advising benchmarks and choose a model, then validate exceptions and backlog measurement against the selected design.

questions.prompt: A university asks to make advising better. Three user groups, an email and spreadsheet workflow, protected records, and a backlog-reduction target are known. What should the architect produce before selecting a solution?

constraints: Public users and owners differ from the internal audience.
Accessibility, privacy, and peak capacity changed.
The internal speed measure is not sufficient evidence.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the public portal had identical users, context, accessibility needs, and traffic contract, existing discovery evidence could carry forward.
details.errorCorrection: Scaling one latency number, copying content, or waiting for tickets does not test external usability or protect employee-only data.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic treats task fidelity, privacy preservation, context utilization, and latency as use-case-specific dimensions measured against actual needs.
details.scenarioApplication: Revisit public user tasks, screen-reader outcomes, employee-note access, peak load, escalation, and service thresholds before selecting the rollout design.
details.transfer: When context or audience changes, reopen discovery for the changed users, data boundaries, and operating envelope.

messages.text: Scaling an internal target does not establish public accessibility, privacy, or the new workflow’s owner.
Labels and a support contact do not replace discovery of public tasks or protect employee notes under the new path.
Internal criteria plus post-launch tickets leave the public accessibility and privacy boundary untested.

feedback.reason: The audience, data, accessibility, and traffic envelope changed, so inherited internal assumptions cannot establish external acceptance.

options.text: Scale the internal latency target for peak traffic, retain internal tasks, and schedule an accessibility audit after the public release.
Publish the copied FAQ with data labels and a support contact, then measure public accessibility and peak load in production.
Keep internal criteria for the first release, add a disclaimer, and route accessibility issues to support while traffic is observed.
Re-interview public users and owners, map changed data and accessibility, model peak load, and define privacy, escalation, and service criteria.

questions.prompt: An internal FAQ assistant is moving to a public portal with non-native speakers, screen-reader users, tenfold peak traffic, and employee-only notes that must stay private. What discovery step is required?

constraints: Known routes, uncertain steps, and side-effect risk are explicit.
Quality, latency, cost, and control measures can be recorded.
The recommendation must remain reviewable by stakeholders.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every request had uncertain steps and no side effects, a deterministic route split would not be needed.
details.errorCorrection: Universal autonomy, hidden controls, and demo preference omit the predictable-workload fit and the evidence needed to operate the agent safely.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says patterns should be shaped to the use case, performance measured, complexity added only when it improves outcomes, and transparency prioritized.
details.scenarioApplication: Map known categories to deterministic routes, uncertain cases to bounded investigation, then list controls and tests that can falsify the recommendation.
details.transfer: Document both why a pattern fits a workload and how its tools, stops, and measures will be verified.

messages.text: Flexibility adds cost and control exposure for predictable requests without evidence of benefit.
Hidden tool and stop behavior prevents stakeholders from reviewing the actual boundary.
A demo preference does not establish operating or side-effect behavior.
Pattern fit and trade-offs let stakeholders inspect the architecture decision.
Explicit tools, stops, tests, and metrics make the constrained behavior verifiable.

feedback.reason: The pattern split and its measurable consequences make the decision reviewable, while tool, stopping, and verification details define the constrained agent boundary.

options.text: Document which request classes fit each pattern and state the expected quality, latency, cost, and control trade-offs.
Use maximum autonomy for both classes because flexibility is expected to improve experience.
Hide tool and stopping details behind the framework so the recommendation stays concise.
Measure only the demo’s answer preference and defer side-effect decisions to operations.
Record tools, stopping boundaries, tests, and metrics that will verify the routing and agent choice.

questions.prompt: A service desk is choosing a deterministic routing workflow for known categories versus a constrained agent for uncertain investigations. Select TWO documentation controls.

constraints: The failure may be in abstraction, tool contracts, or model-visible context.
A direct path can expose the underlying request and response.
Product and operations need an inspectable explanation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the framework emitted complete traces and validated tool contracts, a direct-path comparison might be unnecessary for that incident.
details.errorCorrection: Another hidden layer reduces diagnosability, final-answer preference cannot locate the failing step, and a model swap changes a variable before cause is known.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic says frameworks can obscure prompts and responses and recommends understanding the underlying code before relying on abstractions.
details.scenarioApplication: Replay representative searches through the direct API, capture prompt and tool arguments and responses, run checks, and compare the two paths on reliability and operating cost.
details.transfer: Expose the underlying request path before changing model or architecture when an abstraction hides the failure evidence.

messages.text: A tracing adapter may expose a summary, but the extra abstraction can preserve the hidden behavior causing the inconsistency.
A final answer and owner certification do not show whether context, arguments, or intermediate responses caused the failure.
A model swap changes capability before the framework and tool-contract hypotheses are isolated.

feedback.reason: A direct comparison makes the hidden path observable and separates framework behavior from model or tool causes before another abstraction is added.

options.text: Add a tracing adapter around the framework, normalize prompts and tool calls into an inspectable record, and diagnose from that abstraction.
Treat the final answer as the product contract, ask framework owners to certify hidden prompts, and compare search quality over a fixed sample.
Reproduce a representative search directly, capture prompts, calls, responses, and checks, and compare reliability, cost, latency, and maintainability.
Swap models within the framework, compare answer preference on the same queries, and preserve the hidden tool path while tuning prompts.

questions.prompt: A framework hides prompts, intermediate responses, and tool arguments while a team tries to explain inconsistent search answers; a direct API path is available. What should the team do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the agent later meets the deterministic latency and budget across the full distribution, a broader route can be reconsidered on new evidence.
details.errorCorrection: A tail improvement is not evidence that all requests need agent autonomy; silent fallback changes user-visible behavior without a decision record.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest workflow and adding agentic complexity where it materially improves task performance; architecture choices should be measured against explicit criteria.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the route criteria, measured tail benefit, monthly cost ceiling, deterministic-path latency, owner, and behavior when the cap is reached.
details.transfer: Communicate the supported scope and counterfactual limits of the architecture evidence.

messages.text: The result on 8% of cases does not establish value or cost feasibility for all requests.
Training cannot resolve conflicting evidence that the workflow cannot interpret.
A hidden switch at the budget cap changes behavior and SLA without an agreed boundary.

feedback.reason: The measurements support a hybrid route with explicit cost and latency constraints; they do not support applying the expensive path to known cases or hiding a threshold-driven behavior change.

options.text: Use the agent for all requests until the monthly ceiling is approached, then silently switch to the deterministic path.
Keep known cases deterministic; route only the evidenced ambiguous tail within explicit cost and latency bounds.
Replace every path with the agent because the tail improvement demonstrates the better general architecture.
Keep the deterministic workflow for all cases and describe tail failures as operator training needs.

questions.prompt: A claims team has a deterministic workflow for 92% of requests; the remaining 8% require interpreting conflicting notes. The pilot shows the constrained agent improves resolution on that tail but costs 4x per case. The CFO accepts a fixed monthly ceiling; the operations owner requires the 92% path to retain its latency contract. What should the architecture decision communicate?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the organization formally delegates that risk to the sponsor, the acceptance record can be updated with the delegation and evidence.
details.errorCorrection: A sponsor cannot accept a risk outside their authority, and silence or metric changes do not create the required approval.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Clear criteria and explicit ownership make evaluations and architecture decisions actionable; scenario governance assigns security acceptance to a different owner.
details.scenarioApplication: Separate completed quality evidence from the pending security review, identify the authorized decision maker, and state the launch condition that remains unmet.
details.transfer: Communicate partial evidence without turning it into approval for a different risk domain.

messages.text: Business success criteria do not substitute for the security owner’s decision.
Changing a quality threshold does not resolve an authorization concern.
Silence is not an affirmative decision when the role is responsible for acceptance.

feedback.reason: Passing a quality metric does not close an independently owned security decision; authority remains with the named role that can accept that risk.

options.text: Report the quality evidence as met, keep the security gate and risk acceptance open.
Declare the pilot accepted because the product sponsor owns the business outcome.
Lower the quality threshold so it matches the reviewer’s unresolved concerns and close the gate.
Proceed with a restricted launch and infer security acceptance from the reviewer’s silence.

questions.prompt: A pilot meets its quality threshold, but the security reviewer’s approval is still pending and the acceptance record names the product sponsor as the sole owner of residual risk. The sponsor cannot accept security risk under the organization’s decision rights. What should the architecture recommendation say?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If representative tail evidence met predeclared criteria and its risk owner accepted residual risk, a broader launch could be justified.
details.errorCorrection: A small volume can still carry material harm; model capability and post-launch monitoring do not prove tail behavior.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Success criteria should be relevant to the actual task and distribution; the risk boundary and launch owner are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Show common-path evidence, identify the untested tail, and retain a bounded route or gate until representative tests and authorized acceptance are available.
details.transfer: Communicate distribution-specific evidence, uncertainty, and the condition that changes the design decision.

messages.text: The common-case 99% result says nothing about the untested high-impact segment and cannot support a whole-service readiness claim.
Averaging unknown tail performance into the common-case score imputes results that were never measured.
Model size does not supply representative evidence for the untested tail.

feedback.reason: The aggregate conceals a distinct high-impact segment; the architecture decision must disclose that evidence gap and the condition for proceeding.

options.text: Keep the unvalidated high-impact tail bounded until evidence and an owner decision exist.
Publish 99% readiness because the untested tail is too small to change the aggregate.
Average the untested tail into the common-case score and promise to monitor after release.
Replace the evaluation with a larger model and claim the tail is covered by capability.

questions.prompt: A launch review shows 99% of common requests pass quality checks, but the remaining 1% includes rare high-impact actions with no representative test results. The sponsor asks for a single “99% ready” statement. What should the architect communicate?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If controlled tests show the agent invokes an idempotent action and reconciles timeout outcomes, side-effecting use can be reconsidered.
details.errorCorrection: Flexibility does not resolve repeated writes, and an instruction alone does not provide durable idempotency or recovery.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Architecture should match complexity and control to the task; the scenario’s side-effect and recovery conditions govern selection.
details.scenarioApplication: Present the ambiguous-tail benefit, duplicate-effect evidence, idempotency/reconciliation controls, and a safe boundary until recovery is demonstrated.
details.transfer: Communicate capability together with failure behavior, recovery, and the condition for enabling side effects.

messages.text: Flexibility on ambiguous requests does not address the observed duplicate side effect or establish safe recovery.
Timeout recovery determines whether a consequential action repeats; omitting it leaves a material architecture behavior unspecified.
A prompt instruction cannot guarantee a side effect executes only once.

feedback.reason: The architectural tradeoff includes the observed duplicate side effect, which cannot be dismissed as a prompt-level detail.

options.text: Control duplicate effects and recovery before enabling side-effecting execution.
Select the agent because flexibility is the primary value of an agent architecture.
Select the workflow and omit the timeout cases because they are integration details.
Add a prompt instruction not to repeat actions and treat that as sufficient recovery control.

questions.prompt: A proposed agent can recover from ambiguous requests but sometimes repeats a side effect after a timeout. The workflow alternative is less flexible but exposes an idempotency key and clear operator recovery. What should the architecture recommendation emphasize?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the risk owner approves the exact production scope, update the recommendation with that evidence and expiry conditions.
details.errorCorrection: Quality scores, redaction claims, or deleting the case do not grant a production permission.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Architecture communication should state evidence, assumptions, boundaries and the decision owner for unresolved risks.
details.scenarioApplication: Document the pilot scope, temporary access condition, authorized owner and a viable route that does not use the unapproved access.
details.transfer: Do not turn evidence from a temporary configuration into a broader approval.

messages.text: Removing a known use case hides the unresolved access dependency instead of communicating it.
Redaction is not the named risk owner’s access decision and may not satisfy the access boundary.
Quality evidence does not renew access authority or establish production permission.

feedback.reason: The pilot supports a quality claim under temporary access, not production authority. Keep the technical result and the unresolved approval separate in the recommendation.

options.text: Keep the route conditional on authorized access; report quality and a bounded alternative.
Remove the document class from evaluation so the recommendation can proceed on the common cases.
Ask the model to redact sensitive fields and treat that as approval to keep the agent route.
Recommend the route for all documents because the pilot established quality, and renew access during implementation.

questions.prompt: A routing pilot shows that an agent improves a rare document class. The pilot used a temporary data access exception that expires before production and the risk owner has not approved renewal. What should the architecture recommendation communicate?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the same approved data path later covers both regions, the routing decision can be revisited on that changed fact.
details.errorCorrection: One quality average or blanket design hides a meaningful workload and approval boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A useful architecture decision explains context, evidence, scope and the assumptions that change the selected path.
details.scenarioApplication: Separate consistent notes from conflicting notes, record each region’s allowed data path, and identify the owner who can approve a route.
details.transfer: Communicate the route together with the conditions that make it valid.

messages.text: This ignores the demonstrated conflicting-notes class without resolving its user outcome or permitted route.
A combined score hides which class and region each architecture can serve under the required approvals.
The agent’s data path changes across regions and can be a decision prerequisite, not a post-selection detail.

feedback.reason: The route choice depends on both task class and where its evidence may be processed. A clear recommendation states the measured route benefit and the regional approval condition.

options.text: Use the deterministic route everywhere because it has fewer operational dependencies.
Average the agent and deterministic quality results into one score and select the lower-cost option.
Choose the agent because it handles conflicts better, then treat regional approval as a deployment detail.
Record route evidence, regional boundaries, approval owner, and conditions for each path.

questions.prompt: A product owner asks for a single architecture recommendation covering a low-cost deterministic path and an agent path. The agent is useful only when notes conflict; the notes are currently available in two regions with different data-transfer approvals. What should the decision record do?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A timely owner review with current evidence may renew or replace the decision under the existing process.
details.errorCorrection: Quality stability, date editing, and operational responsibility do not silently renew the exception.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Temporary architecture decisions need explicit ownership and review triggers; the scenario’s expiration condition controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Retain the measured evidence, pause or use the previously approved bounded workflow, and request a documented decision from the named owner.
details.transfer: Treat expiry and renewal as substantive decision conditions.

messages.text: The exception’s time boundary was an approved condition; stable quality does not renew it.
Editing the date without an authorized review changes the record without resolving its condition.
Operating the pilot does not confer the named owner’s risk-acceptance authority.

feedback.reason: The decision record made the exception time-bounded and assigned renewal to an owner. Until that review occurs, the team should honor the existing boundary.

options.text: Continue autonomy because the quality score is unchanged and the expiry was only administrative.
Pause exceptional autonomy until its authorized owner reviews evidence and renewal.
Change the ADR date to the next quarter and complete the review later.
Ask the implementation team to accept the residual risk because they operate the pilot.

questions.prompt: An ADR approved a 60-day autonomy exception for a pilot. The exception has reached day 60; quality is stable, but the named owner has not reviewed new failure evidence or renewed the exception. What should the architect communicate?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the type is formally out of scope with an owned exclusion and safe manual path, the existing route can remain for its validated scope.
details.errorCorrection: Aggregate success cannot establish coverage of a known tail; an unmeasured global change or universal escalation may overcorrect.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Hybrid routing is an architecture choice only when the escalation signal captures the cases that require the stronger path.
details.scenarioApplication: Introduce a type-aware validated gate or direct route, then test false-clear and false-escalation rates, cost, latency and capacity.
details.transfer: Use failure evidence to change the route where the decision boundary actually breaks.

messages.text: The failing slice warrants a corrected route, but the evidence does not yet justify discarding measured cost/latency benefits for all traffic.
A global threshold may increase escalations without proving reliable detection for this document type or preserving the service budget.
The aggregate hides an in-scope slice that fails the escalation trigger and can be silently misrouted.

feedback.reason: The in-scope type bypasses the current trigger, so the routing boundary is invalid for that slice. Correct and validate the route while measuring the whole tradeoff.

options.text: Route the missed type using validated signals, then measure that slice.
Send every request to the capable model immediately to remove all routing complexity.
Lower the confidence threshold globally until the rare type escalates more often.
Keep the route because 95% of the measured requests meet the cost target.

questions.prompt: A team routes 95% of requests through a low-cost classifier and escalates ambiguous cases to a capable model. New acceptance testing finds that a rare document type is consistently classified as “clear” even when it is wrong, so it never reaches escalation; that type is explicitly in scope. What architecture change is justified?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a new independently validated signal separates the difficult slice and the budget owner requires a bounded hybrid, the split may become preferable again.
details.errorCorrection: A lower threshold cannot fix a non-discriminating score; a numerical majority does not erase known in-scope failures.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A hybrid route is justified only when its signal meaningfully separates cases needing the stronger path.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare false-clear results by document family, retire the ineffective gate for this approved scope, and test the resulting path for quality, latency and capacity.
details.transfer: Change the architecture when evidence invalidates the decision boundary, and retain the tradeoff evidence.

messages.text: The evaluation shows confidence does not identify the errors, so this gate repeats the failed signal.
The measured score does not separate errors, so changing its threshold does not repair the route’s inability to identify risky cases.
Each document family has an observed false-clear failure, and aggregate volume does not override the accepted risk and scope.

feedback.reason: The prior hybrid boundary depends on a discriminator that now fails across the in-scope families. With cost explicitly approved, use the path that can meet the requirement and validate its operating envelope.

options.text: Send only low-confidence cases to manual review and call the architecture unchanged.
Keep the hybrid router and lower its confidence threshold until more cases escalate.
Use the approved higher-quality path and verify quality, latency, and capacity.
Keep the cheap route for the 95% majority because the error count is still small in absolute terms.

questions.prompt: A hybrid design sends routine cases through a low-cost route and only ambiguous cases to a more capable model. A new evaluation table shows that every in-scope document family has a material false-clear rate, the confidence score does not separate errors, and the budget owner has approved the cost of one consistent higher-quality path. What architecture choice follows?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a representative handwritten evaluation validated the score and route, the existing architecture might remain appropriate.
details.errorCorrection: A slice-specific boundary can preserve a validated routine route while gathering the missing evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A route is justified by evidence on the inputs it receives and the approved operating envelope.
details.scenarioApplication: Handwritten cases are in scope and the score is confidently wrong on them.
details.transfer: State unvalidated slices and route-specific cost/quality trade-offs explicitly.

messages.text: The evidence supports the high-cost path only for scanned forms; using it universally assumes unmeasured cost and capacity.
A global threshold can alter well-measured traffic without proving it separates handwritten-form errors.
A small in-scope slice can carry material risk; aggregate budget and accuracy do not establish that it is safe.

feedback.reason: The router is unvalidated on an in-scope input class, so bound that class and measure its route before broadening or changing the global threshold.

options.text: Send every claim through the high-cost route because its scanned-form evaluation is stronger.
Lower the shared confidence threshold until more handwritten forms are escalated, then leave the route unchanged.
Constrain or separately route handwritten forms using validated evidence, and compare their quality, cost, and latency with the approved path.
Keep the current route because handwritten forms are a small share of total claims and aggregate cost remains within budget.

questions.prompt: A low-cost route handles routine claims. The high-cost route is approved for disputed evidence, but routing depends on a confidence score that is calibrated only on scanned forms; handwritten forms are in scope and produce confident wrong clearances. What recommendation best addresses the trade-off?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If every task slice met quality and the approved budget allowed the larger path, a simpler uniform route could be justified.
details.errorCorrection: Use per-route and per-slice evidence to choose a feasible boundary under the fixed budget, including misses that do not escalate.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Use per-route and per-slice evidence to choose a feasible boundary under the fixed budget, including misses that do not escalate.
details.scenarioApplication: The confidence threshold catches many errors but also routes easy work, creating a quality-cost constraint.
details.transfer: Compare paths on the evidence, quality, budget, latency, authority, and recovery actually in scope.

messages.text: A threshold that meets budget may still leave costly false-clear errors and hides the quality boundary.
A stronger average score does not establish that universal use fits the fixed budget or latency.
An unfunded overrun is not an accepted architecture trade-off.

feedback.reason: Use per-route and per-slice evidence to choose a feasible boundary under the fixed budget, including misses that do not escalate.

options.text: Raise the threshold until routing volume fits the budget, then report aggregate accuracy.
Send all requests to the larger model because it scored better on the evaluation set.
Compare route quality and cost across thresholds, including false-clear misses at the budget cap.
Keep the current threshold and ask the larger-model team to absorb any spend above the ceiling.

questions.prompt: A proposed architecture sends 70% of requests to a fast model and reserves the larger model for cases above a confidence threshold. Evaluation shows the low-confidence set contains most errors, but the threshold also routes a large share of easy cases. The budget ceiling is fixed. What should the trade-off brief compare?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the security owner had approved the risk or the input boundary excluded links by enforced design, the launch condition could change.
details.errorCorrection: Communicate the passed measures and unresolved risk decision separately, with the owner who can accept or constrain it.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Communicate the passed measures and unresolved risk decision separately, with the owner who can accept or constrain it.
details.scenarioApplication: Embedded links remain in scope but were not covered by the security test; the budget sponsor does not own that decision.
details.transfer: Compare paths on the evidence, quality, budget, latency, authority, and recovery actually in scope.

messages.text: Performance evidence does not answer whether untested links create an accepted security risk.
Budget ownership does not establish security decision authority.
Removing a test input does not remove that input from the in-scope documents or prove the residual path safe.

feedback.reason: Communicate the passed measures and unresolved risk decision separately, with the owner who can accept or constrain it.

options.text: Declare the architecture ready because measurable cost and latency targets passed.
Keep performance evidence separate from the open security gate and its authorized owner.
Ask the sponsor to accept the security risk because they own the product budget.
Remove embedded links from evaluation and launch the route for the remaining document fields.

questions.prompt: A sponsor accepts the measured latency and cost of a document route. Security testing has not covered the document’s embedded links, and the security owner has not accepted the residual risk. The launch board says “all performance targets green.” What belongs in the trade-off communication?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: After the authorized scope is granted and the exception is evaluated, the second route can be considered for rollout.
details.errorCorrection: Preserve the validated low-risk path while expressing the high-impact route as a concrete approval and evidence dependency.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Preserve the validated low-risk path while expressing the high-impact route as a concrete approval and evidence dependency.
details.scenarioApplication: The agent’s scope is proposed but not approved; the deterministic path already meets its bounded summary task.
details.transfer: Compare paths on the evidence, quality, budget, latency, authority, and recovery actually in scope.

messages.text: A design document does not grant deployed tool scope or show an approval occurred.
A universal agent route adds unvalidated authority and discards the proven deterministic path.
Removing an in-scope high-impact exception hides a consequential requirement rather than meeting it.

feedback.reason: Preserve the validated low-risk path while expressing the high-impact route as a concrete approval and evidence dependency.

options.text: Keep validated summaries deterministic; gate the high-impact route on approved scope.
Launch both routes because the agent’s proposed scope is already included in its design document.
Use the agent for every case to avoid maintaining two workflows.
Drop the high-impact exception from measurement so the schedule and quality target remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: For low-impact summaries, a deterministic workflow meets the quality target. A high-impact exception needs a flexible agent, but its reviewer-approved tool scope has not yet been granted. The schedule is fixed. Which recommendation best communicates the trade-off?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If reviewer capacity were provisioned to the measured peak or an approved bounded backlog policy existed, the trade-off could differ.
details.errorCorrection: Average spend does not establish acceptable queue delay during peak periods; route behavior must satisfy time-varying capacity and quality constraints.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Average spend does not establish acceptable queue delay during peak periods; route behavior must satisfy time-varying capacity and quality constraints.
details.scenarioApplication: The same policy fits annual cost but exhausts reviewers at peak hours.
details.transfer: Compare the available paths using the actual hard constraints, failure modes, and accountable owners.

messages.text: Aggregate annual cost hides the peak-period capacity failure.
A threshold should not be changed without checking how its false-clear errors shift.
Unbounded model routing may violate latency and budget constraints and does not guarantee quality.

feedback.reason: Average spend does not establish acceptable queue delay during peak periods; route behavior must satisfy time-varying capacity and quality constraints.

options.text: Keep the same threshold because the annual average cost is within budget and errors are mostly caught.
Raise the threshold until the average reviewer count falls below capacity.
Route every uncertain form to the largest model regardless of latency to avoid human review.
Compare peak queue delay and quality under thresholds, with a safe degraded path.

questions.prompt: A route sends uncertain forms to a human queue. An evaluation shows the threshold catches most errors, but peak-hour cases already consume all reviewer capacity; outside peak hours, the queue has headroom. The annual average cost fits the approved budget. What should the architecture brief compare?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the task were limited to drafts and the agent had no path to persist the recommendation, the validated draft route could be used under that scope.
details.errorCorrection: The preferred path changes persistent records, but its authority and recovery behavior are not yet validated.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The preferred path changes persistent records, but its authority and recovery behavior are not yet validated.
details.scenarioApplication: The write-capable agent reduces handoffs while both permission review and rollback testing remain open.
details.transfer: Compare the available paths using the actual hard constraints, failure modes, and accountable owners.

messages.text: A convenience benefit does not resolve unapproved access or untested recovery.
Temporary write permission still exposes production state without approval or rollback evidence.
Recovery is part of the architecture trade-off for a write path.

feedback.reason: The preferred path changes persistent records, but its authority and recovery behavior are not yet validated.

options.text: Keep the validated draft path; gate record edits on approved scope and tested recovery.
Launch both paths because fewer handoffs outweigh an unfinished permission review.
Give the agent temporary write access and remove it after the first successful week.
Compare only the number of handoffs and leave rollback design to operations after launch.

questions.prompt: An architecture comparison shows one agent path can edit records and another can only draft suggestions. The trusted pre-change checkpoint can be restored.
No dependent work has been built on the unaccepted patch.
Team recovery policy requires restoring the trusted checkpoint after an independent scope violation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the diff stayed within authorized scope and only the invoice fixture failed, a bounded in-place repair with independent rerun could be appropriate; a scope violation changes the recovery boundary.
details.errorCorrection: An in-place bounded fix can be valid after a functional failure when scope remains authorized; here the independent scope violation makes continuing from the diff unsafe, and a smoke run cannot replace the contract check.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done. The scenario requires checkpoint restoration because the independent review found an unauthorized scope change.
details.scenarioApplication: Restore or quarantine the failed diff to the trusted checkpoint, preserve the failed fixture and scope finding, revise the plan against them, and rerun independent checks before another patch.
details.transfer: Distinguish a repairable in-scope functional failure from an unauthorized diff: restore a trusted checkpoint for the latter, and preserve independent evidence in both cases.

messages.text: A bounded in-place fix could be appropriate for an in-scope fixture failure, but the explicit unauthorized scope change makes this diff an untrusted repair base.
A waiver leaves the failed invoice contract unresolved and builds dependent work on a state the independent review did not accept.
A smoke suite may add evidence but cannot turn the failed independent fixture into a passing contract or establish the correct scope.

feedback.reason: The independent scope violation makes the current diff an untrusted continuation point; restoring or quarantining it preserves a trusted baseline, while a failed test alone could support a bounded in-place repair.

options.text: Apply a bounded invoice-only fix in the existing diff and rerun that fixture, since no other behavior changed.
Restore the trusted checkpoint or quarantine the failed diff, preserve evidence, revise the plan, and rerun independent checks before applying another patch.
Keep the patch in place, add a waiver for the invoice fixture, and let owner acceptance follow after dependent work is built.
Retain the diff, rerun a broader smoke suite, and use the resulting green run as the next baseline without resolving the contract failure.

questions.prompt: An AI-assisted patch was applied from a trusted clean checkpoint, but an independent contract test fails on an invoice total and a fresh review confirms that the diff includes an unauthorized file or scope change. The team can restore the trusted checkpoint and retain the failed evidence. What is the next action?

constraints: The changes are independent.
Separate branches are available.
Each result must be tested before merge.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If one change depended on the other, coordinate a sequence or shared handoff instead of treating the work as independent parallel edits; keep any shared service or secret isolation as a separate environment control.
details.errorCorrection: A shared checkout or worktree lets nearby edits and repository test state mix before attribution is established; commit tags alone do not provide separate working directories, and worktrees do not isolate external dependencies.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents worktrees as separate working directories and branches for parallel sessions, and says a fresh worktree may require its own dependency and environment setup. Worktrees do not automatically isolate shared services, ports, or secrets; separate review and merge are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Create a worktree and branch for each independent change, provision its documented environment, run its tests there, and merge only results that have been reviewed.
details.transfer: Use separate worktrees for independent parallel changes, provision each environment, and merge only independently tested and reviewed results.

messages.text: Alternating branches in one checkout still shares checkout files and repository state, so the two test results are not attributable to separate starting states.
A combined diff loses ownership and can hide which change caused a failed test before either result is reviewed.
Commit tags provide history but do not isolate working files or repository setup state while both engineers edit.

feedback.reason: Independent simultaneous edits need separate working directories and branches so checkout files and branch history from one change cannot silently become the other's starting state; external services remain a separate environment concern.

options.text: Use one checkout, alternate branches, and run each test after the other engineer commits before starting the next edit.
Create a worktree and branch per change, set up each environment, run isolated checks, and merge only reviewed results.
Let both engineers edit the shared checkout, then compare the combined diff and test output before choosing a branch.
Share one worktree but tag each commit, assuming nearby files make isolation unnecessary.

questions.prompt: Two engineers need to make independent changes to the same repository at the same time. Their edits touch nearby files, and each change needs its own tests before the results are merged. Which setup fits?

constraints: The worktree setup instructions and dependency manifests are available.
The failure occurs before patch evaluation.
The main checkout can remain a comparison.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If setup were verified and the same test failed after patch execution, investigate the patch against its independent contract instead of repeating environment provisioning.
details.errorCorrection: Changing the model or prompt confuses an environment failure with patch behavior, while copying unreviewed state or testing only in main hides the worktree contract.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents worktrees as separate working directories and branches for parallel sessions, and says a fresh worktree may require its own dependency and environment setup. The order of setup and patch evaluation is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Provision the documented dependencies and environment in the worktree, verify the checkout-specific setup, rerun the same tests, and keep main as a comparison.
details.transfer: Diagnose a fresh-worktree failure as an environment-readiness issue until its dependencies and settings are provisioned and verified.

messages.text: The worktree has not reached patch evaluation, so changing generation variables does not test the actual failure cause.
Unreviewed environment copying can import hidden state and make the new checkout appear valid without proving its documented setup.
Testing only in main cannot establish that the requested branch and its own worktree environment are runnable.

feedback.reason: The command failed before the patch was evaluated, and a fresh worktree has its own setup requirements; repair and verify that environment before attributing the result to the patch or generation variables.

options.text: Change the prompt or model after the worktree command fails, treating the main checkout’s passing tests as evidence against the patch.
Provision the documented worktree dependencies and environment, verify setup, rerun the same tests, and retain main as a comparison.
Copy main’s untracked environment files into the worktree without review, then accept the patch if the command completes.
Abandon the worktree and test only in main, where the dependency directory and environment are already present.

questions.prompt: A fresh worktree checks out the requested branch, but its dependency directory and local environment are absent; the same tests pass in the main checkout. The patch itself has not been evaluated yet. What should happen first?

constraints: The declared scope and independent checks are recorded.
Fresh review found no unmet criterion.
The owner acceptance and next merge or rollout step are documented.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a criterion, independent fixture, scope check, or owner acceptance were missing, block the phase and obtain the missing evidence before accepting.
details.errorCorrection: Open-ended review has no defined stopping condition once the declared criteria pass, while merging without the recorded owner decision loses the lifecycle evidence that supports acceptance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends a fresh-context review of the diff and explicit criteria before counting unattended work as done. The acceptance and stop decision follows the scenario’s complete evidence and owner checkpoint.
details.scenarioApplication: Accept the scoped patch, record the evidence and owner decision, and move to the agreed merge or rollout; reopen only when new evidence or a scope change creates a new decision.
details.transfer: Stop at a defined acceptance boundary when independent evidence and ownership converge; reopen only for a changed risk, requirement, or scope.

messages.text: Additional review without a new risk or unmet criterion replaces the defined acceptance boundary with an unbounded search.
Expanding scope introduces a new change to review and defeats the declared narrow patch instead of closing its acceptance decision.
Passing fixtures do not replace the required recorded owner acceptance and lifecycle evidence.

feedback.reason: The declared scope, independent checks, fresh review, and owner acceptance converge on the acceptance boundary; more review without a new risk or changed requirement adds delay rather than evidence.

options.text: Accept the scoped patch, record evidence and owner decision, and proceed to the agreed merge or rollout; reopen if scope or evidence changes.
Request additional model reviews and broader tests until every hypothetical risk has been discussed, despite all declared criteria passing.
Expand the patch scope before merge so a larger review can search for risks outside the declared acceptance criteria.
Merge without recording owner acceptance because passing independent fixtures make lifecycle evidence self-authenticating.

questions.prompt: A narrowly scoped patch passes the independent contract fixtures, the diff contains only declared files, a fresh-context review finds no unmet criterion, and the owner has accepted the recorded evidence. What is the lifecycle decision?

constraints: The change touches session creation, middleware, and logout.
The developer can review a plan before implementation.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A small change in a well-understood module may need less planning. The unfamiliar cross-module security flow warrants an explicit exploration step.
details.errorCorrection: Branches, isolated tests, and specification review are useful controls, but do not replace learning the actual integration contract before choosing an implementation.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends separating research and planning from implementation and using explicit verification checks after code changes.
details.scenarioApplication: Inspect the session utilities and relevant tests, identify affected modules and security cases, review the plan, and give Claude executable checks to run after the scoped implementation.
details.transfer: In unfamiliar code, establish repository fit before implementation and define observable checks that can challenge the resulting change.

messages.text: Isolation makes changes reversible, but learning conventions only from failing tests can miss untested session and security contracts.
An isolated module can pass its own tests while introducing a competing session architecture that does not fit existing callers.
Reviewing the feature specification without inspecting the repository leaves its current session contracts unknown until after implementation.

feedback.reason: The missing information is the existing repository contract. Exploration before planning and editing prevents a plausible standard implementation from taking the wrong architectural path.

options.text: Create an isolated branch, implement a standard authentication pattern, and use the existing tests to identify differences from the repository’s conventions.
Inspect the repository’s authentication paths, agree on a scoped plan and security checks, then implement and verify the change.
Build the new authentication module in isolation from the existing session utilities, then integrate once its own contract tests pass.
Ask a fresh reviewer to assess the feature specification, implement that reviewed specification, and compare the resulting diff with the current utilities.

questions.prompt: A developer asks Claude Code to add authentication across several modules in an unfamiliar repository. Existing session utilities and security tests are available, but their contracts have not yet been inspected. Which workflow provides the best starting point?

constraints: No interactive discussion is needed for routine repositories.
Failures must be isolated and assigned for review.
Automation can parse structured command output.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Noninteractive execution needs orchestration and result handling. Ambiguous repositories should leave the routine path and receive focused review.
details.errorCorrection: A shared interactive history mixes state, disposable branches do not bound tool authority, and a model’s success summary is not test evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends claude -p for CI and scripts, structured output for programmatic processing, and restricted tools when running unattended.
details.scenarioApplication: Refine the prompt during the pilot, invoke each repository independently with the permitted tools and structured output, run its checks, and retain explicit failed outcomes for the owner.
details.transfer: Scale a repeatable AI-assisted workflow through constrained independent runs with per-unit evidence, not a single growing conversation.

messages.text: Checkpointed summaries help continuity, but one shared session still couples repository state and does not supply the requested independent structured execution records.
A disposable branch limits Git changes, not all tool effects; a central build can also omit repository-specific migration checks.
A confident final summary can be wrong. Skipping checks for apparently routine runs removes the evidence needed to classify success.

feedback.reason: The repeatable task fits noninteractive execution, but safe scaling depends on bounded tools, separate repository state, machine-readable results, and actual verification for each run.

options.text: Run one long-lived interactive session over repositories in sequence, checkpointing its summary after each repository to preserve migration context.
Launch unrestricted noninteractive runs in disposable branches, then use a central build result as the gate for merging the successful-looking changes.
Invoke a separate noninteractive run per repository and classify success from its final prose summary, with tests reserved for repositories that report uncertainty.
Use constrained claude -p runs per repository, collect structured output, execute each repository’s checks, and route failures for review.

questions.prompt: A platform team has a bounded dependency migration to apply to 60 repositories. The prompt, allowed files, and deterministic checks are defined, and unattended runs need repository-specific success or failure records. How should the team scale after a small pilot?

constraints: Provider request identifiers and classified error responses are available.
A bounded reproduction can run in safe mode.
Detailed diagnostics require controlled handling.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More detailed diagnostics may be justified for a specific unresolved incident, but should be collected deliberately in a controlled environment rather than by default.
details.errorCorrection: Prompt hashes do not replace provider request IDs; broad project differences confound isolation; routine full diagnostics collect more sensitive content than the runbook permits.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends safe mode to test plugins, MCP servers, and hooks, and warns that detailed diagnostics may contain conversation content or credentials.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the request identifier and error category for each incident, then use a bounded reproduction to compare customization states. Keep any detailed artifacts under the prescribed sensitive-data controls.
details.transfer: Separate the evidence needed for request correlation from the additional data needed for a bounded local reproduction.

messages.text: A content cluster may help grouping, but it cannot identify the exact provider request and can combine different executions of the same prompt.
Comparing a new minimal project with the full project changes more than the suspected customization, making attribution less reliable than a controlled mode comparison.
Restricted storage limits access but does not satisfy the requirement to avoid routine retention of sensitive prompt-bearing diagnostics.
Request IDs and bounded error metadata connect the failure to support evidence without storing prompt text by default.
Safe-mode comparison and selective re-enablement isolate the customization while retaining the managed-policy boundary.

feedback.reason: Request metadata supplies direct correlation without routine prompt storage. A controlled safe-mode comparison isolates customizations without treating organization policy as a debugging variable.

options.text: Cluster failures by a hash of the prompt and use that cluster identifier as the primary reference in provider support requests.
Retain request IDs, error classes, and bounded timing metadata; enable sensitive diagnostics only in a controlled reproduction.
Create a fresh project configuration containing just the suspected server, then infer the effect of that server by comparing it with the full production project.
Export full session diagnostics into the restricted support archive for every failure so later investigations always have a complete reconstruction.
Compare the reproduction in safe mode and normal mode, re-enable the suspected customization selectively, and preserve managed policy.

questions.prompt: A support runbook must correlate Claude API failures with provider investigations without storing sensitive prompt text. It must also isolate a suspected MCP customization while leaving organization policy intact. Select TWO suitable controls.

constraints: Work can be checkpointed before reducing context.
The same bounded workload can be repeated in normal and safe modes.
Detailed diagnostic artifacts may contain conversation content or credentials.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the controlled reproduction remained slow without customizations and with focused context, profiling in a protected environment would be a reasonable next diagnostic step.
details.errorCorrection: More resources can mask the symptom, profiling alone is less targeted than the available configuration contrast, and changing two variables together does not isolate causality.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends compacting, restarting, and using safe mode to isolate customizations, and warns that heap snapshots can contain conversations and credentials.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve the active work, establish a compact or fresh-session reproduction, compare safe mode with the same workload, and reintroduce plugins, servers, or hooks individually.
details.transfer: When a successful comparison changes several factors, hold the workload steady and reintroduce one factor at a time.

messages.text: A higher limit may reduce resource pressure but does not reveal whether accumulated context or a customization caused the regression.
Protected profiling is legitimate, but the observed safe-mode/fresh-session contrast offers a narrower first isolation test before interpreting a large mixed-state snapshot.
Removing a customization while also compacting context confounds the result; either change could account for the improvement.

feedback.reason: The working comparison changed both context and customizations. A controlled workload with staged context reduction and one-at-a-time re-enablement can distinguish those causes without conflating them.

options.text: Raise the process resource limit and compare completion time on the original session, using the faster result to decide whether customizations need changes.
Checkpoint and reduce context, repeat a fixed workload in safe mode, then re-enable customizations individually; handle detailed diagnostics as sensitive.
Profile the original long-running process first, collect a heap snapshot in restricted storage, and prioritize its largest allocations before testing configuration differences.
Disable the most recently installed customization and compact the session together, then attribute any improvement to that customization and deploy its removal.

questions.prompt: Claude Code consumes unusually high CPU in a large repository. A fresh session with customizations disabled behaves normally, while the affected session contains large build outputs. How should the operator isolate the cause?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a later response changes the spend-cap state or the organization raises the limit, retry can be considered under the new condition.
details.errorCorrection: Blind retries waste attempts on the spend cap, while treating both as permanent loses recoverable rate-limited work.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents retry-after behavior for rate limits and distinguishes spend-cap errors that do not recover through retries until access resumes.
details.scenarioApplication: Classify by the error body/type, honor retry-after for eligible rate limits, and send spend-cap failures to the budget owner with request evidence.
details.transfer: Choose recovery from the provider’s specific failure class and its changing preconditions.

messages.text: A spend cap will not clear merely because the client waits between identical retries.
More concurrency worsens rate pressure and does not change budget access.
A temporary rate limit is not equivalent to malformed or permanently rejected input.

feedback.reason: The response conditions differ: a rate limit may recover after the documented delay, while a spend cap requires the relevant limit or access state to change.

options.text: Treat both 429 responses as permanent invalid requests and stop all CI work.
Honor rate-limit recovery; route spend-cap errors to authorized budget or access action.
Retry both errors with the same exponential schedule until one succeeds.
Increase concurrency so rate-limited calls finish faster and use retries to test whether the spend cap clears.

questions.prompt: A CI request receives a 429 with `retry-after` during a short burst. The same organization also has a spend cap that has been reached. Which recovery decision fits these two conditions?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no HTTP response arrived, there is no provider request ID to propagate and transport diagnostics should be used first.
details.errorCorrection: Timestamp proximity does not uniquely identify a provider request; permanent full-text logging is broader than routine correlation requires.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic’s API errors include request IDs for correlation with application traces and support investigations; sensitive diagnostic retention should remain bounded.
details.scenarioApplication: Capture request ID, local operation ID, error class, and safe timing metadata, with restricted escalation for any additional authorized diagnostic sample.
details.transfer: Preserve correlation evidence at the request boundary while minimizing sensitive payload capture.

messages.text: Full prompt retention is not required for request correlation and increases exposure.
Several requests can share timestamps even at high precision.
A later success does not identify or explain the failed provider request.

feedback.reason: A request ID is the direct provider correlation handle; high-resolution timestamps can still collide and prompt retention creates unnecessary sensitive-data exposure.

options.text: Propagate the provider request ID with local correlation and safe error data.
Log every prompt and complete response permanently so support can search the text.
Increase timestamp precision and assume it uniquely identifies one request.
Retry the call and use the next successful response as the incident record.

questions.prompt: An HTTP error response includes a provider request ID, but the application logs only the user-facing error and timestamp. Support asks which request failed; several calls occurred within the same second. What logging change is most useful?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the provider returns an HTTP error with a request ID, preserve that ID alongside the local operation ID.
details.errorCorrection: A locally generated ID is not a provider ID, full payload logging is unnecessary, and a later retry is a distinct attempt.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Provider request IDs correlate responses; pre-response failures require application-side operation and transport diagnostics.
details.scenarioApplication: Capture a local correlation ID, connection stage, timing, and safe error classification with bounded retention.
details.transfer: Use identifiers from the layer that observed the failure and keep sensitive payload capture bounded.

messages.text: A locally generated value is not a provider-issued request ID and cannot be represented as equivalent.
Full prompt retention cannot reconstruct a provider ID for a request that received no response and adds sensitive data.
A successful retry has a separate request identity and cannot identify the earlier pre-response failure.

feedback.reason: A provider request ID is unavailable before a response; local transport evidence can correlate the failed attempt without pretending to have provider-side identity.

options.text: Record local operation and transport evidence; use provider IDs only when supplied.
Generate a provider request ID locally and tell support it is equivalent.
Log the full prompt and response indefinitely so the missing ID can be reconstructed.
Retry until a response succeeds and use that response ID for the earlier failed attempt.

questions.prompt: A request fails before any HTTP response arrives, so the application has no provider request ID. Support asks for a correlation path, but routine logs must not retain prompts. What should be captured?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the invalid-request payload changes after correction, the new attempt has a new request identity and should be logged separately.
details.errorCorrection: One universal retry loop wastes attempts on invalid input and can violate the supplied rate-limit timing.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The current API errors documentation distinguishes invalid requests from rate-limit responses and provides request IDs for responses.
details.scenarioApplication: Associate the ID with its exact attempt, correct the malformed input before retry, and use `retry-after` for the eligible rate-limit response.
details.transfer: Classify each failure by its own response and changed preconditions.

messages.text: The error classes have different preconditions: retry timing does not repair an invalid request.
This reverses the evidence: the invalid request needs correction, while the 429 supplies a retry condition.
Each HTTP response belongs to its own attempt; the earlier ID does not identify the later request.

feedback.reason: The returned status and metadata distinguish a deterministic request defect from a rate-limited attempt. Preserve each request ID, correct the former, and use the documented wait for the latter.

options.text: Apply the same retry schedule to both because both are unsuccessful requests.
Correct invalid input before retry and honor the eligible rate-limit delay.
Retry the 400 immediately and escalate the 429 to configuration support.
Use the request ID from the 400 to correlate the later 429 attempt as the same provider request.

questions.prompt: A request receives an HTTP 400 `invalid_request_error` with a provider request ID. The same job’s next attempt receives a 429 with `retry-after`. Which recovery plan matches the evidence?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If no HTTP response arrives, no provider request ID exists; use local transport-stage evidence for that attempt.
details.errorCorrection: Full payload logging is unnecessary for correlation, and replacing or reusing identifiers loses which layer observed each event.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic’s current API error documentation includes a unique request ID on responses and recommends sharing it for support investigations.
details.scenarioApplication: Propagate the provider ID into the local trace with the operation ID, error category and bounded timing data.
details.transfer: Preserve correlation handles from both the provider and application boundary.

messages.text: Keeping only the provider ID can break local operation tracing and loses the application-side correlation path.
The successful retry is a different attempt and its request ID does not identify the earlier server error.
Routine full-payload retention is broader than correlation requires and can expose sensitive content.

feedback.reason: The provider request ID supports provider-side investigation, while the local operation ID connects that response to the application trace. Keep both without turning routine diagnostics into permanent prompt storage.

options.text: Store provider and local IDs with safe error timing; govern payload capture separately.
Replace the local operation ID with the provider request ID so only one identifier is stored.
Retry the request and use the eventual successful response ID to represent the earlier 500.
Retain every prompt and response permanently so the request can be found by searching content.

questions.prompt: The API returns an HTTP 500 and request ID, but the application log records only a local operation ID. Support asks for the failing request. What should change in routine telemetry?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If a spend limit is formally raised, a new attempt may proceed under that updated account state.
details.errorCorrection: A generic backoff or new key cannot resolve an account-level cap.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Operational recovery depends on the error class and supplied response metadata, not status code alone.
details.scenarioApplication: Classify each response, wait for the rate-limit retry window, and stop attempts while the spend-cap condition remains.
details.transfer: Use response evidence to choose whether waiting, correction, or owner action can restore service.

messages.text: The response class and retry metadata distinguish different recovery conditions.
Changing credentials does not authorize bypassing the account spend cap and may not change the account limit.
The second response is an account spend-cap condition, not a transient rate-limit wait; retrying cannot clear that state.

feedback.reason: The same status code represents two recovery classes here. Respect server timing for the rate limit; route the spend cap to an authorized account owner.

options.text: Ignore the response body and choose one fixed delay for every 429.
Create a new API key after the second response to bypass the spend limit.
Retry both responses using exponential backoff because the status code is the same.
Wait only on the rate limit; route spend-cap recovery to the authorized owner.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the connection later succeeds and returns an API response, add that attempt’s provider request ID to its own trace.
details.errorCorrection: Invented IDs, an HTTP-class label without a response, and secret-bearing dumps all misstate or over-collect evidence.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Correlation identifiers and failure classes belong to the boundary that generated them.
details.scenarioApplication: Keep the local operation ID with bounded DNS/transport metadata and avoid claiming provider receipt.
details.transfer: State the last proven stage and retain only the metadata needed to diagnose it.

messages.text: An HTTP 500 requires an HTTP response; this trace stopped before a connection and response.
Full payload and environment capture is broader than needed and may disclose secrets; safe transport metadata is sufficient for this stage.
No provider response supplied an ID, so inventing one would misrepresent the boundary evidence.

feedback.reason: The trace stopped before an HTTP response, so there is no provider status or request ID. Preserve local correlation and describe the actual transport stage.

options.text: Record local DNS failure and operation ID; do not invent a provider response ID.
Classify it as a provider HTTP 500 because the operation failed before completion.
Log the full prompt and all environment variables to reconstruct what DNS attempted.
Record a synthetic provider request ID so support can search for the failed call.

questions.prompt: A support trace has a local operation ID and a DNS-resolution failure before any HTTP connection. There is no response status or provider request ID. What is the accurate diagnostic record?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the provider had no status or idempotency contract, the retry policy would need a different bounded escalation path.
details.errorCorrection: The client’s new key causes observed duplicate charges.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A timeout after submission leaves completion unknown, not necessarily failed.
details.scenarioApplication: The provider exposes status lookup and a same-key idempotency contract.

options.text: Retry quickly with exponential backoff and a fresh key so the provider can distinguish attempts.
